ABH-01.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 sent, and nobody could say where it was. A corporate customer sent EUR 50,000 to a supplier. The money left the account. Three days later, nobody could say where it was. One thing to remember: A message sent is not a payment completed.

ABH-02.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 sent, the screening team still retyped it by hand. A corporate sends EUR 50,000 to a supplier. The payment carries full structured ISO 20022 data. Yet the screening team retypes the beneficiary name by hand. One thing to remember: Treat the message as the control point, not the envelope, and the automation follows.

ABH-03.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 20,000 SEPA payment came back, the team treated it as a reject. A SEPA payment of EUR 20,000 failed. The team raised it as a reject and asked the customer to resend it. The customer had already been debited, and the money came back twice. One thing to remember: The stage decides the path.

ABH-04.agenda: Work through this case: Card approved for GBP 850, merchant says not paid. A customer bought goods worth GBP 850 on a card. The terminal said approved. The merchant said the money never arrived. One thing to remember: Authorisation is permission. It is not money.

ABH-05.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 50,000 payment that passed every check and still failed. A EUR 50,000 supplier payment passes validation, screening and the rail check. It still fails at the beneficiary bank. Nobody can say which team owns the failure. One thing to remember: Learn the connections, not the components in isolation, and the domain starts to behave as one system.

ABH-06.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 stuck because the card team never met the rail team. A customer pays EUR 50,000 by card, the merchant is never credited, and the refund takes nine days. The card team says the authorisation was fine. The rail team says settlement was fine. One thing to remember: A professional who maps the joins will always outperform one who memorises the parts.

ABH-07.agenda: Work through this case: USD 25,000 in two days, and nobody could say what it cost. A business sends USD 25,000 to a supplier overseas. It arrives in two days, which looks fast. Then the supplier reports USD 24,100 received, and nobody can explain the missing USD 900. One thing to remember: Judge every cross-border design on all four together, never on one alone.

ABH-08.agenda: Work through this case: The USD 100,000 Letter of Credit with no paper, and no control. A USD 100,000 Letter of Credit goes fully digital. No paper changes hands, and the shipment is released. Then the bank discovers the documents were never properly checked. One thing to remember: Digitisation is a redesign of the control model, not a scan of the documents.

ABH-09.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 50,000 real-time payment the old system could not see. A bank launches real-time payments, API-first design and ISO 20022. A customer sends EUR 50,000 in seconds. The operations team cannot see it anywhere until the next morning. One thing to remember: The winners are the ones who can bridge the two.

ABH-10.agenda: Work through this case: Approved in one click, EUR 75,000 never reached the supplier. A maker raised a corporate payment of EUR 75,000 in one click. Workflow approved it. The supplier never received it. One thing to remember: Approval is not settlement.

ABH-11.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 300,000 corporate payment, stuck between channel and core banking. A corporate sends EUR 300,000 through its channel. The payment never reaches core banking. Nobody can say where it stopped. There are seven hand-offs, and no one owns the gaps between them. One thing to remember: That chain of hand-offs is what makes the flow controllable end to end.

ABH-12.agenda: Work through this case: VND 500,000,000 domestic payment, nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor clears it. A corporate in Vietnam sends VND 500,000,000 to a supplier. The payment sits, unmoving, for hours. The rail is fine. The beneficiary bank is fine. The payment never cleared the preprocessor. One thing to remember: Nothing reaches the rail until the preprocessor has cleared it.

ABH-13.agenda: Work through this case: VND 200,000,000 sent in Vietnam, supplier says it never arrived. A corporate sends VND 200,000,000 to a supplier in Vietnam. The channel says sent. The supplier says nothing arrived. The payment is somewhere in the middle, and reconciliation is the only proof of where. One thing to remember: Each stage has a job, and reconciliation at the end proves the money arrived where it should.

ABH-14.agenda: Work through this case: VND 800,000,000 payment, a duplicate slips past six checks. A corporate sends VND 800,000,000 in Vietnam. The same payment is sent twice by mistake. Six checks pass. The duplicate check is the one that matters. It catches it, minutes before the money moves twice. One thing to remember: Those checks are the reason a payment can be trusted to reach the right account.

ABH-15.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 400,000 cross-border payment, rejected three times, preprocessor was missing. A bank sends EUR 400,000 across borders. It is rejected three times. Each rejection names a different fault. There was no control tower watching the payment before it left. One thing to remember: A strong preprocessor is what makes straight-through processing possible.

ABH-16.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 250,000 payment fails, every layer says the fault is in another layer. A EUR 250,000 payment fails. The technical team blames the data. The data team blames the business rules. The business team blames compliance. Every layer is pointing at another layer. One thing to remember: Each layer catches a different kind of error, and the full lifecycle runs from initiation through to settlement and reconciliation.

ABH-17.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 600,000 payment enters GPP, vanishes before the rail. A EUR 600,000 payment enters the payment hub. It is parsed, validated, mapped and screened. Then it vanishes. The rail never sees it, and core banking never posts it. One thing to remember: Exceptions are handled at each stage.

ABH-18.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 600,000 GPP payment, the mapping that nobody tested. A EUR 600,000 payment goes through GPP. The ISO 20022 mapping was never tested with this message type. The payment fails at mapping, is routed wrong, and posts twice. Three failures, one untested stage. One thing to remember: Each of these is a place where a payment can fail or be delayed, and each needs its own design and test coverage.

ABH-19.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 180,000 corporate payment, the issue has no stage to belong to. A EUR 180,000 corporate payment fails. The support team cannot say where. They have no list of stages to place it against. The issue floats, unowned, for two days. One thing to remember: Knowing the nine steps lets a BA place any issue at the right stage.

ABH-20.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 500,000 on four rails, four views, one customer asking where it is. A bank runs EUR 500,000 a day across four rails. Domestic, cross-border, real-time and high-value each have their own view. A customer asks where a payment is. Four teams give four answers. One thing to remember: One platform means one set of controls and one view of the payment, whatever the rail.

ABH-21.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 750,000 cross-border payment, the weakest hand-off breaks it. A EUR 750,000 cross-border payment crosses seven hand-offs. Six are strong. One is weak. The payment fails at the weak one. The integration was judged by its best hand-off. One thing to remember: Each stage is a hand-off, and the integration is only as strong as the weakest hand-off.

ABH-22.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 900,000 payment works, the lending product beside it breaks. A BA fixes a EUR 900,000 payment flow. The payment works. A lending product that shares the same platform breaks the same week. The BA never looked beyond payments. One thing to remember: Its products cover more of the bank than payments, so a BA must understand the wider platform, not only the payment flow.

ABH-23.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,200,000 a day, channels connected, hub never reached. A bank connects its channels and systems to the payment hub. EUR 1,200,000 a day should flow end to end. It does not. The plumbing was connected, but the nine-step journey was never tested through it. One thing to remember: The integration is the plumbing that makes the nine-step journey possible.

ABH-24.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 paid twice, the retry had no idempotency key. A customer retries a EUR 50,000 payment after a timeout. The retry succeeds. So does the first attempt, a second later. EUR 100,000 leaves the account for a EUR 50,000 payment. One thing to remember: Idempotency matters because a retried call must never create a duplicate payment.

ABH-25.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 API change, the endpoint looked simple, the blast radius was not. A team changes an API endpoint for a EUR 200,000 payment flow. The endpoint looks simple, one field added. Three downstream systems break. Nobody mapped the consumers. One thing to remember: A BA must understand the data, the consumers, the dependencies and the impact of a change.

ABH-26.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 350,000 requirement written without API knowledge, misses the payload gap. A BA writes a requirement for a EUR 350,000 payment flow. The requirement looks complete. Development finds a payload gap on day one. The BA could not see it, because the API was never understood. One thing to remember: Without API knowledge, the BA cannot write a complete requirement or assess the impact of a change.

ABH-27.agenda: Work through this case: An AI agent paid a EUR 12,000 vendor invoice, and no human had authorised it. A vendor invoice for EUR 12,000 was paid on a Tuesday morning. One thing to remember: An agent that authorises itself is not controlled, it is unsupervised.

ABH-28.agenda: Work through this case: An AI agent spent EUR 8,000 on API calls in one weekend, a few cents at a time. An AI agent paid for API calls with stablecoins all weekend. One thing to remember: A thousand tiny payments is still EUR 8,000.

ABH-29.agenda: Work through this case: An AI assistant drafted a BRD in minutes, and the EUR 100,000 settlement leg was missing. A bank asked an AI assistant built for banking to draft a business requirements document for a new payment flow. One thing to remember: Fast drafting is not complete requirements.

ABH-30.agenda: Work through this case: A BRD promised in ten minutes took three days to fix, and the payment was late. A banking chatbot and BRD tool promised the same document in ten minutes instead of three days. One thing to remember: Ten minutes to draft, three days to fix, is not ten minutes.

ABH-31.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 500,000 payment routed wrong after the person who knew the nostro was replaced. A bank replaced its most experienced payments analyst with an AI execution tool. One thing to remember: You can replace a person, not their context.

ABH-32.agenda: Work through this case: A payments team was cut before a migration, and a EUR 300,000 payment stalled with no one left who knew the old flow. A bank cut its payments operations team ahead of a major migration, to save headcount. One thing to remember: Cutting the team did not cut the work.

ABH-33.agenda: Work through this case: A visa programme was suspended overnight, and a payments project lost its team. A payments migration project depended on a team of specialists working abroad on a sponsored visa route. One thing to remember: A policy change is a project risk.

ABH-34.agenda: Work through this case: A programme was suspended, and the whole team assumed their visas were cancelled too. A sponsored visa programme was suspended for major employers. One thing to remember: Panic cost more staff than the policy did.

ABH-35.agenda: Work through this case: A new BA owned onboarding, fees, limits and payments, and a EUR 120,000 payment had no owner. A new corporate banking BA joined a team covering onboarding, entitlements, fees, limits and payments. One thing to remember: A scope list is not an owner.

ABH-36.agenda: Work through this case: A hiring manager received a CV full of regions and roles, and no evidence of a single payment delivered. A payments professional applied for product and senior BA roles across the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Asia, Europe and APAC. One thing to remember: A map with no journey proves nothing.

ABH-37.agenda: Work through this case: A CV listed SEPA, ISO 20022 and SWIFT, and the interviewer still asked: show me one payment. A payments BA applied for Product Owner and Senior BA roles in banking and payments. One thing to remember: Skills name the tools. A journey shows the hands.

ABH-38.agenda: Work through this case: A bank bought payments consulting, and the EUR 200,000 flow still had no BRD. A bank hired payments consulting to cover functional advice, all payment types, BRD and FRD documents, AI use cases and product thinking. One thing to remember: Advice is not a document.

ABH-39.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 50,000 payment query could not reach support, because the booking channel was blocked by location. A customer needed help with a EUR 50,000 payment query. One thing to remember: One channel is no channel when it is blocked.

ABH-40.agenda: Work through this case: A bank expanded to six Asian markets on one payment assumption, and EUR 150,000 in payments stalled. A bank expanded its payments business across six Asian markets: Singapore, Malaysia, China, Vietnam, the Philippines and more. One thing to remember: Six markets, six rulebooks.

ABH-41.agenda: Work through this case: An award-winning AI pilot paid EUR 60,000 with no control owner, and no one noticed. A team won an award for exploring AI and turning ideas into impact. One thing to remember: An award is not a control.

ABH-42.agenda: Work through this case: An award was announced, and the EUR 40,000 payment flow behind it had never been tested. A team announced an award for exploring AI and turning ideas into impact. One thing to remember: An announcement is not a test.

ABH-43.agenda: Work through this case: An award was called a milestone, but the EUR 25,000 lesson behind it was never written down. A team received an award for exploring AI and turning ideas into impact. One thing to remember: A milestone is not a lesson learned.

ABH-44.agenda: Work through this case: A payments desk posting said only one group could apply, and a EUR 90,000 queue waited for staff who never came. A payments operations desk posted a vacancy that said only one group of candidates could apply. One thing to remember: Wording is a staffing decision.

ABH-45.agenda: Work through this case: A bank demanded joining in 30 days, and a EUR 400,000 migration waited six months for a BA. A bank needed a payments BA for a migration moving EUR 400,000 a day. One thing to remember: A 30-day demand with a 60-day notice gets no one.

ABH-46.agenda: Work through this case: Branches opened on Sundays, while EUR 80,000 in weekend payments failed in the app. A bank opened its branches on Sundays. One thing to remember: Branch hours cannot fix an app.

ABH-47.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 70,000 payment queue waited on a festival night, and the only analyst on shift was far from home. On a festival night, a payments operations analyst worked the night shift far from home. One thing to remember: One person on shift is not cover.

ABH-48.agenda: Work through this case: A status update said all green while EUR 110,000 in payments sat unreconciled. A payments team lead posted a polished update: the team was doing well, the work was on track. One thing to remember: A green update does not reconcile a ledger.

ABH-49.agenda: Work through this case: One payment switch kept working while everything around it failed, and EUR 200,000 kept moving. A disaster hit a region and payment systems failed across it. One thing to remember: Resilience is built, not lucky.

ABH-50.agenda: Work through this case: A payments post reached thousands, got the settlement rule wrong, and EUR 500,000 followed the wrong advice. A payments post with a large following explained a settlement rule. One thing to remember: Reach is not accuracy.

ADD-001.agenda: Work through this case: MT103 cleared, the cover held, GBP 40,000 stuck. GBP 40,000 left London for a supplier overseas. The customer was told the payment was sent. The supplier was never paid. One thing to remember: The MT103 is information. The cover is the money. Screening one does not clear the other.

ADD-002.agenda: Work through this case: First payment to a new bank, MT103 never left. EUR 25,000 was sent to a new beneficiary bank for the first time. The customer was told it was sent. Three days later, nothing had arrived. One thing to remember: An RMA is a precondition, not paperwork to finish later. No RMA, no message, no payment.

ADD-003.agenda: Work through this case: IBAN correct, no name, EUR 12,000 in suspense. EUR 12,000 was sent to pay a supplier invoice. The IBAN was correct. The money sat in suspense for a week. One thing to remember: Field 59 must name the person the money is for. An account number is not an identity.

ADD-004.agenda: Work through this case: Reference cut at 16 characters, invoice never matched. EUR 48,000 was paid against a supplier invoice. The supplier was credited in full. The supplier still chased the payment as unpaid. One thing to remember: Credited is not reconciled. A reference the receiver cannot read is a payment the supplier cannot find.

ADD-005.agenda: Work through this case: The intermediary quit the corridor, nobody told routing. EUR 60,000 was sent to a supplier through the usual corridor. The payment was rejected downstream. The intermediary named in the instruction had stopped serving that corridor months earlier. One thing to remember: Reference data without an owner decays. Every routing field needs a named owner and a validation rule.

ADD-006.agenda: Work through this case: Limit cut without warning, the queue filled fast. A correspondent cut its intraday credit limit without warning. The payment engine kept feeding the same corridor. By the afternoon, payments were queuing, then rejecting, and nobody could explain why. One thing to remember: Build routing rules for the bad day, not the quiet one. A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure.

ADD-007.agenda: Work through this case: Purpose code missing, EUR 90,000 held at the border. EUR 90,000 was sent to settle a trade. The purpose code field was left blank. The beneficiary bank held the payment for compliance, and the trade could not settle. One thing to remember: Optional at the front is not optional downstream. Name the system that needs the code, and validate early.

ADD-008.agenda: Work through this case: Charges claimed by MT191, nostro debited months later. A cover payment settled cleanly months ago. Then an MT191 arrived, claiming the intermediary charges. The nostro was debited, reconciliation broke, and nobody remembered the payment. One thing to remember: The cover is not the charges leg. Charges travel separately, by MT191, and can arrive months later.

ADD-009.agenda: Work through this case: CHAPS leg queued, the house completion missed its day. A cross-border payment needed sterling settlement in the UK. The sterling leg went by CHAPS, for a house purchase completion that day. The completion missed its day. One thing to remember: Same day is a promise with a cut-off and a balance behind it. Confirm liquidity before promising the day.

ADD-010.agenda: Work through this case: Salary file a day late, payday moved a day. The monthly salary file went to BACS a day late. Payday moved a day. No one could hurry it back. One thing to remember: BACS does not hurry. A BACS file is a three-day promise, submit it on day one or move payday.

ADD-011.agenda: Work through this case: Faster Payments at 2am, queued till morning. A supplier payment went out at 2am by Faster Payments. It was meant to arrive in seconds. It arrived in the morning. One thing to remember: Around the clock is the scheme. Liquidity is the bank. Check liquidity, not just the rail.

ADD-012.agenda: Work through this case: Mandate silent for 36 months, the collection bounced. A subscription collection was presented after three quiet years. It was returned. No message warned anyone it would happen. One thing to remember: A mandate lapses quietly. Nobody is told. Track its last use or lose the collection.

ADD-013.agenda: Work through this case: Amount changed, notice not updated, debtor disputed. A creditor changed the collection amount for the month. The pre-notification still showed the old amount. The debtor disputed the collection, and it was returned. One thing to remember: The notice is the agreement. When the amount changes, the notice changes first.

ADD-014.agenda: Work through this case: Warehoused Monday, listed Thursday, stopped Friday. A EUR 5 million payment was accepted on Monday for Friday execution. The customer was promised Friday. On Thursday, the beneficiary was added to a sanctions list. One thing to remember: Warehousing stores the promise, not the permission. Re-validate at execution.

ADD-015.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 instant, routed slow to TARGET2. A customer with a EUR 300,000 limit sent EUR 200,000 instantly. It did not arrive instantly. It travelled to TARGET2 instead, slower and costlier. One thing to remember: A rule built on a dead limit is a live defect. When a scheme limit dies, re-check every rule built on it.

ADD-016.agenda: Work through this case: OCT Inst in 60 seconds, the conversion took longer. A cross-border payment was promised in 60 seconds. The euro leg cleared on time. The beneficiary was paid late, and short of the expected amount. One thing to remember: Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are. Prove the conversion before promising 60 seconds.

ADD-017.agenda: Work through this case: FX traded after cut-off, value date slipped a day. A supplier payment was promised with value today. It arrived with value tomorrow. The supplier charged a late fee. One thing to remember: The cut-off decides the value date, not the instruction. Trade before the cut-off or re-promise the date.

ADD-018.agenda: Work through this case: Statement 14 never arrived, the missing credit hid. The MT940 statements arrived every day. The sequence ran 12, 13, 15. Inside the missing statement 14 sat a credit nobody noticed was gone for days. One thing to remember: A missing statement is found in the numbering, not in the money. Check field 28C first.

ADD-019.agenda: Work through this case: Evidence a day late, EUR 4,800 lost to chargeback. A cardholder disputed a EUR 4,800 transaction. The merchant had delivery proof. The proof arrived a day after the scheme deadline, and the merchant bore the loss. One thing to remember: Representment evidence has a deadline. Miss it and the evidence does not exist.

ADD-020.agenda: Work through this case: File retried after timeout, three on-us paid twice. A corporate submitted a pain.001 file with ten payments. The file timed out with no confirmation. The file was re-sent whole, and three payments were paid twice. One thing to remember: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure. Find the outcome first. Never retry a file blind.

INS-001.agenda: Work through this case: The Rs. 4,500 card payment that cleared but never settled. A customer pays Rs. 4,500 by card. One thing to remember: Know the stage, and you know who must act. Authorisation is not settlement.

INS-002.agenda: Work through this case: Same terminal, same Rs. 10,000, two different kinds of money. Two customers each pay Rs. 10,000 at the same terminal. One thing to remember: The terminal looks identical, but the account and settlement implications are entirely different.

INS-003.agenda: Work through this case: Balance was enough, and the Rs. 25,000 payment was still declined. A customer tries to pay Rs. 25,000 by card. One thing to remember: Sufficient funds alone never guarantee approval. The checks decide together.

INS-004.agenda: Work through this case: The settlement that looked fine, and the Rs. 18 lakh that did not reconcile. Card payments clear for the day, and customers see their payments succeed. One thing to remember: A settlement that does not reconcile means money is unaccounted for, even if the payment appeared to succeed.

INS-005.agenda: Work through this case: The Rs. 12,000 chargeback that changed hands three times. A cardholder disputes a Rs. 12,000 transaction. One thing to remember: The reason code is the case, not a label on it. It decides the evidence and who bears the loss.

INS-006.agenda: Work through this case: The app said a EUR 850 payment failed, but the account was debited anyway. A customer sent EUR 850 through a mobile app. One thing to remember: Do not retry until the true status is known, because a blind retry could create a duplicate payment of EUR 850.

INS-007.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 75,000 payment rule nobody could test. A business asks for a rule on EUR 75,000 payments. One thing to remember: Ambiguity handled early is cheap; ambiguity found in testing is expensive.

INS-008.agenda: Work through this case: The requirement that passed review and failed every test. A requirement for a EUR 60,000 payment flow passes review. One thing to remember: Without these four, a requirement cannot be verified and a dispute about whether it was delivered cannot be resolved.

INS-009.agenda: Work through this case: Two stakeholders, one EUR 200,000 decision, no record of why. Two stakeholders disagree over a EUR 200,000 payment flow decision. One thing to remember: Document the decision, who made it and why, because an undocumented compromise will be reopened the next time the same stakeholders meet.

INS-010.agenda: Work through this case: The mid-sprint change that broke the sprint goal. A change is requested mid-sprint on a EUR 100,000 payment feature. One thing to remember: Accepting a change without this assessment silently breaks the sprint goal and leaves the team accountable for a target it never agreed to.

INS-011.agenda: Work through this case: Failed instant payments spike just after 09:00. Just after 09:00 the monitoring dashboard shows a sharp rise in failed instant payments. Customers report payments stuck in pending. The contact centre queue is growing, and nobody has declared an incident yet. One thing to remember: Establish the impact, the affected population, the containment, the ownership, the evidence and the update cadence, so the response is organised from the first minutes.

INS-012.agenda: Work through this case: The Rs. 50,000 payment failed, and three parties pointed at each other. A Rs. 50,000 card payment fails. One thing to remember: Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties.

INS-013.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 200,000 sprint that failed at review. A EUR 200,000 payments sprint reaches review. The increment fails its acceptance criteria. The analyst says the criteria were never clear. The team says the analyst was never there. One thing to remember: An analyst who only appears at review is too late to shape anything.

INS-014.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 300,000 BRD the developers could not build from. A EUR 300,000 payments change has a thick BRD. The developers say it tells them nothing they can build. The business says it already approved the requirements. One thing to remember: The right artefact is the one its reader can act on.

INS-015.agenda: Work through this case: The business asked in plain words, and the system was built in system words. A non-technical stakeholder describes a EUR 40,000 payment need in business language. One thing to remember: Confirm before you write, not after you build.

INS-016.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 100,000 refund story that hid the exception path. A team writes a user story for a EUR 100,000 refund. It says what the user wants and why. In testing, the refund fails on a duplicate payment, and nobody wrote down what should happen. One thing to remember: The wrong form hides the detail that matters.

INS-017.agenda: Work through this case: The missing rule found in UAT, and the EUR 60,000 fix that followed. A missing rule is found in UAT. One thing to remember: Fix the origin, not just the symptom.

INS-018.agenda: Work through this case: The process diagram that misled everyone who used it. A process diagram for a EUR 100,000 payment flow is drawn from assumptions. One thing to remember: A diagram is only as good as its validation.

INS-019.agenda: Work through this case: The requirements signed off in a day, and rebuilt over six weeks. Requirements for a EUR 80,000 payment change are signed off in a day. One thing to remember: Skipping validation does not save time; it moves the cost into development and testing, where fixes are far more expensive.

INS-020.agenda: Work through this case: The UAT that tested the system and missed the business. User acceptance testing is planned for a EUR 110,000 payment release. One thing to remember: Test cases built from this coverage test the business outcome rather than the system mechanics, which is what acceptance testing is for.

INS-021.agenda: Work through this case: The dashboard that said healthy while customers failed. A digital banking dashboard shows adoption climbing. One thing to remember: A KPI set that covers only one of these gives a misleading picture of health.

INS-022.agenda: Work through this case: Customers start onboarding, then vanish at document upload. A bank wants more new retail customers to complete digital onboarding, but only a small share of started applications reach an active account. Customers abandon the journey at document upload and at identity verification. Many who do finish are later held for manual review because documents are unclear or data does. One thing to remember: Map the friction, the document collection, the validation, the screening, the exception handling and the conversion measures, so the redesign targets the stages where customers actually drop off.

INS-023.agenda: Work through this case: The customers failing five times a day that nobody noticed. Customers are failing payments five times a day, every day. One thing to remember: A precise rule plus clean data is the whole method.

INS-024.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 100,000 transaction with no audit trail. A EUR 100,000 transaction is screened and cleared. One thing to remember: Evidence is the control. A control that cannot be evidenced is treated as if it did not happen.

INS-025.agenda: Work through this case: Fast, secure, easy: the gateway brief with no requirements. A retailer sells online and in store and wants a third-party payment gateway for card and instant payments at checkout. The requirements are three words: fast, secure and easy to integrate. Three words, and no one can build from them. One thing to remember: Define the API capabilities, the request and response contracts, the error handling, the security, the retries and the reconciliation, so the provider can be compared on evidence rather than on marketing.

INS-026.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 1 million release report that hid the open risks. A EUR 1 million payments release goes live. The first stakeholder report shows green across the board. A week later, adoption is 12 percent and three critical defects are open. One thing to remember: Reporting that hides the open items is worse than no report at all.

INS-027.agenda: Work through this case: The Rs. 30 lakh loan that stalled between approval and money. A customer is approved for a Rs. 30 lakh loan. One thing to remember: A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream.

INS-028.agenda: Work through this case: The Rs. 40 lakh payment sent on the wrong rail. A customer needs Rs. 40 lakh to reach a supplier today. One thing to remember: The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit.

INS-029.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 60,000 payment vanished between states, and no one could say which state it was in. A customer sent a EUR 60,000 payment. One thing to remember: The state where the evidence stops is where the payment is stuck.

INS-030.agenda: Work through this case: The retailer, the bank API and the missing outcome. A retailer wants its checkout connected directly to a bank's payment API, so orders can be paid without leaving the retailer's site. On a EUR 60,000 day of orders, the question is not how to call the API. It is how the retailer learns whether each payment actually completed. One thing to remember: Walk through the integration in layers and make each layer testable, starting with the contract, then the authentication, the asynchronous status path and the recovery procedures.

INS-031.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 2,500 card payment was declined at authorisation, and the team investigated settlement. A customer tried to pay EUR 2,500 by card. One thing to remember: The wrong stage means the wrong investigation.

INS-032.agenda: Work through this case: Gateway said success, EUR 40,000 never posted. A payment gateway returns success for a EUR 40,000 supplier payment. The channel shows the payment as accepted. Hours later the supplier has not been paid, and the finance team finds no debit in the core banking ledger. One thing to remember: Gateway success does not prove the ledger posted. Check the posting, never trust the channel message.

INS-033.agenda: Work through this case: 500 unmatched out of 20,000, and a INR 40 lakh figure that was not a loss. A bank processed 20,000 transactions in a day. The morning reconciliation showed 500 transactions unmatched between the ledger and the clearing reports. A report called it a INR 40 lakh loss before anyone had investigated a single item. One thing to remember: Unmatched is a question, not a loss.

INS-034.agenda: Work through this case: Approved for Rs. 15 lakh, and the money never arrived. A loan is approved for Rs. 15 lakh. One thing to remember: Check each stage in order rather than assuming the approval was the problem.

INS-035.agenda: Work through this case: App says EUR 4,120, the bank says EUR 3,850. A customer checks the mobile app and sees a balance of EUR 4,120. She calls the contact centre, and the agent's screen shows EUR 3,850. The difference is EUR 270, exactly the amount of a card payment she made that morning. One thing to remember: The EUR 270 difference is the pending card payment, so the two balances are both accurate for what they represent.

INS-036.agenda: Work through this case: Migration rehearsal: thousands of mismatches. A bank migrates from a legacy core system to a new platform. The first rehearsal shows thousands of mismatches: names that do not match, addresses that cannot be placed into the new structured format, dates in different formats, and payment records whose beneficiary details are incomplete. Thousands of customers, and. One thing to remember: A migration without proof at each stage is a hope, not a plan.

INS-037.agenda: Work through this case: The process change that arrived the day before UAT. A process change arrives the day before user acceptance testing on a EUR 180,000 payment release. One thing to remember: Never let a late change silently void completed testing.

INS-038.agenda: Work through this case: The scope that shrank one change at a time. Requirements for a EUR 150,000 payment project change every week. One thing to remember: Without this discipline, weekly changes silently erode the scope and the delivery date.

INS-039.agenda: Work through this case: Two weeks wanted, six estimated, and the EUR 150,000 decision in between. The business wants a EUR 150,000 payment feature in two weeks. One thing to remember: The decision is then about what to deliver and what to defer, not about whose estimate is right.

INS-040.agenda: Work through this case: SCT Inst has no maximum, 10 seconds, payee check mandatory. A bank must change its instant euro payments to match the current scheme rules. There is no longer a scheme-level maximum amount for SCT Inst, execution must complete within 10 seconds, and verification of payee is mandatory for instant euro payments. The change touches the mobile app, the payment engine, the. One thing to remember: Build the impact analysis as a map, not as a list of opinions: start from the change and walk upstream, then walk downstream.

INS-041.agenda: Work through this case: Built exactly to sign-off, and the user still said no. A feature is built exactly to signed-off requirements. One thing to remember: Each cause has a different owner and a different fix, so classifying it correctly is the first step.

INS-042.agenda: Work through this case: Make payments faster: the brief with no user, no baseline, no target. A bank wants to launch an instant payment product for small business customers. The sponsor has asked the team to make payments faster. The request has no named user group, no baseline, no target speed and no statement of the problem customers actually face today. Faster than what, for whom, and by when? Nobody can. One thing to remember: Define the hypotheses, the constraints, the minimum viable product and the success metrics, so discovery ends with a decision rather than with a longer list of ideas.

INS-043.agenda: Work through this case: The supplier file that passes through three screens and a phone call. A bank runs a legacy supplier payment process that has grown by accretion over a decade. A corporate customer sends a payment file, operations staff print exception lists, re-key corrected details into three different screens, phone the customer for missing information, and then release the file late in the day. One. One thing to remember: Design the target process, validate the controls and the operational impacts, and only then change the process.

INS-044.agenda: Work through this case: Build us the solution, said the board, and nobody asked what problem it solved. Senior management asks for a solution for a EUR 200,000 payment problem. One thing to remember: Reframe the ask before you build the answer.

INS-045.agenda: Work through this case: Complete, said the business. Incomplete, said the developers.. The business believes the requirements for a EUR 90,000 payment change are complete. One thing to remember: Close the interpretation gap before development, because it is far cheaper to agree on meaning now than to rebuild later.

INS-046.agenda: Work through this case: The new payment screen nobody used. A new digital payment screen is launched. One thing to remember: Diagnose resistance before you try to overcome it.

INS-047.agenda: Work through this case: The BA who could not prove the EUR 300,000 saving. A process change claims a EUR 300,000 saving. One thing to remember: Measured value is the analyst's evidence, not a claim.

INS-048.agenda: Work through this case: SIT passed clean. Production failed on day one.. A merchant payment API integration passes system integration testing cleanly, every test case returning the expected response. It fails in production on day one. The same calls, the same payloads, and a failure rate climbing by the hour. One thing to remember: The difference between test and production is usually in one of these, and comparing them in a fixed order finds it faster than guessing.

INS-049.agenda: Work through this case: One day to go-live, compliance finds a missing requirement. A bank is one day from deploying an upgrade to its instant euro payment service. UAT is signed off, regression evidence is filed, the deployment window is booked and the customer communications are ready. Late in the afternoon the compliance team raises a requirement nobody recorded: verification of payee is mandatory. One thing to remember: Triage defect versus new scope, quantify the risk and obtain a formal go or no-go decision, because a mandatory compliance obligation cannot be deferred the way new scope can.

INS-050.agenda: Work through this case: New channel live, customers charged twice. A new corporate payment channel goes live. Days later the operations team notices duplicate debits: several corporate customers charged twice for the same instruction, and a few suppliers paid twice. The release passed testing. The duplicates are real. One thing to remember: Establish the affected population using stable identifiers rather than guesswork, and separate confirmed duplicates from suspected ones before remediating.

INS-051.agenda: Work through this case: The behaviour changed in production, and nobody knew which layer broke it. A EUR 50,000 payment behaves differently in production than intended. One thing to remember: Fix at the layer that introduced the fault.

INS-052.agenda: Work through this case: The change that arrived when 70 percent of the sprint was done. A change is requested when 70 percent of the sprint is done. One thing to remember: A late change is a decision, not an instruction.

INS-053.agenda: Work through this case: Two senior stakeholders, opposite outcomes, one undocumented call. Two senior stakeholders want opposite outcomes on a EUR 250,000 payment decision. One thing to remember: A documented decision ends the debate; an undocumented one will be reopened every time the stakeholders meet.

INS-054.agenda: Work through this case: UAT morning one: most collections rejected. A bank is starting user acceptance testing for a new SEPA direct debit collection service. On the first morning the failure rate is critical: most test collections are rejected, mandate references cannot be found, and the test schedule shows collections submitted on the wrong day. The testers are ready. The. One thing to remember: Only then decide whether to continue, fix and restart, or stop, because continuing a test on a broken environment wastes the testers' time and produces evidence that cannot be trusted.

INS-055.agenda: Work through this case: A few customers, one wrong EMI. A bank receives complaints from a small group of loan customers that their monthly EMI is wrong. Most customers are unaffected, which makes the problem harder, not easier. A handful of complaints, and a calculation that is wrong for some loans and right for the rest. One thing to remember: The pattern only emerges when the cases are compared, because the affected loans share a characteristic, such as a particular rate change date, that the unaffected loans do not.

INS-056.agenda: Work through this case: The client said our new process broke their EUR 120,000 payroll run. A client's EUR 120,000 payroll run failed on the first day of the new process. Four hundred salaries were held. The client said the new process had damaged their operations. One thing to remember: Empathy first, evidence second, blame never.

INS-057.agenda: Work through this case: One payment, three different amounts. A cross-border payment complaint shows one amount in the online banking screen, a different amount transmitted by the API, and a third value held in the database. The beneficiary address looks complete on screen, but arrives truncated in the payment message. EUR 8,000 was sent. Nobody can agree what the payment. One thing to remember: Capture the value at each point to find where it changed, using one stable identifier at every layer.

INS-058.agenda: Work through this case: Two weeks to build a Payment API integration. A retailer needs a Payment API integration delivered in a two-week sprint. The checkout must submit payment instructions to the bank, receive a clear acceptance or rejection, and create the order only when the payment outcome is known. Two weeks, and the contract is still unwritten. One thing to remember: The contract definition matters most, so agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion.

INS-059.agenda: Work through this case: The API contract that forgot to say what success means. A bank is publishing a Payment API for corporate customers and retail partners. The first draft of the contract is a list of fields with no rules. It does not say which fields are required, what happens when a field is missing, which error code means what, whether a success response means the payment completed, or how. One thing to remember: Where a field is optional under the message schema but the bank's reporting or product needs it, say so in the contract and state the source the bank will use and the derivation rule.

INS-060.agenda: Work through this case: The defect debate that ran on opinion, not evidence. A system integration testing defect is raised on a EUR 70,000 payment flow. One thing to remember: This assessment keeps defect discussions focused on evidence rather than on opinion.

INS-061.agenda: Work through this case: Hypercare ended on a date, and the EUR 40,000 exceptions were still open. A payment release goes live, and hypercare runs for two weeks. One thing to remember: Hypercare ends when these measures are stable, not when a fixed number of days has passed.

INS-062.agenda: Work through this case: Paid and confirmed, but the shop never saw the order. A retailer runs a checkout where the payment gateway returns a success response. The customer sees a confirmation screen, and then nothing happens. The order system never receives the callback, so no order is created, no goods are picked, and the customer is charged for a purchase the retailer cannot see. One thing to remember: Trace one affected payment end to end using its correlation ID, from the gateway request and response through the payment service state, the event published to the bus, and the callback delivery.

INS-063.agenda: Work through this case: Five teams, one EUR 500,000 outage, five different stories. A EUR 500,000 payment run stopped mid-flight. Business, development, QA, gateway and support each opened their own ticket. Each team worked from a different picture of the same outage. One thing to remember: Without one incident view, teams duplicate effort and the incident lasts longer than it should.

INS-064.agenda: Work through this case: Rs 18,500 debited, the order never arrived. A customer pays Rs 18,500 for an order through a retailer's checkout. The bank account is debited, the payment gateway reports success, and the order remains pending. No confirmation, no dispatch, no delivery date. The money is gone and the goods never move. One thing to remember: Trace the four boundaries in order, the gateway, the bank, the merchant callback and the order creation, to find where the payment outcome was lost.

INS-065.agenda: Work through this case: 300 complaints in 20 minutes, one shape. On a weekday morning between 09:12 and 09:32, a contact centre receives more than 300 complaints with the same shape. Customers report a debit that does not match the payment status shown in the app, or a credit they expected that has not appeared. Three hundred voices, one pattern, and no incident bridge yet. One thing to remember: Containment owns the affected-transaction register, the decision on the next batch and any remediation, while the other workstreams proceed in parallel.

INS-066.agenda: Work through this case: Zero-fee weekend: volume hits 300 percent of peak. A bank launches a zero-fee weekend campaign for retail payments. Within the first hour payment volume rises to 300 percent of a normal peak, three times the usual load. Latency climbs, channel sessions start timing out, and the clearing connector queue grows faster than it drains. One thing to remember: At intake, apply back-pressure, queue or gracefully defer non-critical traffic, show a clear pending state instead of a silent timeout, and throttle campaign traffic to a rate the downstream chain can sustain.

INS-067.agenda: Work through this case: UPI, cards, net banking and wallets all failing on the same day. On the same day, UPI payments fail with timeouts, card payments fail at the gateway, net banking sessions drop before confirmation, and wallet payments fail after the wallet is debited. Four rails, four failure shapes, one very bad day. Is it one cause, or several? One thing to remember: Segmenting the incident this way shows whether there is one cause or several, which decides whether one fix or several are needed.

INS-068.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2 million in payments, and no one could prove where they were. Volumes tripled in an hour during a payment surge. EUR 2 million of payments were in flight. Timeouts rose, and no one could prove which payments had settled and which had not. One thing to remember: Without evidence, incident response is guesswork.

INS-069.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 20,000 payment that could be taken but never refunded. A customer pays EUR 20,000 through a new checkout. One thing to remember: Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete.

INS-070.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 15,000 failed, and the merchant blamed the wrong provider. A merchant's EUR 15,000 of card payments fail in one afternoon. The merchant blames the gateway. The gateway shows every instruction routed correctly. The processor had the outage. One thing to remember: Confusing the two roles means blaming the wrong party when a payment fails.

INS-071.agenda: Work through this case: Screen timed out, EUR 25,000 supplier payment in limbo. A corporate customer submits a EUR 25,000 supplier payment through the online channel. The screen spins, then times out. No confirmation appears and no reference is shown. The payment may have been accepted, executed, or never received. One thing to remember: A timeout is not a failure. It is an unknown, and a retry is safe only once the outcome is confirmed.

INS-072.agenda: Work through this case: The payment page customers kept abandoning. A merchant watches customers abandon the payment page every day. One thing to remember: Abandonment is several problems wearing one label.

INS-073.agenda: Work through this case: The loan approval that took two days, and nobody knew where the time went. Loan approval time rises from hours to days. One thing to remember: Measure the clock, not the opinion.

INS-074.agenda: Work through this case: Every test passed, and UAT still failed. All test cases pass. One thing to remember: A test suite that passes but does not represent the real business journeys gives false confidence and a failed acceptance.

INS-075.agenda: Work through this case: The same change, requested every sprint. The same change is requested every sprint. One thing to remember: Repeat requests are a symptom, not a backlog.

INS-076.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 400,000 upgrade deferred because it was sold as features. A team asks for EUR 400,000 to upgrade the payments platform. The business case lists features: new messages, new screens, new APIs. The steering committee defers it. Again. One thing to remember: A case argued on value gets decided; a case argued on features gets deferred.

INS-077.agenda: Work through this case: The rule the developers guessed, and the EUR 25,000 payment that proved them wrong. A rule for a EUR 25,000 payment is stated as a business sentence. One thing to remember: Precision at the boundary is what makes a rule buildable.

INS-078.agenda: Work through this case: The test that could not pass or fail. A test is written for a EUR 30,000 payment scenario. One thing to remember: Each scenario needs an expected result, because a test without an expected result cannot pass or fail.

INS-079.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 50,000 payments outage customers heard about from Twitter. A payments outage blocks EUR 50,000 of customer payments. Support has no status to give. Customers learn about the outage from social media before the bank tells them. One thing to remember: Reliable updates are part of the fix, not an extra.

INS-080.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 50,000 payment that was correct, and three seconds too slow. A EUR 50,000 payment is validated correctly and posted to the right ledger. The customer abandons it anyway. The payment took three seconds longer than the channel allows, and the session timed out. One thing to remember: Function without fitness for use is not a working payment.

INS-081.agenda: Work through this case: The change nobody could trace, and the release it broke. A change is made to a EUR 120,000 payment flow. One thing to remember: Without traceability, a team cannot prove that what was built is what was asked for, and cannot assess the impact of a change safely.

INS-082.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 500,000 release nobody validated in production. A EUR 500,000 payments change goes live on a Friday. By Monday, adoption is near zero and two defects are open. Nobody can say whether the change delivered what was promised. One thing to remember: A lifecycle without that closing loop leaves value unproven.

INS-083.agenda: Work through this case: The operations analyst whose EUR 30,000 salary pitch listed only a job title. An operations analyst applies for a business analyst role paying EUR 30,000 more. The CV lists the old job title and the old employer. The recruiter cannot see a single BA skill in it. One thing to remember: A mapped skill is a hiring argument; an unmapped job title is just a label.

INS-084.agenda: Work through this case: The interview answer listed tasks, but the EUR 1 million result was missing. A BA walked through a EUR 1 million payments project for ten minutes. The panel heard tasks, tools and meetings. They never heard what the project delivered. One thing to remember: Measurable results matter most, because they prove the work delivered value rather than simply occupying time.

INS-085.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 80,000 interview lost on one confident wrong answer. A candidate interviews for an EUR 80,000 payments BA role. One question is outside their knowledge. They answer confidently, and wrongly. The interview ends there. One thing to remember: Interviewers test judgement and honesty as much as knowledge, and a confident guess that turns out wrong is worse than a clear statement of what is known and what is not.

INS-086.agenda: Work through this case: GBP 4,500 failed three times, and the reason was wrong every time. A customer tried to pay GBP 4,500. It failed three times. Each time the screen said the same thing: declined. One thing to remember: A failure label is not a diagnosis.

INS-087.agenda: Work through this case: Supplier paid twice, EUR 12,000 doubled. A supplier payment appears twice on the account statement for the same amount, to the same supplier, on the same day. The supplier confirms receiving two credits. EUR 12,000 has left the account twice. One thing to remember: Comparing the two sets of evidence shows whether the duplicate came from a client retry, a gateway redelivery or a missing idempotency check.

INS-088.agenda: Work through this case: Refund or reversal: the Rs. 8,000 that was posted twice. A Rs. 8,000 payment should never have completed. One thing to remember: Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow. A refund creates a credit, a reversal unwinds the posting.

INS-089.agenda: Work through this case: HTTP 200, order unpaid, account debited. A fintech partner integrates with a bank's payment API to submit customer credit transfers for its merchants. In testing, the API returns a successful HTTP response, but the merchant's downstream order record is not created. In one case the payment is debited while the merchant dashboard still shows the order as. One thing to remember: A success response that promises completion when it only means receipt will mislead every caller.

INS-090.agenda: Work through this case: Tomorrow, the customer was told, and the money came in two days. A customer sends Rs. 2 lakh and is told the money will arrive tomorrow. One thing to remember: Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, not a generic T+1.

INS-091.agenda: Work through this case: Feature complete, and the business problem still standing. A feature for a EUR 130,000 payment flow is delivered complete, on time. One thing to remember: Measuring the outcome rather than the delivery reveals the gap.

INS-092.agenda: Work through this case: Loan approval: two hours became two days. Loan approval time grows from two hours to two days. One thing to remember: The fix depends on which of these is actually causing the delay, so measure before changing anything.

INS-093.agenda: Work through this case: The change request that came back, again and again. Stakeholders repeat the same change request, release after release. One thing to remember: Each cause has a different fix, and implementing the change again without fixing the cause will only repeat the cycle.

INS-094.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 supplier payment stalled, and no one owned the fix. A EUR 50,000 supplier payment sat unreleased for three days. Every team said it was someone else's job. The BA owned the outcome, but no team reported to the BA. One thing to remember: Authority is borrowed. Clarity is owned.

INS-095.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 250,000 scope dispute nobody wrote down. A EUR 250,000 payments project ends in a scope dispute. The vendor says the extra work was agreed in a meeting. The business says it never approved it. There is no record either way. One thing to remember: If it is not written down, it was not agreed.

INS-096.agenda: Work through this case: Six months learning tools, and still no interview for a payments BA role. A career changer spends six months learning BA tools. The profile lists every tool on the market. No recruiter calls for a payments BA role. One thing to remember: Tools are easy to learn; credibility in a domain is what gets the interview.

INS-097.agenda: Work through this case: Five certificates, but no proof of one real payment project. A BA showed five certificates for a EUR 250,000 payments migration. The panel asked for one artefact from the work. There was nothing to show. One thing to remember: Show the chain, not the certificate.

INS-098.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 60,000 BA role that never found a perfect candidate. A recruiter fills a EUR 60,000 business analyst role. The perfect candidate exists, with the exact domain and skills. The recruiter never finds them, because their profile uses none of the role's words. One thing to remember: Visibility gets the call; evidence wins it.

INS-099.agenda: Work through this case: The unfamiliar EUR 45,000 scenario that rewarded method, not memory. A candidate faces an unfamiliar EUR 45,000 payments scenario in an interview. They have never seen this flow before. They answer in a fixed order, and the panel hires them. One thing to remember: Method is what carries you when knowledge runs out.

INS-100.agenda: Work through this case: Seven questions in, the EUR 750,000 project walkthrough still had no shape. A BA started walking through a EUR 750,000 live payments project. Seven questions in, the panel still did not know the scope, the stakeholders or the outcome. The walkthrough had become a list of tasks. One thing to remember: A walkthrough without structure becomes a list of tasks.

INS-101.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 100,000 was due to settle. Both banks waited for the other to move it.. A EUR 100,000 credit transfer sits ready to settle. Each bank assumes the other will move the funds. The payment waits, and the beneficiary calls to ask where the money is. One thing to remember: INDA or INGA decides who moves the funds. Read it first.

INS-102.agenda: Work through this case: File accepted, EUR 120,000 supplier still unpaid. A company sends a supplier file for EUR 120,000. The bank replies: file accepted. Finance tells the supplier the money is on its way. Three days later the supplier says nothing arrived. One thing to remember: File accepted means receipt only. A payment is seven stages, and mistaking acceptance for settlement hides failures.

INS-103.agenda: Work through this case: The MT103 has no town name. pacs.008 demands one.. An MT103 arrives for a EUR 45,000 payment, and it must be translated into pacs.008. The MT103 carries no structured address. pacs.008 requires a town name and a country code, and the town cannot be invented. Guessing writes false data onto the payment. A blank fails validation. The payment is stuck between two message. One thing to remember: Handle the gap with explicit translation rules, enrichment from a trusted source, and exception governance for every field the old message cannot supply.

INS-104.agenda: Work through this case: Migration team changes the network, the messages stay broken. A bank starts an ISO 20022 migration for a EUR 50,000 payment flow. The team plans a network change. Months later the messages still fail validation. The network was never the problem. One thing to remember: SWIFT is the network. ISO 20022 is the standard. Changing one changes nothing about the other.

INS-105.agenda: Work through this case: A customer paid INR 50,000 by UPI in seconds. The banks settled hours later.. A customer pays INR 50,000 by UPI. The debit shows at once and the merchant confirms receipt in seconds. The payment then fails in reconciliation, and the team treats it as a customer failure. One thing to remember: Instant to the customer, settled later between banks.

INS-106.agenda: Work through this case: Collections moved to D-1 to be faster. EUR 90,000 of collections failed on day one.. A creditor moves direct debit submission forward to D-1. EUR 90,000 of collections go out on the new date. They fail at the first step, because the file cut-off and the scheme calendar were never checked. One thing to remember: D-1 is an operational commitment, not a diary change.

INS-107.agenda: Work through this case: The correspondent cut the limit without warning. A correspondent cuts an intraday credit limit without warning. The routing engine keeps feeding the same corridor, EUR 300,000 of payments queue up, and rejects arrive that nobody can explain. The corridor was fine yesterday. The limit changed, and the engine never noticed. One thing to remember: A routing decision nobody can reconstruct is a control failure, not a routing outcome.

INS-108.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 to a new corridor. The intermediary could not serve it, and the payment died.. A EUR 200,000 payment is sent down a new corridor. The instruction names an intermediary that holds no settlement relationship there. The payment dies downstream, and message mapping, routing data and routing logic all look equally guilty. One thing to remember: Start from the agent chain, not from the mapping.

INS-109.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,500 return and EUR 1,500 refund land the same day, team nets them. Two EUR 1,500 amounts land on the same day. One is a return, one is a refund. The team nets them and closes both cases. Both cases are still open, and both are now wrong. One thing to remember: Each has its own trigger, timeline and accounting treatment, so handle them as separate events even when they land together.

INS-110.agenda: Work through this case: A Request to Pay for EUR 3,000 had no date. Three systems settled it on three different days.. A SEPA Request to Pay for EUR 3,000 arrives with no requested execution date. One system derives a date, one asks the customer, one applies a rule. The same request settles on three different dates. One thing to remember: No date on the request means no single payment date.

INS-111.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 500,000 payment passed sanctions. The check that should have run first ran last.. A EUR 500,000 payment is screened by four controls. The controls were reordered for speed, and one ran after the payment it was meant to stop. The payment passes, and the control that assumed a predecessor had run never fires. One thing to remember: Control order is a risk decision, not a performance tweak.

INS-112.agenda: Work through this case: 90 percent of a remittance file lands in repair. A corporate customer sends a daily remittance file with thousands of supplier payments, worth EUR 2.4 million. One thing to remember: The queue is a symptom, not the problem. Fix the data at the source.

INS-113.agenda: Work through this case: The reject reason the customer must never see. A EUR 50,000 payment is rejected. One thing to remember: Precise inside, careful outside. The reason shown must pass the privacy rule first.

INS-114.agenda: Work through this case: Ten million a month, and the peak is the only number that matters. Five new clients bring ten million transactions a month, roughly 330,000 a day on average. The average looks comfortable. Then payroll and supplier files arrive in concentrated morning windows, and the busiest hour is already at about 70 percent of measured capacity. The average fits. The peak does not. One thing to remember: Convert the growth into throughput, concurrency, queue depth, storage, monitoring and resilience requirements before the clients go live.

INS-115.agenda: Work through this case: One extra hour, and every deadline moves. The business asks for the customer cut-off to move one hour later. One hour sounds small. But a cut-off is not a single time, it is the end of a deadline chain: channel cut-offs, scheme windows, liquidity checks and operational staffing. Move the hour, and every deadline in the chain moves with it. One thing to remember: Judge the extension on four things, downstream scheme windows, liquidity for the extra hour, staffing to run it, and exception handling for payments that still miss the new cut-off.

INS-116.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 held at the border. The purpose code was optional at the front, mandatory at the back.. A customer sends EUR 80,000 abroad and leaves the purpose code blank, because the screen says it is optional. Downstream, a system that mandates the code holds the payment. Nobody owns the repair, so the payment waits while the customer calls. One thing to remember: Optional at the front, mandatory at the back, is a defect.

INS-117.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 150,000 payment that could not go instant. A customer sends a EUR 150,000 instant payment. One thing to remember: The scheme maximum is the hard gate, not the customer limit.

INS-118.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 120,000 routed to a bank that stopped serving the corridor years ago.. A EUR 120,000 payment is routed through an intermediary named in the reference data. The bank stopped serving that corridor years ago, and nobody updated the data. The payment is rejected, and the same bad intermediary is used again next week. One thing to remember: Reference data without an owner decays.

INS-119.agenda: Work through this case: The vendor feature that worked everywhere except where it mattered. A vendor demos a capability the bank needs. One thing to remember: A demoed feature is not a usable feature. Verify the configuration level first.

INS-120.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 20,000 returned because the requirement quoted the rulebook. A EUR 20,000 payment is returned by the beneficiary bank. The developers say they built exactly what the requirement said. The requirement quoted the scheme rulebook, word for word. One thing to remember: Jargon left in a requirement produces a system that does the wrong thing confidently, so plain, precise wording is a quality control, not a courtesy.

INS-121.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 850 collected on the wrong day, and the debtor never agreed. A utility collects EUR 850 by direct debit. The money leaves the debtor's account three days early. The debtor demands it back, and the bank has to refund it. One thing to remember: A collection only works when the mandate, the Creditor Identifier and the scheme rules are all set up correctly.

INS-122.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,200 collected under the wrong Creditor Identifier. A business collects EUR 1,200 by SEPA Direct Debit. The debtor bank cannot match the collection to any creditor. The collection is rejected, and the business is paid late. One thing to remember: No correct identifier means no collection can be initiated or matched to the right creditor, so the identifier is a gating data item, not a label.

INS-123.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 600 collection was rejected. The mandate evidence was in three systems, and none of it matched.. A EUR 600 collection is rejected for a missing or invalid mandate. The mandate evidence is scattered: a paper scan in a shared drive, an online consent in another system, an amendment as a free-text note. The rejection cannot be explained, and the customer is not convinced either. One thing to remember: A mandate is a lifecycle, not a record.

INS-124.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5,000 debited on the due date, settled two days later. A creditor expects EUR 5,000 on the due date. The debtor is debited on that date, exactly as planned. The creditor's account shows nothing for two more days. One thing to remember: Confusing them produces wrong value dating and reconciliation breaks, so each date must be tracked as a separate fact.

INS-125.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2,000 collected, and nobody knew which corner failed. A EUR 2,000 direct debit collection fails. The creditor blames its PSP. The PSP blames the clearing system. The debtor bank says it never received the file. One thing to remember: Each corner owns a distinct responsibility, so when a collection fails the model pinpoints exactly which party owns the failure.

INS-126.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 600 collected, but the debtor was never told the amount changed. A creditor raises a subscription from EUR 500 to EUR 600. The debtor is debited EUR 600 without warning. The debtor disputes the collection and gets it refunded. One thing to remember: If the amount changes and the pre-notification is not updated, the debtor can dispute the collection, so the notice and the file must stay in step.

INS-127.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 3,000 collection late because one of three calendars was closed. A EUR 3,000 direct debit is due on a Monday. The creditor's bank is open, the debtor's bank is open. The collection still does not complete that day. One thing to remember: Planning on a single calendar, such as only the creditor's own business calendar, is what produces late debits.

INS-128.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 900 refund refused because the team counted the wrong days. A debtor claims a EUR 900 refund inside the scheme window. The bank refuses, saying the window has closed. The debtor appeals, and the scheme says the bank counted wrong. One thing to remember: The discipline is simple: check the calendar for each timeline before computing any date.

INS-129.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, creditor bank closed, collection never sent. A creditor plans a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday. The debtor bank is open. The scheme is open. The creditor bank is closed for a holiday. The collection is never sent. One thing to remember: The creditor must plan for its own closure days, not just the debtor's, because its own calendar is a hard gate on submission.

INS-130.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4,000 collection due Friday, debtor bank closed, debit lands Monday. A creditor sends a EUR 4,000 collection for Friday. The creditor bank is open. The scheme is open. The debtor bank is closed for a holiday. The debit lands on Monday, and the creditor had promised the money for Friday. One thing to remember: The debtor PSP calendar matters as much as the creditor's: it fixes the real debit date.

INS-131.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 12,000 in collections due, both banks open, clearing closed. EUR 12,000 in collections is due today. Both banks are open and working. Nothing settles. The clearing mechanism between them is closed. One thing to remember: Both banks being open is not enough: the infrastructure between them must also be open.

INS-132.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 950 debited with permission, customer wants it back in week seven. A debtor authorised a direct debit of EUR 950. Seven weeks after the debit, the debtor asks for the money back. The creditor calls it an exception. It is not an exception. It is a scheme right. One thing to remember: A refund inside this window is a normal scheme right, not an exception.

INS-133.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,100 taken without authorisation, claim arrives in month twelve. A debtor finds a direct debit of EUR 1,100 on the statement. The debtor never authorised it. Twelve months have passed. The creditor says it is too late. It is not. One thing to remember: An unauthorised claim is a different process from an authorised refund, with a longer window and different evidence.

INS-134.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2,000 comes back, the ledger books it as the wrong event. EUR 2,000 comes back after a direct debit. The ledger books it as a refund. It was a return, started by the debtor bank because the account could not be debited. The timeline, the message and the accounting are all wrong now. One thing to remember: Treating them as the same thing causes wrong messages, wrong timelines and wrong ledger entries.

INS-135.agenda: Work through this case: USD 25,000 cross-border in two days, domestic instant in seconds. A customer sent USD 25,000 overseas. A domestic instant payment the same morning arrived in seconds. The cross-border payment took two days. One thing to remember: A chain is only as fast as its slowest hop.

INS-136.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 10,000 to a non-euro account, euro leg done in seconds, rest waits hours. A customer sends EUR 10,000 from Europe to a non-euro account. The euro leg finishes in seconds. The customer expects the whole payment done. Nothing happens for hours while the other leg is processed. One thing to remember: The two legs must be explained separately, with their own coverage and responsibilities.

INS-137.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 25,000 instant payment, three steps fast, one step slow, promise broken. A bank promises EUR 25,000 instant payments. The channel is fast. The engine is fast. Clearing is fast. Settlement is slow. The customer promise breaks, even though three steps are instant. One thing to remember: The work is to find which step is the bottleneck and optimise it, rather than assuming the rail alone makes the payment instant.

INS-138.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5,000 sent abroad, beneficiary receives EUR 4,850, rate never shown. A customer sends EUR 5,000 abroad. The beneficiary receives EUR 4,850. The customer was never shown the rate, the fees, or how long the rate held. The price was agreed after the fact, which is no agreement at all. One thing to remember: Transparency means showing the total cost and the applied rate before the customer confirms.

INS-139.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 40,000 traced to the last bank, and still nobody knew where the money was. A EUR 40,000 payment is sent across three banks. The sender traces it with the UETR to the last bank in the chain. The last bank confirms it received the instruction. The beneficiary still has no money. One thing to remember: A UETR proves the payment exists and can be tracked, but it does not by itself prove where the money is or that it settled, so tracking and settlement evidence must never be confused.

INS-140.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 to a supplier, paid in full, cannot be matched to any invoice. A company pays a supplier EUR 30,000. The money arrives in full. The supplier cannot match it to any invoice. The payment carries no structured remittance data, so the cash sits unallocated. One thing to remember: Structured data is what makes a payment reconcilable and compliant at the same time.

INS-141.agenda: Work through this case: Two instant payment systems connected by API, and a EUR 10,000 payment still failed at clearing. Two banks connected their instant payment systems through an API. One thing to remember: Connected is not interoperable.

INS-142.agenda: Work through this case: A father in India sent INR 50,000 to Singapore with just a mobile number, and the transfer failed on scope. A father in India sent INR 50,000 to a family member in Singapore using only the recipient mobile number. One thing to remember: Live does not mean everything is covered.

INS-143.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 instant payment, FX quote expires while screening runs. A bank sends EUR 80,000 instantly to a non-euro account. The FX quote is locked at 09:00. Screening runs long. At 09:04 the quote has expired, and the payment cannot settle at the promised rate. One thing to remember: The FX provider is a dependency in the payment chain, and its failure modes must be designed for.

INS-144.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000 instant dollars promised, no dollars to settle with on Monday morning. A bank promises instant dollar payments. On Monday morning a customer sends USD 100,000. The rate is competitive. The system is ready. There are not enough dollars to settle with. One thing to remember: The constraint is liquidity, not conversion, and it must be managed by treasury, not just by the payment engine.

INS-145.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 5,000 payment had to clear in 10 seconds, and the sanctions check needed 40. A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment. One thing to remember: A 10-second payment still needs its controls.

INS-146.agenda: Work through this case: A fraudster moved EUR 9,000 out of an account in 20 seconds, before the customer noticed. A fraudster gained access to a customer's account. One thing to remember: Seconds to settle means seconds to steal.

INS-147.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 60,000 payment, app says pending, engine says processed, ledger says nothing. A customer sends EUR 60,000 abroad. The app says pending. The engine says processed. The ledger has no posting. Three systems, three truths, one customer on the phone. One thing to remember: A payment whose state cannot be stated cannot be managed.

INS-148.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 15,000 instant payment failed after the debit, and both banks pointed at different contracts. Two banks connected their instant payment systems. One thing to remember: A connection is not an agreement.

INS-149.agenda: Work through this case: A customer confirmed a EUR 8,000 transfer, then found the real cost was EUR 8,400. A customer sent EUR 8,000 across borders. One thing to remember: A hidden cost is a broken promise.

INS-150.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 45,000 across two instant systems, timeout, customer taps send again. A customer sends EUR 45,000 across two fast payment systems. The screen times out. The customer taps send again. Now the bank has two instructions and one debit, and nobody knows if the money moved. One thing to remember: The safe handling is to establish the true state, never retry blindly, and use an inter-PSP investigation to resolve the uncertainty.
