INS-151.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 45,000 payment carried rich remittance data, and the last bank in the chain threw it away. A EUR 45,000 payment was sent with structured purpose and remittance data. One thing to remember: Data that does not survive the chain helps no one.

INS-152.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 10,000 credited in seconds, settled the next day. A customer sends EUR 10,000 by instant payment. The beneficiary sees the credit within seconds and ships the goods. The next morning, the sending bank discovers the interbank settlement never completed. One thing to remember: A payment can look instant to the customer while the interbank settlement is still pending, so the screen is never proof of finality.

INS-153.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 60,000 payment from Europe to India took four days, and neither side could say where it was. A European buyer paid an Indian exporter EUR 60,000. One thing to remember: A chain is not a corridor.

INS-154.agenda: Work through this case: First collection for EUR 850 rejected, mandate was never set up. A creditor sends its first collection for EUR 850 under a new mandate. The file is built, checked and sent. The scheme rejects it the same day. The mandate was never set up. One thing to remember: A first collection on an incomplete mandate is rejected, so put the setup check before the file is built.

INS-155.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 450 mandate was amended twice. The collections could not be traced to it.. A EUR 450 mandate is amended when the customer changes bank accounts. The amendment is recorded under a new reference. When the collections are challenged, none of them trace back to the mandate that authorised them. One thing to remember: One mandate, one reference, for its whole life.

INS-156.agenda: Work through this case: Same debtor, same EUR 850, wrong sequence, collection fails. A creditor collects EUR 850 from the same debtor every month. This month the collection is marked recurring. The debtor bank treats it under the wrong rules and it fails. It was the first collection under a new mandate. One thing to remember: Mark each collection first or recurring from the mandate state, never from a guess.

INS-157.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 750 collected on 3 days' notice, with no agreement to prove it. A creditor collects EUR 750 with only 3 days' notice. The debtor disputes the collection. The creditor cannot prove the debtor ever agreed to shorter notice. One thing to remember: A shorter notice with no agreement behind it leaves the collection open to dispute, so the evidence is as much part of the collection as the notice itself.

INS-158.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 25,000 collected from a customer who cancelled. The file was built on last month's data.. A collection file goes out for EUR 25,000. It includes a customer who cancelled, and an amount changed after the file was built. The file is submitted after the scheme deadline, and the refunds and complaints arrive together. One thing to remember: A collection file is a scheme submission, not a spreadsheet job.

INS-159.agenda: Work through this case: A customer cancelled a EUR 800 collection. The money was still debited.. A customer asks billing to cancel a EUR 800 collection. Billing deletes it from the file. The file is already with the creditor PSP, so the debit goes ahead anyway. One thing to remember: After submission, deletion stops working. Cancellation takes over.

INS-160.agenda: Work through this case: A member cancelled. A clerk revoked. The EUR 300 collection was debited anyway.. A member cancels a membership and expects no further collection. A billing clerk revokes the next EUR 300 collection instead. The wrong mechanism is used for the collection's state, and the member is debited anyway. One thing to remember: Same word, different mechanism. State picks it.

INS-161.agenda: Work through this case: A duplicate EUR 1,100 collection settled. Someone deleted it, and reconciliation broke.. A duplicate EUR 1,100 collection settles by mistake. Someone deletes the settled entry to fix it. Reconciliation now has a hole where the money went, and the audit trail is gone. One thing to remember: Settled money is reversed, never erased.

INS-162.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 3,200 collection returned, reason code unread for four days. A collection of EUR 3,200 is returned. The pacs.004 carries a reason code. Nobody on the returns team can read it consistently. The creditor finds out four days late, with no clear explanation. One thing to remember: If the returns team cannot interpret the reason codes consistently, creditors find out days late with no clear explanation.

INS-163.agenda: Work through this case: A business was collected under Core. It claimed a refund the creditor never expected.. A business is collected under SDD Core for EUR 5,000. The debtor claims a refund the creditor assumed did not exist. The creditor had run one process for both schemes, and the differences were hidden. One thing to remember: Two schemes, two risk profiles. One process hides them.

INS-164.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 250,000 from Europe to India, and nobody owned the journey. A European buyer pays an Indian exporter EUR 250,000. The payment crosses four legs: a domestic euro rail, a cross-border bridge, an FX conversion and a domestic Indian rail. Each participant reports only its own leg. The payment is late, and the chain of calls begins: exporter to buyer, buyer to bank, bank to bridge. One thing to remember: Give the corridor a named owner for the whole journey, with every leg mapped to its rail, FX step, settlement and compliance check.

INS-165.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 140 transfer arrived short by 11.39 percent. The customer was told the fee was small.. A customer sends EUR 140 abroad. About 11.39 percent disappears in fees before it arrives. The customer was quoted one small fee, and nobody split the total into its parts. One thing to remember: One transfer, three stacked charges. Split the total to see them.

INS-166.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 20,000 payment worked on UPI, then failed on FedNow for a reason no engineer could see. A bank connected to instant payment systems in several markets: UPI in India, SCT Inst in Europe, and FedNow and RTP in the United States. One thing to remember: Same payment, different rulebook.

INS-167.agenda: Work through this case: One generic field set swallowed a EUR 30,000 payment's remittance data, and no one could reconcile it. A EUR 30,000 payment crossed two corridors, and each corridor sent slightly different fields. One thing to remember: Similar is not identical.

INS-168.agenda: Work through this case: USD 5,000 still took four days, despite the G20 targets. A small business sends USD 5,000 to a supplier overseas. It takes four days and costs USD 180 in fees. The corridor team points at the G20 targets and says payments are getting faster. One thing to remember: A business analyst uses the objectives to judge whether a corridor design is actually improving the customer outcome, which is the only test that matters.

INS-169.agenda: Work through this case: A mobile number pointed at the wrong account, and INR 25,000 went to a stranger. A customer sent INR 25,000 to a family member using a mobile number. One thing to remember: Resolution is a payment control, not a lookup.

INS-170.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 70,000 to a supplier, screen says pending, supplier says unpaid. A company sends EUR 70,000 to a supplier. The screen says pending. The supplier says it has not been paid. The clerk cannot say where the money is, because the status hides every step in the middle. One thing to remember: Customer-facing statuses must stay accurate while the underlying processing is still pending.

JEB-A01.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 250 payment went out wrong, and the team sent the wrong message to fix it. A legitimate EUR 250 payment was executed in error. One thing to remember: Settled means return, not cancel.

JEB-A02.agenda: Work through this case: No pacs.002 after 20 seconds, EUR 5,000 gone, and the customer asked for it to be sent again. A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment. One thing to remember: No confirmation is not a failure. It is a question.

JEB-A03.agenda: Work through this case: camt.055 sent after settlement: EUR 75,000 already gone. A customer asks to cancel a EUR 75,000 payment. One thing to remember: camt.055 stops a payment. It cannot undo one. Check the lifecycle first.

JEB-A04.agenda: Work through this case: SAR 250,000 left the account, the beneficiary was paid, and the nostro showed nothing. A SAR 250,000 payment left the customer account and was sent onward. One thing to remember: A missing entry is not a missing payment.

JEB-A05.agenda: Work through this case: pacs.009 cover rejected, but the EUR 40,000 payment had not failed. A pacs.009 cover is rejected with FF01, invalid account number. One thing to remember: A rejection code is a clue, not a verdict. The rejection alone must never trigger the refund.

JEB-A06.agenda: Work through this case: The customer asked for Citi, the payment went through Chase. A customer sends a USD 250,000 payment and names Citi New York as intermediary. One thing to remember: Routing follows the governing rule, not the message alone. Update the SSI first, or override explicitly.

JEB-A07.agenda: Work through this case: One pacs.008 for EUR 5 million went to the wrong system, because the route code was never read. A pacs.008 for EUR 5 million was sent. One thing to remember: The pacs.008 is the instruction. The BAH plus BizSvc is the route.

JEB-A08.agenda: Work through this case: Treasury saw EUR 18 million and thought EUR 2 million was lost. Treasury expects EUR 20 million. One thing to remember: An advice is not a payment. pacs.009 ADV gives treasury sight, it does not move money.

JEB-A09.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5 million valid on Monday, failed on Friday. A EUR 5 million payment is accepted on Monday for Friday execution, against a EUR 6 million balance. One thing to remember: Warehousing is a commitment to re-check, not a guarantee. Re-validate at execution.

JEB-A10.agenda: Work through this case: A USD 10 million payment was two days late, and the interest bill proved the value date mattered more than the booking. A USD 10 million payment was delayed by two days. One thing to remember: Value date drives interest, not booking.

JEB-A11.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 6 million to pay, EUR 7 million showing, and the money arrives too late. A treasurer must pay EUR 6 million at noon. The account shows EUR 9 million opening balance and EUR 4 million coming in. The EUR 4 million arrives at 4pm. The payment fails at noon. One thing to remember: With a EUR 9 million opening balance, EUR 4 million coming in and a EUR 6 million payment to make, the intraday view shows EUR 7 million only if the incoming payment arrives in time, so relying on camt.053 alone misses the intraday picture entirely.

JEB-A12.agenda: Work through this case: camt.056 sent, EUR 60,000 stuck in silence. A bank asks for EUR 60,000 back with a camt.056. One thing to remember: Every waiting state needs a way out. Design the exit before the wait begins.

JEB-A13.agenda: Work through this case: Ten payments promised, seven pacs.008 sent, three 'missing'. A corporate submits a pain.001 file with 10 payments. Only 7 pacs.008 messages reach the next bank. Operations raises an incident: 3 payments are missing. One thing to remember: A pain.001 is therefore a promise that payments will be made, not a guarantee of a pacs.008 for each one.

JEB-A14.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 100,000 payment was tracked to the wrong person, and tracking could not stop it. A EUR 100,000 payment was sent to the wrong beneficiary. One thing to remember: Tracking shows. Recall recovers.

JEB-A15.agenda: Work through this case: One settlement code was mapped wrong, and a EUR 150,000 payment was debited twice. A EUR 150,000 payment arrived with the settlement code INGA. One thing to remember: A code is a business decision, not a field.

JEB-B01.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2,500 debited, success shown, beneficiary never credited. A customer sends EUR 2,500 on a payment app. The account is debited at once. The app shows Payment Successful. The beneficiary never receives the money. One thing to remember: A payment therefore stands confirmed only when the receiving side returns a status, so trust the confirmation, not the debit.

JEB-B02.agenda: Work through this case: 3,000 payments arrived at once, and the SLA broke on sequencing. Thousands of payments arrive together. One thing to remember: Control order is a business decision, not a technical default. Sequential for validation, parallel for screening.

JEB-B03.agenda: Work through this case: One leg of a USD 250,000 payment failed, and the team nearly recalled the leg that was fine. A USD 250,000 cover-method payment went from India to Europe. One thing to remember: Check the cover before recalling it.

JEB-B04.agenda: Work through this case: The team asked for pacs.009 and got the wrong one. A EUR 100,000 cover payment needs to move. One thing to remember: A message name is not a use case. Name the use case, the scheme and the business context.

JEB-B05.agenda: Work through this case: The German Direct Debit flow met the Dutch customer, and failed. A Direct Debit process defined for Germany works well there. One thing to remember: Reuse is a delivery choice, not a business decision. Check the local rule first.

JEB-B06.agenda: Work through this case: A pacs.002 RJCT arrived for USD 180,000, and the bank nearly refunded money it did not have. A USD 180,000 cover-method payment was sent. One thing to remember: A rejection is not a refund.

JEB-B07.agenda: Work through this case: One statement line, 400 entries, and one missing. A settlement batch holds 400 entries under one statement line worth EUR 850,000. One thing to remember: Reconcile the batch, not the entry. One missing entry breaks the whole group.

JEB-B08.agenda: Work through this case: Treasury needed one answer before cut-off, and camt.053 could not give it. Treasury waits on a EUR 30 million Nostro credit before releasing an outgoing payment. One thing to remember: Choose the message by the decision it must support, not by its definition alone.

JEB-B09.agenda: Work through this case: A flawless pain.001, a USD 200,000 payment in the wrong engine. A customer sends a flawless pain.001 for USD 200,000. One thing to remember: The message provides the clues, and the business rules determine the route.

JEB-B10.agenda: Work through this case: A regulatory deadline and a EUR 1 million client project collided, and the team was told to pick one. A team had two pieces of work: CBPR+ structured-address work for a regulatory date, and a strategic client Cash Pooling project worth EUR 1 million. One thing to remember: Phase both, not either-or.

JEB-B11.agenda: Work through this case: The loan consent that quietly opened EUR 50,000 of data. A customer applies for a loan and taps consent to share financial data. The lender pulls EUR 50,000 of account history, investments and more. The customer thought they had agreed to share one bank statement. One thing to remember: Good consent states its purpose and duration plainly, with a clear way to withdraw, in plain language anyone can follow.

JEB-B12.agenda: Work through this case: The API said 200 OK, and the EUR 80,000 payment was still rejected. An API call returns HTTP 200. One thing to remember: API success is not a business decision. Start with the decision the process needs to make.

JEB-B13.agenda: Work through this case: A camt.055 arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment, and the team sent a camt.056 before asking where the payment sat. A camt.055 cancellation request arrived for a EUR 75,000 payment. One thing to remember: A cancellation request only asks. It does not guarantee.

JEB-B14.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 10,000 loan offered by a bank the customer never joined. A customer holds a salary account with one bank. A different bank offers them a EUR 10,000 loan at a better rate. The customer asks: how can a bank I never joined offer me a loan? One thing to remember: That reframes the competitive question: not how to become your bank, but how to become the provider chosen for the next financial need.

JEB-C01.agenda: Work through this case: VoP said No Match, GBP 12,000 went anyway. A payer sent GBP 12,000 to a supplier. Verification of Payee returned No Match. The payer carried on, and the money went to the wrong account. One thing to remember: No Match is a warning, not a verdict.

JEB-C02.agenda: Work through this case: The optional field that stopped a EUR 120,000 cover payment. In a four-bank cover payment, Bank A sends pacs.008 to Bank B and a pacs.009 cover to intermediary Bank C. One thing to remember: Optional in the message, mandatory for the flow. A field marked optional can still be required to make the payment work.

JEB-C03.agenda: Work through this case: USD 10,000 to India: one message, or two?. A US bank sends USD 10,000 to HDFC Bank in India, for an INR account. One thing to remember: Serial or cover is a settlement decision, not a wording choice. Decide by accounts and currency.

JEB-C04.agenda: Work through this case: The team heard MT was dead, and stopped planning for it. The CBPR+ November 2026 deadline is announced as the end of MT for cross-border payments. One thing to remember: MT is retiring, not retired. The end date is not the same for every message.

JEB-C05.agenda: Work through this case: The optional address field that cost EUR 12,000 in deductions. A pain.001 is sent without the sending business agent address and postcode. One thing to remember: A field status describes the message, not the process. Ask whether the field is needed for the process.

JEB-C06.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 90,000 payment that waited for a check it did not need. A EUR 90,000 payment enters the engine. One thing to remember: Sequential for validation, parallel for screening. Order follows dependency.

JEB-C07.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 1 million project that stalled on one unasked question. A EUR 1 million payments project stalls in its third month. Compliance says the requirement was never theirs. Developers say the requirement was never buildable. The BA says everyone agreed it in the workshop. One thing to remember: When a stakeholder does not know an answer, the BA helps them understand the question and reach it, because that translation is what makes the requirements workable, and asking the right questions is the core of stakeholder management, not a soft skill on the side.

JEB-C08.agenda: Work through this case: The MT103 that lost its address in translation. An MT103 arrives for a EUR 60,000 payment. One thing to remember: MT to MX is a business mapping exercise, not a format change. Get the mapping right early.

JEB-C09.agenda: Work through this case: A candidate could name every recall message, and still could not explain a EUR 20,000 recall. A candidate was asked to explain a EUR 20,000 recall. One thing to remember: A list of messages is not a journey.

JEB-C10.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 45,000 payment that failed in the place nobody planned for. A EUR 45,000 payment is processed with the wrong details, and the verification of payee check fails. One thing to remember: Design for failure, or failure designs the day. Plan for all three places a solution can fail.

JEB-C11.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 25,000 vanished from the dashboard, but the money never moved. A customer opens an aggregator app and sees EUR 25,000 across their accounts. One day the dashboard shows EUR 0. The customer calls the bank in a panic. The money is still there. One thing to remember: The single most important role of the aggregator is consent management, because it never holds the funds it connects you to.

JEB-C12.agenda: Work through this case: Four messages, one recall, and a EUR 35,000 question no one could answer. A EUR 35,000 payment needed recalling. One thing to remember: Connect the journey first. Debate second.

JEB-C13.agenda: Work through this case: Three accounts, one app, and a EUR 5,000 fee to see them. A customer holds accounts at three banks. One app promises to show all three in one place. To see them, the app demands the customer open a new account with it. One thing to remember: A customer should not need a new bank account merely to view other accounts.

JEB-C14.agenda: Work through this case: Schedule it for next week: the five rules hidden in one sentence. A customer asks to schedule a EUR 25,000 payment for next week. One thing to remember: A requirement that cannot be written as a rule is not a simple requirement. Decode it, do not just document it.

JEB-C15.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 8,000 insurance claim the bank app could not see. A customer opens their bank app to check an EUR 8,000 insurance claim. The app shows their bank accounts perfectly. It shows nothing about the insurance, the pension or the mortgage. One thing to remember: The difference is scope: Open Banking is banking data, Open Finance is the customer whole financial life.

JEB-D01.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 10,000 SDD collection fell on a national holiday abroad. The team moved the due date.. A EUR 10,000 SDD collection is due on a day that is a national holiday in another country. The team moves the due date, assuming the holiday stops the collection. The collection was valid all along, because the interbank leg runs on TARGET. One thing to remember: TARGET governs the interbank leg. National holidays do not.

JEB-D02.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 4,000 collection was presented on D-1. The team thought the window had closed at D-14.. A EUR 4,000 collection is presented to the inter-PSP space. The team thinks D-14 was the deadline, so the collection must be late. D-14 opens the window, D-1 closes it, and the collection is inside it. One thing to remember: D-14 opens the window. D-1 closes it.

JEB-D03.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2,500 collected Monday, debited Tuesday, customer complains. A creditor collects EUR 2,500 by direct debit. The creditor is funded on Monday, the due date. The debtor sees the debit on Tuesday. The debtor complains the money was taken late. It was not. One thing to remember: Three dates, three events. The split is a calendar effect, not an error.

JEB-D04.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 60,000 payment was processed, but by mid-morning there was still no credit. The customer called, and nobody could trace it.. A EUR 60,000 cross-border payment is processed. By mid-morning the beneficiary still has no credit. The customer calls, and the team has no live trace, so one query becomes hours of back-and-forth. One thing to remember: No trace turns one question into an investigation.

JEB-D05.agenda: Work through this case: An instant payment of EUR 5,000 left the account at once. The beneficiary received nothing.. An instant payment of EUR 5,000 is debited at once. The beneficiary receives nothing. The team assumes it was rejected and the money is on its way back, but the payment is stuck, not rejected. One thing to remember: Find the outcome first. Rejected and stuck are not the same.

JEB-D06.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 15,000 payment reached the beneficiary in 10 seconds. Compliance had not finished checking it.. A EUR 15,000 payment reaches the beneficiary in 10 seconds. The AML and sanctions checks run longer than the payment window allows. The team wonders whether instant means the checks can be skipped. One thing to remember: Instant means compliance at payment speed, not no compliance.

JEB-D07.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5,000 to another country, no link to send it on. A bank wants to send EUR 5,000 instantly to a country its system has never paid. It has no link to that country's instant system. Building one link for every country would take years. So the payment waits. One thing to remember: Connect once, reach many countries. A central platform replaces a web of bilateral links.

JEB-D08.agenda: Work through this case: INR 50,000 from India to Singapore, instant at last. A worker in India sends INR 50,000 to family in Singapore. In the old world it would take days and cost a visible fee. This time it arrives instantly. Two instant systems talked to each other. One thing to remember: Linked systems give faster and more transparent payments. Instant systems can interoperate.

JEB-D09.agenda: Work through this case: Two instant rails were connected by API. A EUR 30,000 payment still could not cross.. Two payment systems are connected with an API. A EUR 30,000 payment is sent across the bridge. It fails, because messaging, rules, clearing, settlement and compliance never lined up. One thing to remember: Interoperability demands more than connectivity.

JEB-D10.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 50,000 payment went missing. The beneficiary could not prove it had been sent.. A EUR 50,000 payment is sent across borders. The beneficiary says it never arrived. The team searches by amount and date, and finds three matching payments. One thing to remember: One reference for the whole journey. Without it, there is no track.

JEB-D11.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 40,000 payment crossed borders in 60 seconds. The beneficiary got exactly what was expected.. A EUR 40,000 cross-border payment is sent under OCT Inst. Payment and settlement complete in 60 seconds. The non-euro leg is converted before the beneficiary is paid, so the amount lands exactly as expected. One thing to remember: Speed is not the test. Reliability and rule-following are.

JEB-D12.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 25,000 payment left Europe for outside it. It cleared in 10 seconds, around the clock.. A EUR 25,000 payment starts in Europe and goes outside it. The euro leg and the leg outside the euro area both have to work. OCT Inst clears it in 10 seconds, and the team assumes the speed is the point. One thing to remember: Speed is not the point. An efficient, consistent and compliant process is.

JEB-D13.agenda: Work through this case: USD 1,000 sent abroad, USD 60 gone in cost, three days gone in time. A customer sends USD 1,000 to family abroad. USD 60 disappears in cost. Three days pass before it arrives. The same amount moves in a second at home. One thing to remember: Reaching people in remote areas needs processing systems, not just mobile apps.

JEB-D14.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2,000 at midnight on Sunday, no bank open, payment still instant. A customer sends EUR 2,000 at midnight on a Sunday. No branch is open. No banker is at a desk. The payment still arrives instantly. The phone is only the front door. One thing to remember: Behind the mobile phone sits a payment ecosystem of many interacting parts.

JEB-D15.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 20,000 instant in Europe, stuck for hours outside it. A customer sends EUR 20,000 instantly inside Europe. It arrives in seconds. The same customer sends EUR 20,000 just outside Europe. It takes hours, and no one can say why. The rail was instant. The payment was not. One thing to remember: Cross-border payments become truly instant only when rules are clear, systems are aligned, and technology works with people.

JEB-E01.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 100K limit was removed. A EUR 200,000 payment went to TARGET2 anyway.. The EU Instant Payments Regulation removes the EUR 100K scheme maximum for SCT Inst. A customer with a EUR 300K bank limit sends EUR 200,000 instantly. The old routing rule still sends anything above EUR 100K to TARGET2, and the payment takes the slow road. One thing to remember: Two live rules, one payment, two different outcomes.

JEB-E02.agenda: Work through this case: pacs.004 arrived. The debtor is still waiting.. A pacs.004 arrives, and the operations team credits the debtor at once. The EUR 85,000 payment was a cover payment, a pacs.009, and the pacs.008 instruction was never rejected. The debtor has been credited for a payment that was never returned, and the original instruction is still live. One thing to remember: A pacs.004 only says a payment was returned, so crediting the debtor on receipt is an event-to-action shortcut that skips the questions that matter.

JEB-E03.agenda: Work through this case: The platform handled today easily. Then five new clients arrived, and it fell over at 9am.. Payment traffic peaks between 7am and 10am, and today the platform copes. Five clients in the pipeline could add 10 million transactions a month. Nobody asked when they onboard, what their peaks look like, or whether the workload itself changes. One thing to remember: Peak behaviour defines performance demand, not monthly volume.

JEB-E04.agenda: Work through this case: 90 percent of a remittance file failed, and the repair queue could not cope. A remittance file worth EUR 480,000 arrived for processing. One thing to remember: A repair queue is not a file correction process.

JEB-E05.agenda: Work through this case: The engine was open, but the USD 100,000 payment had nowhere to go. A customer sent a USD 100,000 international payment on a day the USA was open and France was closed. One thing to remember: An open engine does not mean a ready payment journey.

JEB-E06.agenda: Work through this case: AC06 became MS03, and nobody could say why. A return code mapping changes: AC06 for a blocked account becomes MS03, reason not specified. It looks like a one-line change. Then the receiving bank asks why, the compliance team asks who approved it, and the payment engine cannot explain which blocked accounts produce AC06 at all. One thing to remember: The real gap is found by comparing what the ecosystem understands today with what the requirement expects, then tracing the chain and deciding which system changes and who agrees the mapping.

JEB-E07.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 250,000 payment went to the wrong intermediary, and the engine looked guilty. A EUR 250,000 payment reached the wrong intermediary bank. One thing to remember: Correct logic on wrong data still routes wrong.

JEB-E08.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 75,000 payment, no route found, reject or repair?. A EUR 75,000 payment arrives with no route the system can determine. The system offers the easy answer: reject it. A competitor would repair it, find another route, and send it through. The customer would never know the difference, except in the result. One thing to remember: The most valuable question is what the business wants the system to do when this situation occurs.

JEB-E09.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 45,000 payment, every mandatory field filled, still fails. A Eurozone customer payment for EUR 45,000 arrives. Reference, account number and customer name are all filled. The debtor postal address has no street name. The payment fails downstream. The form said it was complete. One thing to remember: Some missing fields are business rules that will fail the payment in processing.

JEB-E10.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 100,000 sent to T2, Bank B waits for a payment that is already settled. Bank A sends EUR 100,000 to Bank B. Bank B waits for settlement before crediting the beneficiary. Settlement already happened. Bank B is waiting on a model that no longer applies. One thing to remember: The distinction is not the message format but the architecture.

JEB-E11.agenda: Work through this case: INR 10,000 arrives instantly, the banks settle it later. Customer A at Bank A sends INR 10,000 to Customer B at Bank B. Customer B sees it instantly. The two banks have not settled a rupee between them yet. Both statements are true at the same time. One thing to remember: Ask instant at which layer, and who pays for the infrastructure.

JEB-E12.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 payment, the team cannot say who clears it. A EUR 80,000 payment is stuck. The team knows the message is pacs.008. It cannot say who transports it, who clears it, or who settles it. Three different jobs are being treated as one. One thing to remember: Ask separately what the standard is, who transports the message, who clears it, and who settles it.

JEB-E13.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 150,000 engine change, a downstream failure nobody traced. A team changes the payment engine for a EUR 150,000 daily flow. The change passes testing. A week later a downstream system fails on a status it no longer recognises. Nobody traced the change past the engine. One thing to remember: In payments a point left to clarify later can become an expensive production problem.

JEB-E14.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 from Bank A to Bank C, who actually settles it?. Bank A asks Bank B to move EUR 200,000 onward to Bank C. Bank B does it. Finance asks who settled the money. The team names Bank B. Bank B only carried the instruction. One thing to remember: Naming the Settlement Agent makes the debit and credit entries and the nostro movements straightforward.

JEB-E15.agenda: Work through this case: Intermediary Agent 2 was optional, so a EUR 80,000 payment was left waiting. A EUR 80,000 cover payment was sent with Intermediary Agent 2 left out. One thing to remember: Optional in the message does not mean unnecessary in the flow.

JEB-F01.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 25,000 payment was rejected for a format fault. Reject or repair? The team guessed.. A EUR 25,000 payment is rejected for a format fault. The team rejects it again without checking where the fault sits. The fault was in the bank's own pacs.008, and a mapping fix would have saved the payment. One thing to remember: A format fault is a diagnosis, not a verdict.

JEB-F02.agenda: Work through this case: The customer cut-off is 3:25 PM. The deadline is 4:00 PM.. A customer submits a EUR 70,000 payment at 3:30 PM and expects it out today. The downstream deadline is 4:00 PM. The payment misses the day, and the customer is told the cut-off was 3:25 PM, a time that appears nowhere in the product. One thing to remember: A payment BA should ask what time the payment must be out of the file, whether the deadline is hard, and whether tiers are needed in the requirements.

JEB-F03.agenda: Work through this case: ISO 20022 ready? Eight gaps say otherwise. A bank is migrating to ISO 20022, and the project plan says the business is ready. The messages are mapped, the build is on track, and the go-live date is set. Then the first customer payment journey breaks, because nobody aligned the processes, the hand-offs, the training, the data quality or the control teams. One thing to remember: A migration plan must close these eight gaps before it can claim the business is ready.

JEB-F04.agenda: Work through this case: The payment is visible end to end. Why not the complaint?. A EUR 55,000 cross-border payment is debited, and the customer can track it end to end across linked payment systems. Then the payment goes wrong, and the customer raises a complaint. The complaint cannot travel the same way, and the hardest cross-border problem is back: nobody knows where the payment is. One thing to remember: That is why interlinking is a way of thinking about payments, not only a connectivity project.

JEB-F05.agenda: Work through this case: The consent arrived late. The 500 payments were still moving.. A set of 500 payments is being cancelled. A negative camt.029 arrives while the payment engine is still processing the set. Then a beneficiary consent arrives, after the expected timeframe, for payments that may already be on their way back. One thing to remember: Treating a late consent as merely late misses the point, since it can still reflect sound business behaviour.

JEB-F06.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 45,000 payment came back. The pacs.004 said returned, but nobody knew why.. A EUR 45,000 payment is returned by pacs.004. The team knows it was returned, but not why it failed. The investigation starts from the return alone, and steers the technical team to the wrong process. One thing to remember: Read the reason code, then investigate. Never the other way round.

JEB-F07.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 900 direct debit failed for insufficient funds. The scheduler retried it in the wrong order.. A EUR 900 direct debit fails because the account cannot fund it. The scheduler retries in first-in-first-out order and fails again. The salary credit lands two days later, and the D+5 window is almost gone. One thing to remember: D+5 is a window, not a penalty. Collect when the balance can fund it.

JEB-F08.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 1,500 collection was rejected. The team resubmitted it, and it was rejected again.. A EUR 1,500 collection is rejected. The team resubmits it at once, with no timing rule. It is rejected again, because the resubmission was never tied to the original timing. One thing to remember: Define the resubmission timing rule first, then resubmit.

JEB-F09.agenda: Work through this case: The rejected direct debit that landed in a third-party account. A direct debit collection of EUR 9,500 is rejected by the debtor bank. Normally it returns to the creditor bank, authorising it to debit the originator's account. This time the collection is booked to a designated third-party account instead, and the operations team is not sure the booking was ever allowed. One thing to remember: A BA cannot necessarily refuse a requirement, yet challenging it remains the BA responsibility.

JEB-F10.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 300 a month, no mandate, no direct debit. A business wants to collect EUR 300 a month from a customer by direct debit. It sends the first collection straight away. The bank rejects it. There was no mandate, and a direct debit without one does not exist. One thing to remember: The journey runs from mandate through collection, rejection, return and refund.

JEB-F11.agenda: Work through this case: Due date 15 October. Five calendars broke, and the SDD timeline broke with them.. A collection is due on 15 October, with due date, settlement date and debit date all the same. A new national holiday is declared after planning, and one PSP is closed. The team assumes the due date moves, and the collection fails. One thing to remember: Design the timeline for the broken assumptions, not only the happy flow.

JEB-F12.agenda: Work through this case: Mandate signed, EUR 1,200 collections stop a year later. A creditor collects EUR 1,200 a month by direct debit. A year later the collections start failing. The mandate was signed, filed, and then forgotten. Nobody owned it after creation. One thing to remember: Mandate management is part of the payments journey, not only administration.

JEB-F13.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 20,000 cross-border payment arrived in seconds. The customer still could not see what it cost.. A EUR 20,000 cross-border payment arrives in seconds. The customer cannot see the FX cost, cannot trace the payment, and the remittance data is too thin for the checks. Speed was delivered, and almost nothing else was. One thing to remember: Instant is only one piece. Speed without the rest is not a transformation.

JEB-F14.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 2,000 collection was made by mistake. The team used one cancel button for all three stages.. A creditor realises a EUR 2,000 collection was made by mistake. The team reaches for one generic cancel requirement. The collection is already in the clearing flow, and the generic cancel does nothing. One thing to remember: Stop a mistaken collection by its lifecycle stage.

PAI-C001.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 75,000 sent serial, returned cover, and the trail went cold. A EUR 75,000 payment goes out by the serial method. The beneficiary bank returns it, but by the cover method. The operations team cannot match the return to the original payment. One thing to remember: The method chosen governs tracking, charging and returns, so it must be identified before any of those are handled.

PAI-C002.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 60,000 MT202 with no customer behind it, and the team paid it anyway. An MT202 for EUR 60,000 arrives at a bank. The team treats it as cover for a customer payment and releases the funds. There was no customer payment behind it at all. One thing to remember: Both move money between banks, yet only the COV answers to a customer instruction, and that distinction is what trips people up.

PAI-C003.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 90,000 MT103 arrived in minutes, the funds took three days. A EUR 90,000 payment instruction reaches the beneficiary bank in minutes. The beneficiary calls to ask where the money is. The funds are still working through the correspondent chain, three days later. One thing to remember: The price is reconciliation: the two legs must match on amount and reference, and any mismatch becomes an exception.

PAI-C004.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 120,000 sent on an MT202, and the beneficiary never existed. A bank sends EUR 120,000 to another bank on an MT202. The receiving bank asks: which customer is this for? There is no customer. The MT202 was never a customer payment. One thing to remember: Every customer payment starts with an MT103, and an MT202 appears only when a separate funds leg is required.

PAI-C005.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 35,000 credited to the wrong account because field 59 was never read. A EUR 35,000 payment arrives at a bank. The operations team credits it using the account in the remittance text. The real beneficiary, named in field 59, never receives it. One thing to remember: In a serial payment each bank reads both fields from the MT103 it receives and forwards the message to the next bank in the chain.

PAI-C006.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 screened against the wrong name, because field 50 was skipped. An EUR 80,000 payment is screened and cleared. Days later, compliance finds the ordering customer was on a watchlist. The screening had checked the name in field 72, not the ordering customer in field 50. One thing to remember: The two fields answer different questions: field 50 says who is paying, field 72 says what else the receiver needs to know.

PAI-C007.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4,000 refunded under SDD B2B, and the scheme said it could never happen. A business debtor claims a EUR 4,000 refund on a direct debit. The bank pays it, no reason asked. The creditor protests: this was an SDD B2B collection, and B2B grants no refund right. One thing to remember: The schemes differ on refunds and mandate checks, so using the wrong one is a real error, not a paperwork slip.

PAI-C008.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 25,000 SEPA payment rejected for the wrong reason code. A EUR 25,000 SEPA payment is rejected. The team fixes the message format and resends it. It is rejected again, with the same reason code. One thing to remember: That is why an MT103 and a pacs.008 can carry one underlying SEPA payment, the pacs.008 being its ISO 20022 form.

PAI-C009.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 18,000 recalled by camt.056, and the bank waited for a pacs.004. A customer asks for EUR 18,000 back after a payment was credited in error. The bank sends a camt.056 recall request. Then it waits for a pacs.004, and nothing arrives for a week. One thing to remember: The two are often confused, yet they do opposite jobs: the pacs.004 moves the money back, while the camt.056 asks for the money back.

PAI-C010.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 12,000 paid twice from one pacs.008 file. A bulk pacs.008 file pays a supplier EUR 12,000. The same supplier is paid EUR 12,000 again the next day. The file contained the same transaction twice. One thing to remember: Duplicate detection is therefore a pre-processing discipline, not a post-payment investigation.

PAI-C011.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 came back, but the return was sent to the wrong bank. A beneficiary bank returned EUR 80,000. The originator bank waited for it. The return never arrived, because it was sent straight to the originator instead of back through the chain. One thing to remember: A return travels the chain in reverse, or it travels nowhere.

PAI-C012.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 arrived back, but no one could say which payment it was. EUR 80,000 arrived back at the originator bank. The credit sat in the account for two days. No one could say which payment it belonged to. One thing to remember: Without those references a return is only a credit with no story.

PAI-C013.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 120,000 recalled, and the recall had to cross three banks. A customer asked for EUR 120,000 back. The payment had already crossed an intermediary bank. One message could not bring it back, because the money sat at the end of a chain. One thing to remember: A recall is a chain of messages, not a single message.

PAI-C014.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 60,000 returned, and both ends claimed the return was theirs to start. EUR 60,000 had to come back. The originator bank said it would start the return. The beneficiary bank said it would start the return. Both were right, and the team argued about it for a day. One thing to remember: The message is identical in both cases. Only the initiating bank and the reason differ.

PAI-C015.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 45,000 recall sent, and the only answer was silence. A EUR 45,000 payment went to the wrong beneficiary. The originator bank sent a camt.056 recall. Days passed. No answer came, and no one could close the case. One thing to remember: No camt.029 means no closure. Silence is not an answer.

PAI-C016.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 returned with a reason code no bank recognised. EUR 30,000 came back as a pacs.004. The reason code on it did not exist in the scheme rulebook. The next bank in the chain rejected the return, and the money sat in limbo. One thing to remember: A reason code is a controlled vocabulary, not a free-text field.

PAI-C017.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 95,000 rejected, and the pacs.002 said nothing useful. A EUR 95,000 pacs.008 was rejected. The pacs.002 that reported it named the payment and nothing else. The originator bank spent a day guessing what had gone wrong. One thing to remember: A pacs.002 without status and reason leaves the originator guessing.

PAI-C018.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 announced, but the funds had not arrived yet. An MT103 announced EUR 200,000 to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary called, asking where the money was. The funds leg had not arrived yet, and the beneficiary had not been credited. One thing to remember: MT103 first, funds later, is normal. Crediting early is the error.

PAI-C019.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 cover arrived, and it looked like an ordinary transfer. EUR 200,000 arrived at the beneficiary bank as an MT202 COV. Nothing on it said which customer payment it was for. An MT103 for the same amount was waiting, unmatched, and the beneficiary was not credited. One thing to remember: The reference is the bridge between the information leg and the funds leg.

PAI-C020.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 150,000 cover sent to the wrong bank. A EUR 150,000 cover payment was sent. The MT202 COV went to a bank that held no settlement account for it. The funds landed where no one expected them, and settlement stopped. One thing to remember: The address is part of the settlement design, not an administrative detail.

PAI-C021.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 150,000 cover rejected, and the refund went to the wrong bank. A EUR 150,000 cover payment was rejected. The bank holding the funds sent them back. They went to the wrong bank, and one exception became two. One thing to remember: A return sent to the wrong bank creates a second exception on top of the first.

PAI-C022.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 90,000 cover, and two different ordering customers. A EUR 90,000 cover payment arrived. The MT103 named one ordering customer. The MT202 COV named a different one. The operations team spent a day arguing over who had sent the payment. One thing to remember: Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg.

PAI-C023.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 75,000 cover, and field 72 sent the funds to the wrong place. A EUR 75,000 cover payment was sent with a free-text instruction in field 72. The next bank read it the wrong way. The funds went to the wrong place, and settlement stopped. One thing to remember: Put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects.

PAI-C024.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000 sent, USD 99,850 received, and no one could explain the gap. A customer sent USD 100,000 by serial payment. The beneficiary was credited USD 99,850. USD 150 had vanished, and no one at the bank could explain where it went. One thing to remember: In a serial payment, every deduction in the chain lands on the beneficiary.

PAI-C025.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000 sent, two deductions, one credit that did not add up. USD 100,000 was sent through two intermediary banks. Each took a charge. The beneficiary bank could not prove the final credit was right, because the fields that explain the deductions were missing. One thing to remember: Without fields 71A and 71F, the beneficiary cannot reconcile the credit against the amount sent.

PAI-C026.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000, and the charges were counted twice. A USD 100,000 payment mixed serial and cover legs. Charges were deducted on the serial leg, then charged again on the cover leg. The beneficiary was short, and the customer was charged twice for the same journey. One thing to remember: Know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive.

PAI-C027.agenda: Work through this case: USD 85,000 return that tried to jump the chain. A USD 85,000 MT103 was returned. The return was sent straight to the originator bank. It never arrived, because the chain it had travelled on was skipped. One thing to remember: A return is not a new payment. It is the original payment travelling backwards.

PAI-C028.agenda: Work through this case: USD 40,000 sent to an account that did not exist. USD 40,000 was sent to a beneficiary account. The account number was wrong. The beneficiary bank could not credit anyone, and the customer asked where the money was. One thing to remember: An invalid account is the most common reason for a return, and the handling never changes.

PAI-C029.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 60,000 settled, and the recall had nowhere to go. A customer asked for EUR 60,000 back after the payment had settled. The originator bank sent a camt.056 recall. The clearing house did not support the message, so the recall went nowhere. One thing to remember: Know which clearing systems support a recall before promising a customer a payment can be taken back.

PAI-C030.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 110,000 recalled after the beneficiary had already spent it. EUR 110,000 was paid to the wrong beneficiary. By the time the customer noticed, the beneficiary had already spent it. The recall went out anyway, and the customer expected the money back. One thing to remember: Once the money has been spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

PAI-C031.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 70,000 recall for a third party, sent to the wrong bank. A EUR 70,000 recall was made in favour of a third-party beneficiary. The recall was sent straight to the third party. It sat unread, because the third party was never meant to receive it. One thing to remember: The third party never receives the recall directly. It receives the result through the bank that acts for it.

PAI-C032.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 55,000 recall rejected, with a reason code that did not belong there. A EUR 55,000 recall was refused. The refusal came back as a pacs.004 carrying the reason code GVC. GVC is not a code for a return, so the handling was wrong, and the case had to be reopened. One thing to remember: A reason code must match the message and the situation.

PAI-C033.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 25,000 stuck, and the team sent a camt.056 when they needed a camt.026. EUR 25,000 could not be applied by the receiving bank. The team sent a camt.056 to recall it. Nothing happened, because a recall asks for money back, and this payment needed a report that it could not be applied. One thing to remember: One asks for money back. The other reports it could not be applied.

PAI-C034.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 180,000 returned without a pacs.004, and the chain lost the link. EUR 180,000 had to come back. The returning bank sent the funds by another route, not a pacs.004. The money arrived, but no bank in the chain could prove which payment it belonged to. One thing to remember: Using another route breaks the link, which is why the pacs.004 is the expected message for a return.

PAI-C035.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 130,000 cover, screened on one leg and missed on the other. A EUR 130,000 cover payment was screened and cleared. The MT103 was checked. The MT202 COV was not. The funds leg carried a sanctioned party, and the payment went through anyway. One thing to remember: Screening one leg only leaves a gap a regulator will find.

PAI-C036.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 130,000 cover, and the two legs disagreed by EUR 500. A EUR 130,000 cover payment arrived. The MT103 said EUR 130,000. The MT202 COV said EUR 129,500. The beneficiary bank would not credit a cent until someone explained the EUR 500 gap. One thing to remember: A mismatch is not a minor data error. It is a break in the link between the information leg and the funds leg.

PAI-C037.agenda: Work through this case: USD 95,000 serial recall that tried to skip a bank. A USD 95,000 serial MT103 had to be recalled. The originator bank sent the recall straight to the beneficiary bank. It failed, because the bank that was skipped still held the funds. One thing to remember: A recall that skips a bank cannot work, because the bank that was skipped still holds the funds.

PAI-C038.agenda: Work through this case: USD 50,000 to a bank that is not on SWIFT. USD 50,000 had to reach a bank that is not a SWIFT member. The MT103 could not be sent to it directly. The payment sat for a day while the team argued whether it could be sent at all. One thing to remember: Non-membership does not stop the payment. It adds a step to the chain.

PAI-C039.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 65,000 MT103 arrived with field 57 empty. An MT103 for EUR 65,000 arrived with field 57 empty. It named no beneficiary bank. The receiving bank held it, unsure whether the payment was broken or meant to be handled in house. One thing to remember: Read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission.

PAI-C040.agenda: Work through this case: Parent paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries, and the screening landed on the wrong party. A parent company paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries with one MT101. The bank reported all three payments under the parent. Screening and accounting landed on the wrong party for every one of them. One thing to remember: Report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party.

PAI-C041.agenda: Work through this case: pacs.008 passed the clearing system. Where is the pacs.002?. A EUR 75,000 payment is sent through the clearing system to the beneficiary bank. The pacs.008 has gone. The beneficiary bank is waiting, the customer is asking, and nobody can say where the status reply is. One thing to remember: An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own.

PAI-C042.agenda: Work through this case: Debited, rejected, and the EUR 20,000 must come back. The originator bank deducts EUR 20,000 from the customer for a payment. The payment never reaches the beneficiary, because the clearing system rejected it. The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the money is sitting with the clearing system. One thing to remember: The customer sees a deduction with no payment, and the return is what makes the customer whole.

PAI-C043.agenda: Work through this case: The MT103 in a language nobody at the bank speaks. A EUR 15,000 payment is sent to a beneficiary bank in a country whose language is not English. The names and addresses in the message are in the local language. The operations team stares at the MT103 and wonders whether it can even be processed. One thing to remember: Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows the fields.

PAI-C044.agenda: Work through this case: Two banks, no account between them, EUR 40,000 still arrives. A customer wants to transfer EUR 40,000 to a bank that holds no account with the sending bank. There is no direct relationship, no nostro, no vostro. The payment still arrives. One thing to remember: The chain exists precisely to connect banks that have no direct relationship.

PAI-C045.agenda: Work through this case: We hold each other's accounts. Do we still need an intermediary?. The ordering bank and the beneficiary bank already hold accounts with each other. A EUR 90,000 international payment needs to move between them. The operations team still routes it through an intermediary, paying the fee and adding a day, out of habit. One thing to remember: The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved.

PAI-C046.agenda: Work through this case: One misspelt name in field 50, EUR 30,000 sent back. An MT103 for EUR 30,000 is sent to pay a supplier. The ordering customer name in field 50 is misspelt by one letter. The payment comes back. The supplier is unpaid, and the ordering customer cannot understand why one letter stopped EUR 30,000. One thing to remember: The return is therefore a data-quality failure, not a funds failure, and it is fixed by correcting the name and resending.

PAI-C047.agenda: Work through this case: Sent EUR 5,000, the employee received EUR 4,940. An ordering customer pays an employee EUR 5,000 with an MT103. An intermediary bank deducts its charges on the way. The employee receives EUR 4,940, and asks why EUR 60 is missing. The ordering customer has no answer, because nobody explained the charge rule before the payment was sent. One thing to remember: The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer rule matters before the payment is sent.

PAI-C048.agenda: Work through this case: Faster Payments is not SEPA with a different name. A team that knows SEPA is asked to build the flow for UK Faster Payments and BACS. They reach for the SEPA messages, because the concepts look the same: initiation, clearing, status reporting. Then the first GBP 25,000 payment fails, because the UK messages are not the SEPA messages. One thing to remember: An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK equivalent, rather than starting from nothing.

PAI-C049.agenda: Work through this case: The sterling leg went through CHAPS. The payment still had to leave the UK.. A cross-border payment needs sterling settlement in the UK, so the team routes the domestic leg through CHAPS. The CHAPS leg settles cleanly in central bank money. Then the payment stops, because nobody arranged the leg out of the UK, and the GBP 120,000 sits in London. One thing to remember: The cross-border leg itself still needs a correspondent or a scheme to carry the payment out of the UK, so CHAPS is one leg of the journey, not the whole journey.

PAI-C050.agenda: Work through this case: Faster Payments settles in seconds. Salaries still run on BACS.. Faster Payments settles a payment in seconds. Yet every month, a business with 2,000 employees pays salaries through BACS, a system older than most of its staff. The faster rail is there, and the business still chooses the slower one. One thing to remember: The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better.

PAI-C051.agenda: Work through this case: GBP 10,000 crossed borders with no SWIFT message at all. A customer sends GBP 10,000 to a beneficiary abroad. No SWIFT message is sent for either leg. The beneficiary is paid, on time, and the sending bank never touched the correspondent chain. One thing to remember: The model works because the provider nets the flows across its customers, and it is a different design from the correspondent banking chain.

PAI-C052.agenda: Work through this case: The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars.. A cover payment is sent, and the two legs carry different currencies. The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars. The operations team assumes one of them is wrong, and holds the EUR 150,000 payment. One thing to remember: The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can differ.

PAI-C053.agenda: Work through this case: Cancelled, recalled, disputed: three words, three different acts. A EUR 40,000 SEPA payment has gone wrong. The team argues about whether to cancel it, recall it, or dispute it, as if the three words meant the same thing. They do not, and picking the wrong one sends the wrong message. One thing to remember: The three are often confused because they all undo a payment, but they apply at different stages and they use different messages.

PAI-C054.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 40,000 MT103 STP stopped because one field used the wrong option. An MT103 STP for EUR 40,000 was sent to straight-through processing. It stopped for manual handling. One field had used an option other than A, and the system could not identify the bank. One thing to remember: Any other option leaves the bank to work out who the party is by hand.

PAI-C055.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 120,000 credited twice because a notification was sent as an MT103. EUR 120,000 was credited to a customer. The bank then sent an MT103 to report the credit. The receiving bank read it as an instruction to pay, and debited the account a second time. One thing to remember: An instruction is not a notification. Sending one as the other moves money twice.

PAI-C056.agenda: Work through this case: USD 75,000 MT103, and the intermediary was named in the wrong field. A USD 75,000 MT103 travelled through an intermediary bank. The intermediary was named in field 55 instead of field 56. The funds went for reimbursement through a bank that was never meant to handle them. One thing to remember: Field 56 names the intermediary. Field 55 names the reimbursement bank. Swap them and the funds go astray.

PAI-C057.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 90,000 debited, and the customer demanded proof that never came. EUR 90,000 was debited on an MT103 instruction. The customer asked for proof of the debit. No MT900 ever arrived, and the customer assumed the payment had failed. One thing to remember: A payment can settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged.

PAI-C058.agenda: Work through this case: USD 250,000, no account relationship, and the wrong route chosen. A Canadian bank had to pay USD 250,000 to a United States beneficiary. It held its dollars with Wells Fargo. The beneficiary held its account with Citibank New York. The bank sent a single serial MT103, and the payment had nowhere to settle. One thing to remember: Account relationships decide the route. No relationship means cover, not serial.

PAI-C059.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 45,000 MT103 arrived, and the team could not read it in MX. A EUR 45,000 payment arrives as an MT103. The bank's new ISO 20022 platform cannot map it. The team treats it as a new kind of payment and builds a new process for it. One thing to remember: The two families describe the same payments, so a team moving from MT to MX only has to learn the new names for the same legs.

PAI-C060.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 cover arrived EUR 150 short. An MT103 announced EUR 200,000. The cover arrived for EUR 199,850. An intermediary had taken its EUR 150 charge from the cover, and the beneficiary bank refused to credit the short amount. One thing to remember: A cover that arrives short of the announced amount is an exception, not a normal deduction.

PAI-C061.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 100,000 MT103 refused before it was even read. EUR 100,000 was due to a beneficiary. The MT103 was sent. The receiving bank's system refused it outright, before anyone read it, because no RMA existed for the sender. One thing to remember: The RMA is a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

PAI-C062.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 100,000 cover rejected even though the amounts agreed. A EUR 100,000 cover payment arrived with the amounts matching exactly. The beneficiary bank rejected it anyway. Sequence B of the MT202 COV did not mirror the MT103. One thing to remember: A mismatch in sequence B stops the funds even when the amounts agree.

PAI-C063.agenda: Work through this case: USD 175,000 with no SSI on file, and no one knew where to send it. USD 175,000 had to be paid to a beneficiary bank. The sending bank had no standing settlement instruction on file for that bank. No one knew which correspondent to send the funds to, and the payment waited. One thing to remember: Without an SSI, the sender must find the correspondent before the payment can move.

PAI-C064.agenda: Work through this case: USD 175,000 took the long route when a shorter one was on file. USD 175,000 was sent by the preferred route. It took three days. A shorter route was on file the whole time, and no one used it because the preferred instruction felt like an order. One thing to remember: Preferred is an option, not an order. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one will complain.

PAI-C065.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 80,000 sent to the wrong bank because field 57a was read the same way twice. EUR 80,000 was sent in a cover payment. The team read field 57a the way it works in a serial MT103. The funds went to the beneficiary bank's correspondent instead of the beneficiary bank. One thing to remember: The same field number points at a different bank in each leg.

PAI-C066.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 140,000 cover treated as a different kind of payment. A EUR 140,000 cover payment arrived. The team treated it as a different kind of movement from a serial payment. They built separate handling for it, and the cover leg stalled while they worked out rules that already existed. One thing to remember: The cover is the same serial mechanism carrying the funds leg of a customer payment.

PAI-C067.agenda: Work through this case: The beneficiary bank has a BIC that cannot receive messages. A EUR 65,000 payment is addressed to a bank whose BIC has the digit 1 in position 8. That marks it as non-connected: a SWIFT participant that cannot receive messages directly. The MT103 bounces, and the payment has nowhere to go. One thing to remember: The same pattern appears in bank groups where SWIFT communication is centralised at the head office and the head office forwards payments to subsidiaries and branches.

PAI-C068.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 200,000 MT103 sent by a corporate, and the chain rejected it. A corporate with its own BIC sends an MT103 for EUR 200,000 direct to a clearer. The clearer rejects it. The corporate's payment never enters the chain. One thing to remember: The rule is simple: corporates instruct, banks pay.

PAI-C069.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,200 in charges taken from a EUR 200,000 cover. A EUR 200,000 cover payment arrived EUR 1,200 short. An intermediary had taken its charges straight from the cover. An MT191 then arrived, claiming the same charges again. One thing to remember: An MT191 in a chain is the charges leg, not the payment itself.

PAI-C070.agenda: Work through this case: USD 60,000 sent in dollars, credited short after a double conversion. USD 60,000 was sent to a United States dollar account. The beneficiary was credited short. An intermediary had converted the payment twice on the way, and no one had asked for a conversion. One thing to remember: A payment sent in dollars to a dollar account that arrives short after a double conversion has gone wrong.

PAI-C071.agenda: Work through this case: The instruction was complete. The payment waited for the currency.. A customer instructs a EUR 80,000 payment in a foreign currency, with every field complete and every check passed. The payment does not move. Hours pass, and the instruction sits untouched, waiting for something the customer never sees. One thing to remember: A payment can therefore wait for the bank's currency position to be settled, even when the instruction itself is complete.

PAI-C072.agenda: Work through this case: USD 45,000 missing for two weeks, and everyone said to wait. USD 45,000 was sent to a supplier. Three days passed. Then a week. Then two. Everyone said to wait a little longer, while the supplier threatened to stop deliveries. One thing to remember: If the money has not arrived after two weeks, there is definitely a problem.

PAI-C073.agenda: Work through this case: Five returns in six weeks over one wrong field. A payment sent to Australia was returned five times over six weeks. Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A. The code was right there in the message, in field 72 and in field 52A, where the receiving bank could see it. It still came back, five times. One thing to remember: The beneficiary bank had also been taken over and its SWIFT code had changed, so the sender had to use the new code in field 57A before the payment could be applied.

PAI-C074.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000, and the beneficiary received less than the sender instructed. A sender instructed USD 100,000 with field 71A as BEN. The beneficiary was credited as if the instruction had been SHA. The beneficiary received less than the sender had instructed, and the bank copy showed a different code from the sender's instruction. One thing to remember: A bank copy that shows SHA where the sender instructed BEN is a discrepancy worth querying.

PAI-C075.agenda: Work through this case: USD 100,000 credit that did not match the equation. USD 100,000 was instructed. The beneficiary bank credited an amount that did not fit the charges equation. The operations team could not say whether the credit was right, because no one had checked the arithmetic. One thing to remember: 32A equals 33B plus 71G minus all the 71F charges. If the equation does not balance, something is wrong.

PAI-C076.agenda: Work through this case: Two legs, one payment, one thread: the UETR. A EUR 110,000 payment passes through a correspondent bank on its way abroad. The correspondent sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender, and the outgoing payment to the next bank. Two legs, two messages, and the reconciliation team cannot prove they are the same payment. One thing to remember: No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent.

PAI-C077.agenda: Work through this case: USD 500,000 nostro debited twice, because two banks read one account. A bank holds USD 500,000 in a nostro account with another bank. Both banks debit the same account for the same payment. The account goes short, and neither bank can say why. One thing to remember: There is only one account, and the two words simply say which side of it each bank is standing on.

PAI-C078.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 55,000 MT103 with a BIC stuffed into field 57B. A EUR 55,000 MT103 arrived with field 57B carrying a BIC. The receiving system could not route it straight through. The payment stopped for manual handling, because a BIC must never be passed in option B. One thing to remember: Option A is the default whenever a BIC is available.

PAI-C079.agenda: Work through this case: USD 80,000 to a US bank, and the clearing account was a guess. USD 80,000 was sent to a United States bank. Field 57A carried only the BIC. The receiving bank had several clearing accounts, and the operations team had to guess which one the payment was for. One thing to remember: The BIC alone is valid, but the UID removes any doubt about which clearing account should be used.

PAI-C080.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 70,000 payment read backwards, because nobody knew whose copy it was. An operations team investigates a EUR 70,000 payment. The stored message says it is an output message. The team concludes the bank received it. The bank had actually sent it. One thing to remember: An operator reading a stored message must therefore know which bank's copy it is looking at before deciding what block 2 means.

PAI-C081.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 110,000 debited from the wrong nostro account. A bank held three euro accounts with the same correspondent. EUR 110,000 was debited from the wrong one. Liquidity planning for the week broke, because field 53B had never named the account to debit. One thing to remember: Field 53B exists to say exactly which account must be debited.

PAI-C082.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 35,000 remittance reference that broke the 16-character limit. A EUR 35,000 payment carried a remittance reference in field 70. The reference after /RFB/ ran past 16 characters. The beneficiary's system could not match it, and the payment sat unreconciled. One thing to remember: A field 70 that repeats a code or overruns the limit is not a valid instruction.

PAI-C083.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 150,000 for two suppliers, squeezed into one MT103. A corporate must pay two suppliers EUR 150,000 in total. It sends one MT103 naming both. The second supplier is never paid, and the first is paid the full amount. One thing to remember: Trying to name two beneficiaries in a single MT103 is not possible, because the message has nowhere to put the second one.

PAI-C084.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 48,000 credited to the named beneficiary when it belonged further on. EUR 48,000 was sent to a named beneficiary. The funds were meant for an account beyond that beneficiary. The beneficiary bank credited the named beneficiary directly, because no instruction told it to look further. One thing to remember: Without the code, the bank has no instruction to look beyond the beneficiary named in field 59.

PAI-C085.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 55,000 valued a day late, because field 32A was read as the send date. A EUR 55,000 payment is sent on a Monday. The receiving bank makes the funds available on Wednesday. The beneficiary complains the value date was wrong, and the bank cannot explain it. One thing to remember: The currency in field 32A is the currency the receiver's bank actually receives, which is why it can differ from the currency the ordering customer instructed in field 33B.

PAI-C086.agenda: Work through this case: A future-dated MT103 for EUR 200,000, offered as security. An MT103 value-dated far in the future is presented to a bank, and the holder asks the bank to discount it. EUR 200,000, dated months ahead, offered as if it were money already promised. The bank declines, and the holder cannot understand why a payment instruction is not a promise. One thing to remember: If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer.

PAI-C087.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 160,000 late, and the MT103 copy proved nothing. EUR 160,000 was late by four days. The customer produced a copy of the MT103 as proof the money had moved. The copy proved nothing, and the bank could not trace the payment from it. One thing to remember: A copy of an MT103 on its own proves nothing about whether the money moved.

PAI-C088.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 22,000 ordering name rejected for spilling onto a second line. An ordering customer had a long company name. It ran over two lines in field 50K. The receiving bank rejected the MT103, saying a name must fit on one line. One thing to remember: The standard does not restrict the name to the first line, so a name split across lines is valid.

PAI-C089.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 140,000 cover arrived from a bank the announcement never named. An MT103 announced EUR 140,000 and named the correspondent that would send the cover. The cover arrived from a different bank entirely. The beneficiary bank could not match the two legs and would not credit the beneficiary. One thing to remember: The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree.

PAI-C090.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 70,000 MT103 with an IBAN but no name. An MT103 for EUR 70,000 arrived showing only the beneficiary's IBAN and address in field 59. No name at all. The beneficiary bank held the payment, unable to confirm the account belonged to the person the payment was meant for. One thing to remember: A missing name leaves the bank unable to confirm the account belongs to the right person.

PAI-C091.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 payment rejected because the name had one wrong character. A EUR 30,000 payment names a beneficiary with characters from their own script. The SWIFT network rejects the message outright. The beneficiary waits while the name is rewritten. One thing to remember: Names and addresses must be written with the characters the SWIFT set allows, or the message will not be accepted.

PAI-C092.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 85,000 MT101, and the two references pointed at two different owners. An MT101 for EUR 85,000 carried two references. Field 20 and field 21R showed different values. The operations team treated them as the same reference, and the reconciliation broke. One thing to remember: Field 20 belongs to the sender. Field 21R belongs to the ordering customer.

PAI-C093.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 120,000 paid by a parent, and the beneficiary thanked the wrong company. A parent company paid EUR 120,000 on behalf of a subsidiary. The beneficiary thanked the parent for a payment the subsidiary had really made. The subsidiary's own records showed nothing, because the beneficiary had been told the payment was from the subsidiary, and no one had read the field that said so. One thing to remember: The beneficiary sees the parent as the sender and the subsidiary as the party the payment is really from.

PAI-C094.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 95,000 drawn on the parent's account with no authority on file. A subsidiary instructed a EUR 95,000 payment from its parent company's account. The payment went through. No authorisation was on file, and the parent only found out when the statement arrived. One thing to remember: The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender is not the owner of the account being debited.

PAI-C095.agenda: Work through this case: One MT101 for EUR 500,000 across six banks, or six MT101s. A large corporate held accounts at six banks. It had to pay EUR 500,000 across them.
