The team prepared six separate MT101s, one per bank, and spent a day on work one message could have done. One thing to remember: The forwarding service is a genuine value-added service, and the concentrating bank charges for it.

PAI-C096.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 2 million payroll split across five MT101s, and one arrived late. A EUR 2 million payroll order was too big for one MT101. It was split across five messages, numbered 1 of 5 to 5 of 5. Message 4 arrived a day late, and the bank processed the rest without it. One thing to remember: Banks hold a chained message until every message in the chain has arrived.

PAI-C097.agenda: Work through this case: One MT101, three transfers, and the team built three processes. A corporate uses an MT101 to move EUR 40,000 between its own accounts. It uses the same message to pay a domestic supplier EUR 25,000. It uses it again to pay an overseas supplier EUR 60,000. The bank built three separate processes for the same message. One thing to remember: The same message therefore serves a corporate moving money between its own accounts and a corporate paying a supplier abroad.

PAI-C098.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 15,000 moved inside one bank, and the team still sent an MT103. EUR 15,000 moved between two accounts at the same bank. The team sent an MT101, then an MT103 as well. The MT103 went nowhere, because the payment never left the bank. One thing to remember: An MT103 is only required when the beneficiary's bank is different from the debtor's bank.

PAI-C099.agenda: Work through this case: The MT101 debited the customer. Where did the money sit?. A corporate customer sends an MT101 to pay its suppliers. The debtor's account is debited at once. But the suppliers are not paid yet, and the EUR 95,000 sits somewhere inside the bank, on an account nobody on the customer side can see. One thing to remember: The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement.

PAI-C100.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4 million statement, and the closing balance appeared twice. A EUR 4 million statement was split across several MT940 messages. An intermediate message carried tag 62F, the final closing balance. The client system treated the statement as finished and never generated the messages that followed. One thing to remember: There is only one closing balance for the whole statement.

PAI-C101.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4 million statement, and the intermediate balance dates did not match. A EUR 4 million statement arrived as several MT940s. The intermediate balance dates did not match the last entry in each message. The receiver questioned the statement, even though the balances themselves were right. One thing to remember: Receivers care most that the balances themselves are correct.

PAI-C102.agenda: Work through this case: A statement with 900 entries arrived as one MT940, and the rest never came. A statement with 900 entries was sent as a single MT940. Only the first entries arrived. The rest never came, because a single MT940 can carry only a limited number of entries. One thing to remember: The sequence number rises with each message, so the receiver can rebuild the order.

RUN3-001.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 22,000 SEPA payment rejected, and the beneficiary bank never knew it existed. A customer sends EUR 22,000 by SEPA credit transfer. The beneficiary calls to say nothing arrived. The beneficiary bank says it never saw the payment at all. One thing to remember: A fault spotted later, at the beneficiary bank itself, travels back as a pacs.004 return instead, because receipt has already happened by then.

RUN3-002.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 pacs.008 rejected, and the pacs.002 was booked as a payment. A EUR 50,000 pacs.008 was rejected. The pacs.002 that reported it was booked as a debit. The same payment was counted twice, and the books no longer balanced. One thing to remember: Booking the status report itself as a debit or credit would count the same payment twice.

RUN3-003.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 credit advice arrived in a format the receiver could not read. EUR 30,000 landed in a customer's account. The credit advice arrived as a camt.054. The receiver's system could only read MT900, so the customer was never told the money had arrived. One thing to remember: The receiving side must be ready to read either format when the advice arrives.

RUN3-004.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 12,000 SDD collection, silence for a week, and the team assumed it had failed. A EUR 12,000 direct debit collection went out as a pacs.007. A week passed in silence. The team assumed the collection had failed and sent it again, and the debtor was debited twice. One thing to remember: Silence after pacs.007 is normal, not failure.

RUN3-005.agenda: Work through this case: A pacs.004 arrived for EUR 50,000. Return or refund? Nobody could tell.. A pacs.004 for EUR 50,000 lands in the queue. The customer is waiting for an answer. The team cannot tell whether it is a return or a refund. One thing to remember: One message, two events. Read the initiator.

RUN3-006.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,200 collected with no mandate. The debtor claims it back, 12 months later.. A EUR 1,200 direct debit was collected every month. Twelve months later the debtor says there was never a valid mandate. The creditor is sure the 8 week refund window has closed. One thing to remember: 8 weeks needs a mandate. No mandate means 13 months.

RUN3-007.agenda: Work through this case: The MT950 arrived at noon. The team ignored it, and the day went wrong.. An MT950 for the account arrived at noon. The team treated it as tomorrow's statement and ignored it. By close of business the account was short and nobody knew why. One thing to remember: End of day is the default. Intraday is the agreement.

RUN3-008.agenda: Work through this case: Twenty transactions, one closing balance, and EUR 4,000 that did not add up.. An MT950 shows twenty transactions and a closing balance. The closing balance is EUR 4,000 out from the opening balance plus the entries. The team trusts the balance and moves on. One thing to remember: Field 61 repeats. Field 62F must add up.

RUN3-009.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 300,000 of advices, and the day-end statement disagreed. A corporate receives MT900 and MT910 advices all day for EUR 300,000 of movements. At day end the MT950 statement arrives. The statement total does not match the advices. One thing to remember: The two must reconcile, since the advices and the statement describe the same day from different angles.

RUN3-010.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 95,000 'confirmed' by instruction, but the credit never landed. A corporate is told EUR 95,000 is on its way. It treats the funds as received and releases goods. The credit never lands, because the instruction was never a posting. One thing to remember: On receipt, the owner can treat the funds as received, with certainty that the account was credited.

RUN3-011.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 75,000 moved. The statement shows it. Nobody knows why.. EUR 75,000 leaves the account. The MT940 shows the movement in field 61. The customer asks why it moved, and the team has no answer. One thing to remember: Field 61 shows money moved. Field 86 shows why.

RUN3-012.agenda: Work through this case: The treasurer thought EUR 2 million was available. It was not.. The treasurer reads the MT940 and sees EUR 2 million. A payment of EUR 2 million is released against it. The payment fails. The funds were never available that day. One thing to remember: 62M, 64 and 65 answer different questions.

RUN3-013.agenda: Work through this case: One MT940 never arrived. Nobody noticed for a week.. A week of statements arrives, and one MT940 is missing. Every transaction in the week still reconciles. The gap is found only when a customer disputes a payment from the missing day. One thing to remember: 28C is the first completeness check.

RUN4-001.agenda: Work through this case: USD 250,000 in the mirror, and zero in the real nostro. A bank needs USD 250,000 from its nostro account. Its own books, the mirror nostro, show USD 250,000 available. The real account at the other bank shows zero. One thing to remember: The mirror is kept in the real account's currency, so a USD nostro carries a USD mirror, and the mirror lets a bank work out what the real account should show.

RUN4-002.agenda: Work through this case: USD 10,000 in a French bank account, sitting in New York. A customer opens a USD 10,000 account with a bank in France. The customer checks the balance in Paris and sees USD 10,000. The actual dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA. One thing to remember: The correspondent then advises the French bank with an MT103, and only on that advice is the customer's account credited.

RUN4-003.agenda: Work through this case: USD 1 million nostro opened, and the first payment bounced on zero. A bank opens a new USD nostro and promises a USD 1 million payment from it the same day. The payment bounces. The account opened at zero, and nobody had funded it. One thing to remember: Where the bank already holds the currency in an account elsewhere, it simply instructs that bank to move the funds across, with no FX deal needed.

RUN4-004.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 8,000 sent 'on SWIFT' inside one country, and it never arrived. A customer sends EUR 8,000 to another account in the same country. The sending bank routes it on SWIFT. The payment never arrives, because the domestic system never sees it. One thing to remember: Local networks carry local payments and SWIFT carries payments that cross a border; the two worlds stay separate.

RUN4-005.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 100,000 of currency bought at the wrong price, because bid and ask were read backwards. A customer sells EUR 100,000 of foreign currency to the bank. They expect the higher price they saw quoted. They receive the lower one, and the bank keeps the difference. One thing to remember: A base currency exporter therefore watches the ask price, while a base currency importer watches the bid price.

RUN4-006.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 quoted the wrong way round, and the deal was priced in the wrong currency. A euro area bank quotes EUR/USD for a EUR 50,000 deal. The dealer prices the deal in dollars. The customer is charged in the wrong currency, and the deal has to be rebooked. One thing to remember: Keeping this the right way round matters, because the direct and indirect quotes describe the same pair from opposite sides.

RUN4-007.agenda: Work through this case: Dealer buys EUR/USD, expects dollars, gets euros. A dealer buys EUR/USD for EUR 500,000. The quote is 1.1635. He expects USD 500,000 to land in the account. Instead EUR 500,000 arrives, and USD 581,750 leaves it. One thing to remember: Every buy or sell in EUR/USD refers to EUR, the base currency, never to USD.

RUN4-008.agenda: Work through this case: A small bank sent EUR 500,000 abroad. It owned no correspondent anywhere.. A small bank needs to send EUR 500,000 to a supplier overseas. It holds no correspondent account in that currency. The payment still goes through, and the customer never asks how. One thing to remember: No correspondent of your own does not mean no route abroad.

RUN4-009.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 250,000 went to the wrong correspondent. The instructions were published years ago.. A EUR 250,000 payment is sent to a correspondent named in the payment engine. The correspondent no longer serves that currency. The payment is rejected, and the team discovers the instructions were never updated. One thing to remember: Published instructions go stale. Stored instructions go stale faster.

RUN4-010.agenda: Work through this case: The nostro showed EUR 1 million. The mirror showed something else.. A EUR 1 million credit lands on the nostro. The mirror account still shows the old balance. Treasury funds the day on a balance that is already wrong. One thing to remember: Mirror nostro moves transaction by transaction, never in a batch.

RUN4-011.agenda: Work through this case: A debit on the nostro, a credit on the mirror, and a team that read it backwards.. A EUR 300,000 debit hits the nostro. The mirror shows a credit of EUR 300,000. The team reports a gain, and treasury releases funds that were never there. One thing to remember: Mirror nostro always shows the opposite sign, by design.

RUN4-012.agenda: Work through this case: An FX deal for EUR 800,000 settled a day late. The trade was placed at 4pm.. A EUR 800,000 FX deal is traded late in the day. The team expects settlement on the tenor date. The funds arrive a day later, and a payment misses its value date. One thing to remember: After the cut-off, the trade day is tomorrow.

RUN4-013.agenda: Work through this case: Treasury bought EUR 5 million of FX. The nostro was still empty.. Treasury buys EUR 5 million to fund the day's payments. The mirror account shows the credit. The payments still fail, because the real nostro was never checked. One thing to remember: Treasury funds the nostro. The mirror only records it.

RUN4-014.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 400,000 crossed two countries. The money never left the country it started in.. A EUR 400,000 payment crosses borders between two banks. The SWIFT message travels internationally. The money itself settles locally, and the customer is charged the international price anyway. One thing to remember: Same country, same clearing. The message travels, the money stays local.

RUN4-015.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 150,000 payment to Germany went by MT202 COV. SEPA would have cost less.. A bank outside Europe instructs its French correspondent to pay EUR 150,000 to a German customer. The payment goes out as an MT202 COV. It arrives late and expensive, when SEPA would have done it faster and cheaper. One thing to remember: A euro leg in Europe belongs on SEPA, not on an MT202 COV.

RUN4-016.agenda: Work through this case: USD 20,000 in cash, handed over in Paris. The dollars were in New York.. A customer with a USD account in France asks for USD 20,000 in cash. The real dollars sit with the bank's correspondent in the USA. The branch hands over the cash anyway, and the account is debited the same amount. One thing to remember: Cash on hand is not the nostro. The debit is what balances it.

RUN4-017.agenda: Work through this case: French bank, German bank, dollars settled in New York. A French bank sends USD 500,000 to a German bank. Two European banks, an American currency, and a payment that never leaves the United States to settle. The treasurer expects a cross-border journey. Settlement takes one domestic step. One thing to remember: The sender finds the German bank's US correspondent in its Standing Settlement Instructions and states it in the MT103.

RUN4-018.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 600,000 of goods shipped. The documents were perfect. The bank paid nothing.. An exporter ships EUR 600,000 of goods under a documentary collection. The documents are in order and the buyer pays. The exporter then asks the collecting bank for the money, and the bank says it owes nothing. One thing to remember: A collection intermediates. It never promises payment.

RUN4-019.agenda: Work through this case: The letter of credit is issued. How does the money move?. A letter of credit for USD 250,000 is issued with an MT700. The documents are accepted. Now the beneficiary asks a simple question: how does the money move? The MT700 does not say. One thing to remember: Either route moves the funds under the credit once the documents have been accepted.

RUN4-020.agenda: Work through this case: France before SEPA: PNS, TBF, then CORE. Before SEPA, France already ran EBA systems for interbank payments alongside high value systems called PNS and TBF. Then SEPA arrived, and CORE, the retail clearing system, came after it to process XML format files. Old systems, new systems, and a market that changed underneath them, with a EUR 2 million retail file. One thing to remember: The market infrastructures changed greatly with the SEPA project, with old and new systems sitting side by side for a time.

RUN5-001.agenda: Work through this case: A customer paid GBP 250 by card. The merchant was paid before the customer was.. A customer pays GBP 250 by card on Monday. The merchant is paid at settlement on Tuesday. The customer pays the issuer weeks later, after the statement arrives. One thing to remember: The merchant is paid before the cardholder pays.

RUN5-002.agenda: Work through this case: GBP 1,000 spent on day one of the cycle. No interest for 45 days. Spent on day 29, far less.. A cardholder spends GBP 1,000 on the first day of the billing cycle. The statement arrives, and the cardholder pays in full 21 days later. No interest is charged, and the cardholder assumes every purchase gets 45 days free. One thing to remember: The free window depends on the day you spend, not the card you hold.

RUN5-003.agenda: Work through this case: A merchant pays GBP 100 in card fees. GBP 80 of it goes to a bank the customer never sees.. A merchant accepts a card payment and pays GBP 100 in merchant service charges. About GBP 80 of that goes to the issuer. The merchant asks the customer to cover it, and the customer refuses. One thing to remember: Interchange is the acquirer paying the issuer. The merchant bears it.

RUN5-004.agenda: Work through this case: Merchant pays per card sale, holder pays nothing per sale. A shop takes EUR 10,000 in card sales in a week. The owner expects the cardholders to carry the cost. Instead his own statement shows a charge on every single sale. The cardholders paid nothing per transaction. One thing to remember: The merchant pays per card sale. The holder pays nothing per transaction, only the annual fee and interest on an unpaid balance.

RUN5-005.agenda: Work through this case: RuPay: the scheme that is also the clearing house. A RuPay card payment of Rs 12,000 is made between two RuPay member banks. The issuer expects the transaction to clear through a separate clearing house. It does not. The scheme clears it itself. One thing to remember: When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, they clear their transactions through RuPay itself rather than through a separate clearing house.

RUN5-006.agenda: Work through this case: Monthly fee stays flat, processing fee follows every sale. A merchant pays EUR 200 a month to a processor. In a quiet month he still pays EUR 200. In a busy month the bill jumps to EUR 1,400. He complains the monthly fee has gone up. It has not. One thing to remember: The monthly fee is fixed. The processing fee is per transaction, so it rises and falls with volume.

RUN5-007.agenda: Work through this case: Two merchants, same volume, wildly different scheme bills. The cards were different.. Two merchants each process the same volume. One takes mostly one scheme's cards, the other the other scheme's. Their scheme bills look nothing alike, and neither merchant can explain why. One thing to remember: Same volume, different scheme bill. The card mix decides it.

RUN5-008.agenda: Work through this case: Cheque for EUR 25,000 clears, the paper never arrives. A customer deposits a cheque for EUR 25,000. The paper cheque is lost in the post on its way to the paying bank. The money still clears. The branch had expected the paper to be essential. It was not. One thing to remember: Cheque clearing now runs on images, not on the movement of paper.

RUN6-001.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 500,000 bill refused at first presentment, never returns. A seller presents a bill for EUR 500,000 for acceptance. The drawee refuses to sign. The seller plans to present it again next week. It will never return for a second acceptance. One thing to remember: Dishonour by non-acceptance describes refusal at first presentment, and the instrument never returns for a second acceptance.

RUN6-002.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 500,000 bill looks complete, the payee is not named. A bill for EUR 500,000 arrives for discounting. It names a bank, it looks official, it looks complete. The payee is not identified without ambiguity. The bill is not valid. One thing to remember: Payor and payee must both be identified without ambiguity, and the drawee must have accepted the instrument.

RUN6-003.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 500,000 payment on a blockchain network, and no one could say who settles it. A EUR 500,000 payment was sent across a blockchain payment network. One thing to remember: A shared ledger is not a settlement account.

RUN6-004.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,000,000 moves on a network where every bank is a node. EUR 1,000,000 moves between banks on a blockchain payment network. A customer asks which single system processed it. There is no single system. Every participant processed it. One thing to remember: Each institution operates as a node and takes a direct part in processing transactions.

RUN6-005.agenda: Work through this case: Blockchain for payments: four questions nobody has closed. A EUR 40,000 payment is proposed on a shared ledger, and the room is full of confidence. Then four questions land, and nobody in the room can answer any of them. Who sees the confidential fields? Who maintains the ledger? What format does it use? And can one network really span domestic and cross-border payments? One thing to remember: A single network spanning domestic and cross-border payments is achievable if the industry aligns on common standards.

RUN6-006.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 3,000 SEPA payment, customer blames the clearing system. A customer sends EUR 3,000 by SEPA credit transfer. A fee appears on the statement. The customer complains the clearing system charged him. The clearing system charged nothing. One thing to remember: The clearing system itself levies no interchange fee for processing the transaction.

RUN6-007.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 2 million day settled in three moves, not two thousand. Two banks exchanged 2,000 payments in a day, worth EUR 2 million in total. One thing to remember: Netting turns thousands of payments into a handful of positions.

RUN6-008.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 10,000,000 cleared but not settled, the team used the wrong word. EUR 10,000,000 in payments is cleared for the day. Operations reports the day as settled. It is not settled. The money has not moved. The team used the wrong word, and the wrong word hid the gap. One thing to remember: The term CSM is preferred because it makes the link between clearing and settlement explicit.

RUN6-009.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 4 million in net debits, and the settlement account was not a bank account. At the end of the clearing cycle, three banks owed a combined EUR 4 million in net debits. One thing to remember: The mechanism moves the money, it does not hold it.

RUN6-010.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 50,000 payment arrived after cut-off, and the cycle had already closed. A EUR 50,000 payment was sent five minutes after the clearing cut-off. One thing to remember: Cut-off is a wall, not a suggestion.

RUN6-011.agenda: Work through this case: Who sends the pacs.002? It depends on the rail.. A EUR 30,000 payment is sent, and the status reply never arrives. The team waits for the beneficiary bank to answer. On this rail, the beneficiary bank was never the one who answers. One thing to remember: On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them.

RUN6-012.agenda: Work through this case: A bank was EUR 3 million short at settlement, and the last check caught it. A bank ended the clearing cycle EUR 3 million short on its settlement account. One thing to remember: The last check before settlement is the one that saves the cycle.

RUN6-013.agenda: Work through this case: An indirect participant sent EUR 200,000 it did not have, and the direct participant paid for it. An indirect participant sent a EUR 200,000 debit through its direct participant. One thing to remember: Sponsoring a participant means carrying its risk.

RUN6-014.agenda: Work through this case: The indirect participant the central bank never sees. An indirect participant sends EUR 20,000 through its direct participant. The payment moves, the direct participant's account is debited, and the central bank watches it all happen. The central bank sees the direct participant, and nobody else. One thing to remember: The central bank sees only the direct participant, even when the payment belongs to the indirect participant, and oversees the direct participant as a whole rather than dealing with the indirect participant.

RUN6-015.agenda: Work through this case: Cycle 00 arrived. The indirect participant got nothing.. A direct participant signs up for scheme cycle 00. The cycle 00 transactions arrive, and the direct participant receives them all. The indirect participant, who never signed up, receives nothing, and its customers wait for payments that were never forwarded. One thing to remember: In SCT Inst some indirect participants connect directly to the mechanism and files move immediately, so no cycles exist there.

RUN6-016.agenda: Work through this case: Small bank sends EUR 5,000,000, has no direct link, still holds a central bank account. A small bank sends EUR 5,000,000 in payments every day. It has no direct connection to the settlement system. A customer assumes it holds no central bank account. Every bank holds one. One thing to remember: A bank stays indirect because connecting directly demands complex infrastructure, worthwhile only with enough volume.

RUN6-017.agenda: Work through this case: Two fields in pacs.008 tell you who really paid. A EUR 28,000 pacs.008 arrives, and the operations team cannot tell whether the payer was a direct participant or an indirect one. The answer is in the message, in two fields they never thought to read together. One thing to remember: Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant.

RUN6-018.agenda: Work through this case: A pacs.008 worth EUR 120,000 failed validation, and no one could say which rule it broke. A pacs.008 worth EUR 120,000 failed validation. One thing to remember: The MDR is the rulebook, not the team's memory.

RUN6-019.agenda: Work through this case: MT103 for EUR 250,000 cannot carry the data the MX can. A bank sends an MT103 for EUR 250,000. The beneficiary bank asks for remittance data the MT103 cannot carry. The payment arrives, the data does not. The format ran out of room. One thing to remember: MT is giving way to MX over time, yet both standards serve the same situations today.

RUN6-020.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 25,000 pacs.008 arrived, and the beneficiary waited until the next day. A EUR 25,000 pacs.008 arrived at the beneficiary bank on the settlement day. One thing to remember: The settlement day is the deadline, not the start of the window.

RUN6-021.agenda: Work through this case: One MT101 for EUR 60,000 in payables, and the ERP only spoke one language. A corporate had EUR 60,000 in payables to send: domestic transfers, a cheque payment, and a cross-border payment. One thing to remember: One format from the ERP, every payable covered.

RUN6-022.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 90,000 MT101 arrived at the concentrating bank, and the bank passed it on untouched. A corporate sent one MT101 worth EUR 90,000 to its concentrating bank, covering three destination banks. One thing to remember: Forward the instruction, do not rewrite it.

RUN6-023.agenda: Work through this case: Corporate sends MT101 for EUR 120,000, bank cannot read the extra data. A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 120,000. It wants to attach rich remittance data for its supplier. The MT101 has no room for it. The supplier is paid, but cannot match the payment. One thing to remember: ISO 20022 is far richer, so pain.001 holds far more information than MT101 can.

RUN6-024.agenda: Work through this case: TAG 21 never leaves the MT101. A corporate customer sends an MT101 for EUR 18,000, with TAG 21 filled in for its own reporting. The MT103 that follows carries no TAG 21. The customer calls to ask where their reference went, and the operations team cannot explain why it stopped. One thing to remember: TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain.

RUN6-025.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 15,000 SEPA payment on an MT101, and the bank said it could not carry it. A corporate sent a EUR 15,000 SEPA payment on an MT101. One thing to remember: MT101 can carry SEPA, but only as far as the information fits.

RUN6-026.agenda: Work through this case: An MT101 for EUR 40,000 arrived, and the debit and the money took different messages. A corporate sent an MT101 for EUR 40,000 to its bank. One thing to remember: MT101 instructs, MT103 carries.

RUN6-027.agenda: Work through this case: The cheapest rail that still arrives on time. A debtor bank must send a EUR 75,000 payment, and the treasurer wants the cheapest route. The cheapest route takes three days. The beneficiary needs the money tomorrow, and the cheapest rail that arrives on time is not the cheapest rail. One thing to remember: Routing rules set up in the payment engine apply that choice automatically, including for bulk MT101 and pain.001 files.

RUN6-028.agenda: Work through this case: MT101 sent for EUR 90,000, team waits for money that has not moved. A corporate sends an MT101 for EUR 90,000. The beneficiary bank waits for the money. Nothing arrives. The team is waiting on an instruction, not a payment. One thing to remember: MT101 instructs the payment, MT103 moves the money.

RUN6-029.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 600 mandate unused for three years, no one told the creditor. A creditor holds a mandate for EUR 600 a month. No collection runs under it for three years. On the fourth year the creditor sends a collection. It is rejected. The mandate expired silently. One thing to remember: The mandate simply lapses quietly after three years without use.

RUN6-030.agenda: Work through this case: E-mandates need a router. It does not have to be a CSM.. A creditor bank needs to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks across the SEPA area. The team assumes only a clearing and settlement mechanism can do it. The mandate for EUR 2,000 a month waits while they look for a CSM to hire. One thing to remember: The operating model defines two services for this: routing and validation, each delivered by a service provider, and either service can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM.

RUN6-031.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 3,000 direct debit arrived with no mandate, and the creditor bank paid it anyway. A pacs.003 direct debit for EUR 3,000 arrived at the creditor bank. One thing to remember: No obligation to check does not mean no risk.

RUN6-032.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 15,000 on-us transfer built on a different standard, breaks reconciliation. A bank moves EUR 15,000 between two accounts it holds itself. A team builds it on a different message standard from interbank payments. Reconciliation breaks, because the two standards do not line up. The payment never left the bank. One thing to remember: An on-us transfer travels on the same message standards as any other payment.

RUN7-001.agenda: Work through this case: A store voucher for R1,000 shoes worked, and the customer asked why it could not pay anywhere. A customer bought shoes worth R1,000 with a clothing store voucher. One thing to remember: A closed loop payment works inside its loop, and only there.

RUN7-002.agenda: Work through this case: A customer tried to pay EUR 10,000 with a promissory note, and the bank said no. A customer walked into a bank with a promissory note for EUR 10,000 and asked to pay with it. One thing to remember: Legal does not mean accepted.

RUN7-003.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 2,000 card payment through a wallet arrived in seconds, but the bank account was debited two days later. A customer paid EUR 2,000 by card through a wallet. One thing to remember: The same payment can look instant and delayed at the same time.

RUN7-004.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 5,000 wallet transfer failed, and the money was in the other account all along. A customer tried to move EUR 5,000 from a mobile wallet to a bank account. One thing to remember: Same owner, different accounts, different balances.

RUN7-005.agenda: Work through this case: A card worked in every SEPA country, but the cash still did not travel. A traveller used a bank card in five SEPA countries on one trip. One thing to remember: Cards finished, cash still catching up.

RUN7-006.agenda: Work through this case: Cancelling a SEPA payment: the right message each time. A customer asks to cancel a EUR 12,000 SEPA payment, and the team reaches for camt.056. The payment is a direct debit, not a credit transfer. The camt.056 goes nowhere, and the debit is collected anyway. One thing to remember: Corporations may also send camt.055 through their bank to cancel a pain.008: an unexecuted transaction is cancelled, while an executed one is reversed by the bank with pacs.007 instead.

RUN7-007.agenda: Work through this case: An MT103 for EUR 75,000 was sent to the wrong application, and the payment vanished from view. A bank sent an MT103 for EUR 75,000 to another bank. One thing to remember: The right network, the wrong application.

RUN7-008.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 8,000 foreign cheque, the bank cannot tell what type it is. A customer deposits a cheque for EUR 8,000 from another country. The deposit slip says "foreign cheque". The bank cannot process it. Foreign is not a complete type. One thing to remember: The word foreign only says where the cheque comes from, and the type must be named as well.

RUN7-009.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 1,500 card payment was guaranteed, and the merchant asked who actually paid for that promise. A merchant accepted a EUR 1,500 card payment. One thing to remember: Interchange pays for the guarantee, not the network.

RUN7-010.agenda: Work through this case: USD 2,000,000 trade, no rule says which instrument comes first. A buyer and seller agree a USD 2,000,000 trade. The buyer asks which instrument starts it, letter of credit or bank guarantee. There is no rule that answers that. The team waits for a rule that does not exist. One thing to remember: Greater appetite for security on both sides calls for more sophisticated payment techniques.

SCN-01.agenda: Work through this case: One payment, two amounts: USD 100,000 in, USD 99,400 out. A customer instructs a cross-border payment of USD 100,000. One thing to remember: The amount gap always has a rule behind it. Compare pacs.008 against what clearing settled.

SCN-02.agenda: Work through this case: The payment settled, but Treasury funded from a stale screen. A payment settles correctly. One thing to remember: The payment settled, but the bank was making funding decisions from outdated data.

SCN-03.agenda: Work through this case: One extra hour at the branch, and the RTGS payment bounced. A branch cut-off for RTGS is extended by one hour. One thing to remember: A cut-off is a contract, not a clock setting. Moving it means re-validating everything that depends on it.

SCN-04.agenda: Work through this case: A pacs.008 for EUR 60,000 was rejected. The team sent a pacs.004 to fix it.. A pacs.008 for EUR 60,000 is rejected before settlement. The pacs.002 carries status RJCT and a reason code. The team opens a return, even though no money has moved. One thing to remember: RJCT before settlement means repair, not return.

SCN-05.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 90,000 payment settled, then failed. The team tried to fix it with a status report.. A EUR 90,000 payment settles, then turns out to be wrong. The team sends another pacs.002 to fix it. Nothing moves, because a status report never moves money. One thing to remember: After settlement, only a return moves money.

SCN-06.agenda: Work through this case: Credited already? The recall is only a request. A EUR 18,000 payment has been credited to the wrong beneficiary. The sender bank wants the money back. It has no power to command it back. It can only ask. One thing to remember: A rejection leaves the sender with a commercial claim outside the payment rails, so the camt.056 must go out fast, while the funds are still there.

SCN-07.agenda: Work through this case: Two legs settled, two returns needed. A EUR 60,000 cover payment settles twice over: the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover that moved funds between correspondents. The customer payment is returned. The team closes the case, and the nostro ledger still disagrees by EUR 60,000. One thing to remember: Both legs post to the Nostro ledger, so reconciliation must pair all four messages, instruction, cover, return of instruction, and return of cover.

SCN-08.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 40,000 credited to a closed account. The beneficiary bank sent it back itself.. EUR 40,000 is credited to an account, then found to be closed. The beneficiary bank does not wait to be asked. It sends the money back itself, and the sender waits for a recall that never comes. One thing to remember: The beneficiary bank can send the money back itself.

SCN-09.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 70,000 held on a party name that looked wrong. The team rejected it outright.. A EUR 70,000 payment arrives with ultimate debtor details that look wrong, but are not proven wrong. The team rejects it outright. A legitimate payment dies, and the customer loses a supplier deadline. One thing to remember: Uncertain means ask, not kill.

SCN-10.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5,000 debited, failed, and the books disagree. A 5,000 euro SEPA credit transfer debited the account. It failed between the engine and clearing. The customer is EUR 5,000 down, the books say the payment went, and reality says it never arrived. One thing to remember: Establish the true state across core banking, payment engine, ISO 20022 messages, clearing, settlement and accounting, and rule out duplicates before touching anything.

SCN-11.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 110,000 payment timed out. The team retried it blind, and paid twice.. A EUR 110,000 payment times out mid-chain. Nobody knows whether it settled. The team retries it, and the beneficiary is paid twice. One thing to remember: A timeout is an unknown, not a failure.

SCN-12.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 180,000 was covered but never credited. The instruction and the money took different roads.. A EUR 180,000 cross-border payment is sent by cover. The pacs.009 cover arrives, but the pacs.008 instruction does not. The beneficiary bank cannot credit the customer, and the money sits unmatched. One thing to remember: Instruction one way, money another. Both must arrive.

SCN-13.agenda: Work through this case: USD 75,000 from India to the USA vanished between hops. The tracker showed the last good hop.. A USD 75,000 payment leaves India for the USA. It never reaches the beneficiary. The team searches the whole chain at once, and finds nothing. One thing to remember: Trace leg by leg, from the last good hop.

SCN-14.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 95,000 payment timed out mid-chain. The recall was the brake, and it was pulled too late.. A EUR 95,000 payment times out mid-chain with its state unknown. The team debates whether to recall it. By the time the recall goes out, the credit has completed, and the recall cannot undo it. One thing to remember: A recall is a brake, not a reverse gear.

SCN-15.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 40,000 payment stopped, but which stop is it?. A customer asks to stop a EUR 40,000 payment. Operations logs it as a return. The payment had not settled yet, so there was nothing to return. The stop fails, and the money still moves. One thing to remember: Reject, return and cancellation are separated by one boundary: settlement.

SCN-16.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 55,000 returned, and the team treated it as a cancellation. It was a payment in reverse.. EUR 55,000 settles to the wrong beneficiary. A pacs.004 comes back through the chain. The team files it as a cancellation, with no charges, no references and no controls. One thing to remember: A return is a payment in reverse.

SCN-17.agenda: Work through this case: pacs.002 says rejected, EUR 40,000 still sits in the account. A EUR 40,000 payment is rejected. The team waits for the money to come back. Nothing comes back, because nothing ever left. They were waiting on a status report, not a payment. One thing to remember: A pacs.002 reports a status and moves nothing. A pacs.004 moves money back.

SCN-18.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 300,000 payment went quiet for a day. Nobody owned it, and nobody called the customer.. A EUR 300,000 payment passes its expected window with no status update. It sits on a dashboard, flagged but unowned. The deadline passes, the customer calls first, and the team starts from zero. One thing to remember: A flag without an owner is decoration.

SCN-19.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 130,000 payment went missing. The investigation started with a free-text email.. A EUR 130,000 payment goes missing and a customer complains. The investigation starts with a free-text email to the correspondent, with no references. Days pass, the case has no deadline, and the backlog grows. One thing to remember: Investigations run on rails, not instinct.

SCN-20.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 60,000 cross-border payment, six messages, one missing link. A customer sends EUR 60,000 abroad. The bank can see the payment left. It cannot say where it is now. The team is reading one message, not the chain. One thing to remember: Every step can branch into an exception with its own message, so the message set is the lifecycle.

SCN-21.agenda: Work through this case: Small breaks, ignored for months, added up to a USD 2 million surprise before the audit.. Small uncleared items pile up for months, each one looking harmless. Volumes rise, and a USD 2 million discrepancy appears just before an audit. The team had optimised the manual workaround, never the process that created the breaks. One thing to remember: Fix the process that creates the break, not the workaround.

SCN-22.agenda: Work through this case: Duplicate payouts: 90 percent recovered, 10 percent still missing. A payout batch fires twice, and suppliers are paid double. The team starts diagnosing the cause while the batch is still running. More duplicates are being created while they investigate, and 10 percent of the duplicated value is still missing. One thing to remember: The cause here was a retry firing twice after a timeout through an idempotency gap, and the permanent fix is idempotency keys on every payout plus real-time reconciliation flagging double credits.

SCN-23.agenda: Work through this case: A surname parked a 28 million dirham letter of credit for 8 working days.. A legitimate 28 million dirham letter of credit is stopped by a fuzzy sanctions match on a common surname. It sits parked for 8 working days. The screening team treats every alert the same, and the real business waits. One thing to remember: Most alerts are false positives. Triage by risk, not by queue order.

SCN-24.agenda: Work through this case: A USD 500,000 payment matched the sanctions list. The funds froze, and the trail mattered.. A USD 500,000 payment matches a name on the sanctions list. The payment is held at once and no funds move. The analyst wonders whether to release it quietly and move on. One thing to remember: A list match stops the payment. The trail proves the decision.

SCN-25.agenda: Work through this case: USD 85,000 left a customer's account. The bank called it authorised, and refused to pay it back.. A scammer posing as a bank representative wins remote access to a victim's computer. USD 85,000 leaves from the victim's own login and device. The bank classifies the payment as authorised, and the customer loses everything. One thing to remember: Valid payment, deceived customer. Authorised is not the same as safe.

SCN-26.agenda: Work through this case: P1 hit mobile banking, service back in 40 minutes, cause still unknown. A P1 incident struck mobile banking, fund transfers and ATMs. Transfers worth EUR 500,000 queued while customers waited. The war room restored service in about 40 minutes. The cause was still unknown. One thing to remember: Restored is not resolved.

SCN-27.agenda: Work through this case: Acknowledged, then lost: the broker died before replication. A payment is charged once. The retry charges it a second time. Nothing alerted, because each component behaved exactly as designed, and the failure lived in the interaction between them. One thing to remember: Fix the guarantees, acks=all with idempotent producers and dedup keys on every payment, add the transactional outbox pattern, and keep reconciliation as the backstop.

SCN-28.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 payment timed out, the fault was made at the very first step. A payment of EUR 30,000 timed out. The team blamed the network and the receiving bank. The fault was made at the very first step, when the message was created. One thing to remember: The symptom is downstream. The cause is upstream.

SCN-29.agenda: Work through this case: One empty parameter passed QA, staging and a small rollout. At full volume it broke everything.. A new flow passes QA, staging and a small rollout. At full volume a parameter everyone assumed was always filled comes back empty. Partner API calls fail, reconciliation mismatches, and the fix takes three hours while trust takes far longer to rebuild. One thing to remember: The parameter everyone assumed was filled is the one that breaks you.

SCN-30.agenda: Work through this case: GBP 125,000 left. No trace, no rejection, no return.. A 125,000 pound international payment left the sender. It never arrived. No rejection, no return, no confirmation. The beneficiary is waiting, the sender is asking, and the payment has vanished from every screen that matters. One thing to remember: Never re-send until the original is accounted for, because a duplicate is worse than a delay, and keep both sender and expectant beneficiary updated.

SCN-31.agenda: Work through this case: One mule account looked like a case. Linked together, they were a network moving millions.. Small transfers arrive from unrelated sources into one account. The funds leave within minutes of credit, and almost nothing is retained. The team treats the account as a single case, while the network keeps moving. One thing to remember: Read the network, not the case.

SCN-32.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 250,000 held for three days on a name mismatch. The status said Pending, and the team read it as rejected.. A EUR 250,000 payment sits uncredited for three days. The pacs.002 shows Pending, and the team treats it as a rejection. The beneficiary bank is holding the payment, waiting for the name to be corrected. One thing to remember: Pending is a hold, not a rejection.

SCN-33.agenda: Work through this case: Payments fail only at 11 AM, EUR 90,000 queue stuck. Every day at 11 AM, payments start timing out. A queue of EUR 90,000 in payments stalls. By noon everything works again. The team keeps fixing the code. The code is fine. One thing to remember: Peak-only failures mean capacity. All-day failures mean code or data.

SCN-34.agenda: Work through this case: Processed, timed out, then paid twice. A core banking API processes a EUR 35,000 transaction. Then it times out before responding. The caller, believing it failed, re-submits a completed transaction, and the customer is debited twice. One thing to remember: The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first.

SCN-35.agenda: Work through this case: The bank moved its cut-off. The fintech kept sending on the old one, and every payment settled late.. A bank moves its transaction cut-off time and tells no one. The fintech keeps sending on the old settlement window. Requests are accepted, then processed in a later cycle, with green dashboards and no errors anywhere. One thing to remember: Most incidents are coordination failures, not bugs.

SCN-36.agenda: Work through this case: UPI debit landed. The credit never did.. A UPI payment is made for Rs 45,000. The sender account is debited. The receiver is never credited, and the credit acknowledgement timed out somewhere between the two banks. One thing to remember: The mitigations are globally unique transaction references, idempotent processing at each bank, compensating transactions such as auto-reversal, and settlement-level balancing at the end of the cycle.

WC-01.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 180,000 sent, the instruction arrived, the money did not. A supplier in another country was owed EUR 180,000. The payment left the ordering bank on Monday morning. By Friday, the supplier had received nothing. The ordering bank insisted the money had been sent. One thing to remember: An instruction without its cover is a promise the beneficiary bank cannot keep.

WC-02.agenda: Work through this case: Tracker said credited, the beneficiary saw nothing for a week. A customer sent USD 95,000 to a family member abroad. The gpi tracker showed the payment as credited. The family member checked the account twice a day for a week. No money ever arrived. One thing to remember: Credited at the bank is not the same as available to the beneficiary.

WC-03.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 42,000 returned 11 days later, after it was spent. A beneficiary received EUR 42,000 on a Monday. By the following week, the money was spent. Eleven days after the credit, a pacs.004 return arrived. The bank debited the account, and the balance went negative. One thing to remember: Available on the statement is not the same as beyond return.

WC-04.agenda: Work through this case: OUR charges, USD 60 deducted anyway, nobody owned it. A corporate customer paid USD 60,000 to an overseas supplier. The customer chose OUR, so the supplier would receive the full amount. The supplier received USD 59,940. The customer was also charged a fee at the sending bank, and nobody could explain the missing USD 60. One thing to remember: OUR is an instruction to the chain, not a guarantee the chain will obey.

WC-05.agenda: Work through this case: FX converted at the wrong leg, USD 1,800 vanished overnight. A customer sent EUR 100,000 to be paid in US dollars. The rate on the morning of the instruction was agreed and confirmed. The beneficiary received USD 1,800 less than the confirmed figure. The bank said the rate had moved. The customer said the rate had been agreed. One thing to remember: The leg that converts owns the rate, and the delay that moves it.

WC-06.agenda: Work through this case: False positive froze a hospital payment for three days. A payment of EUR 75,000 was sent to pay for urgent medical equipment. The payment never left the bank. A sanctions screening match froze it in the queue. The hospital waited, and the equipment supplier waited, while the case sat with compliance. One thing to remember: Holding a payment is also a decision, and it has a cost.

WC-07.agenda: Work through this case: Nostro shortfall at cut-off, GBP 250,000 queued, deal failed. A payment of GBP 250,000 had to settle on Friday. The funds were debited from the customer on Friday morning. The payment never left the bank that day. On Monday, the deal it was funding had already failed. One thing to remember: A queued payment the customer does not know about is a broken promise, not a delay.

WC-08.agenda: Work through this case: Timeout, resend, EUR 30,000 paid twice. A supplier was owed EUR 30,000. The supplier was paid twice. The customer was debited twice. Both payments looked correct, and both had different tracking references. One thing to remember: A timeout is a missing answer, not a failed payment. Ask before you resend.

WC-09.agenda: Work through this case: Field 70 truncated the invoice data, USD 120,000 unallocated. A payment of USD 120,000 arrived in full and on time. The beneficiary could not match it to any invoice. The remittance information had been cut in half. Three teams spent a week arguing about whose system had lost the data. One thing to remember: A payment without its remittance data arrives as money and lands as a mystery.

WC-10.agenda: Work through this case: Account existed, IBAN rejected three times, check digits wrong. A payment of EUR 55,000 was rejected three times. The reject reason said the account number was invalid. The beneficiary insisted the account existed, and it did. Both sides were certain, and both sides were right. One thing to remember: Validating the format is not the same as finding the account.

WC-11.agenda: Work through this case: 40 percent owned by a listed person, block or release?. A payment of USD 200,000 was ready to go to a long standing trading partner. A routine review found the partner was 40 percent owned by a listed person. The payment was not clearly blocked, and not clearly safe. Three options sat on the table: block, release, or escalate, and each one carried a risk. One thing to remember: Not on the list is not the same as safe. Ownership and control decide.

WC-12.agenda: Work through this case: Cut-off passed in another time zone, a day of interest lost. A customer instructed a payment of EUR 500,000 late in the afternoon. The payment was value dated the next day. The customer lost a full day of interest on half a million euro. The bank said the cut-off had passed. The customer said the instruction was sent in time. One thing to remember: A cut-off the customer cannot see is a surprise, not a rule.

WC-13.agenda: Work through this case: Route closed mid-flight, 40 payments stranded, no plan. A correspondent bank withdrew from a payment route on a Tuesday. Forty payments were already in transit on that route. Some were held, some were returned, and some simply vanished from the tracker. Customers with deadlines that week had no idea their route no longer existed. One thing to remember: A route exit is foreseeable. A rerouting plan made after it happens is already late.

WC-14.agenda: Work through this case: Rs 480 crore stood still while three banks waited for each other. A busy settlement morning, and the RTGS queue stopped moving. Three banks each had a large payment ready to send. Each bank was waiting for money to arrive before it could pay. Nobody had failed. The queue had tied itself in a circle. One thing to remember: In RTGS, liquidity is about sequence and timing, not just the total balance.

WC-15.agenda: Work through this case: Forty seconds late, and 4,200 salaries waited a full day. The salary file was ready. The approvals were done. The upload finished forty seconds after the cut-off. That was enough to move 4,200 salary credits to the next working day. The rail was still running. The product window was not. One thing to remember: A cut-off is a customer promise in disguise, so it must be visible before it bites.

WC-16.agenda: Work through this case: Rs 62 crore short, and a same-day promise already made. The corporate customer had been promised same-day credit. The settlement account did not have the funds to keep that promise. Treasury saw a liquidity problem. Operations saw a queue. The customer saw a promise. One of the three views had to give way before the end of the day. One thing to remember: Never promise a settlement time that the settlement account has not confirmed.

WC-17.agenda: Work through this case: Rs 86,000 debited, and the status stayed on processing for three days. The customer paid a supplier from a mobile app. The money left the account within seconds. The supplier said no payment had arrived. For three days the only status anyone could show was processing. One thing to remember: Processing is not a status, it is an unresolved payment that needs an owner and a deadline.

WC-18.agenda: Work through this case: Two taps, two debits, and every party pointed at another party. The first tap seemed to fail, so the customer tapped again. Both payments settled. The merchant was paid twice for one purchase. Getting one payment back took longer than making both of them. One thing to remember: A retry without a status check is a second payment, not a second attempt.

WC-19.agenda: Work through this case: A blurred cheque image, a wrong return code, a customer blamed. A supplier cheque for Rs 3,80,000 was deposited on a Monday. It came back unpaid two days later. The return memo said insufficient funds. The account had held more than enough funds all week. One thing to remember: A return reason code is a fact about the customer, not a back office label.

WC-20.agenda: Work through this case: Seven debits of Rs 12,400, and a mandate the customer denied. Seven monthly debits left the account, each for Rs 12,400. The customer said the mandate had never been signed. The creditor said the mandate was valid and the service had been used. The bank sat between a customer demanding a refund and a creditor demanding payment. One thing to remember: A mandate is only as good as the consent evidence behind it.

WC-21.agenda: Work through this case: One bad record in 12,000, and a file rejected whole. A bulk debit file held 12,000 records. One record carried a mandate reference that did not exist. The system rule said reject the whole file. Rejecting it would delay 11,999 collections that were perfectly valid. One thing to remember: Rejection granularity is a business decision, not a system default.

WC-22.agenda: Work through this case: The clearing house stopped on month-end, banks settled alone. On the last working day of the month, the clearing house went down. Millions of items were already queued. Salaries, pensions and supplier payments all depended on that day value date. Waiting meant missing month-end. The fallback meant settling without the centre. One thing to remember: A fallback that has never been rehearsed is a hope, not a plan.

WC-23.agenda: Work through this case: USD 4.2 million paid, and the other leg never arrived. The bank paid its side of a foreign exchange deal on time. The counterparty failed before paying its side. The bank had sent USD 4.2 million and received nothing. The loss was not a market move. It was the full principal. One thing to remember: In foreign exchange, paying first without payment versus payment is lending the full principal unsecured.

WC-24.agenda: Work through this case: An urgent USD 18,000 supplier payment took the wrong rail. The supplier deadline was that evening, and the payment was urgent. The operator chose the cheapest rail, because it said instant. The payment could not reach an overseas account at all. By the time the mistake was clear, hours had been lost. One thing to remember: The right rail is decided by destination, currency and deadline, not by the fee on the screen.

WC-25.agenda: Work through this case: A structured address the legacy system could not read at all. The migration went live on a Monday, with structured addresses. By Tuesday the repair queue held 1,800 payments. Straight-through processing fell by a third in a single day. The messages were correct. The systems downstream were not ready. One thing to remember: A migration is finished when every downstream system can read the new format, not when the first message goes out.

WC-26.agenda: Work through this case: 250,000 settled at the central bank, in the wrong currency. The instruction said EUR 250,000. The settlement account was debited in USD 250,000. The numbers matched. The currency did not. By then it had settled in central bank money. One thing to remember: Currency is part of the amount, so a payment with the wrong currency is a wrong payment, even when the number matches.

WC-27.agenda: Work through this case: Nine days, one pacs.028, and no pacs.029: the payment nobody could find. A customer sent EUR 18,500 to a supplier overseas. The money left the account on a Monday. By Friday, the supplier said nothing had arrived. The customer called every day after that. Nine days passed, and nobody could say where the money was. One thing to remember: An investigation sent is not an investigation answered.

WC-28.agenda: Work through this case: The camt.056 recall arrived, but the money had already been withdrawn. A corporate customer sent EUR 40,000 to the wrong supplier account. The error was spotted within the hour. A camt.056 recall was sent the same morning. The beneficiary bank replied that the funds had already been withdrawn. The money was gone, and the recall had nothing left to recall. One thing to remember: A recall asks for the money back. It does not bring it back.

WC-29.agenda: Work through this case: The scam victim asked for a recall, and the account was already empty. A customer was tricked into sending GBP 22,000 to a fraudster. The payment was authorised by the customer, in the bank's app. By the time the customer realised it was a scam, the money had moved on. The bank was asked to recall it. The beneficiary account was already empty. One thing to remember: A recall after the money is gone is recovery, not reversal.

WC-30.agenda: Work through this case: The wrong person was credited EUR 25,000, and the bank could not take it back. A payment of EUR 25,000 was credited to the wrong account. The intended beneficiary never received it. The account that received it belonged to a different customer of the same bank. The operations team asked for the funds to be debited back. The answer was no, not without the account holder's consent. One thing to remember: Crediting the wrong account does not give the bank the right to debit it.

WC-31.agenda: Work through this case: The same bulk file was paid twice, and nobody noticed until the second debit. A corporate customer uploaded a bulk payment file on a Monday morning. The file contained 240 salary payments. The upload timed out, so the customer uploaded it again. Both uploads were processed. Every employee was paid twice, and the customer discovered it from its own staff. One thing to remember: A file processed twice is not a duplicate. It is two payments.

WC-32.agenda: Work through this case: The treasurer asked for yesterday's value date, and the answer was not simple. A corporate treasurer called on a Tuesday morning. A payment of EUR 2,000,000 should have gone out on Monday, but it had not. The treasurer asked for the value date to be set to Monday. The difference was one day of interest, and a covenant report that would look different. One manager had to decide whether to agree. One thing to remember: A value date is a fact about when money moved, not a field to be edited.

WC-33.agenda: Work through this case: The pacs.002 said rejected, but the debit had already happened. A customer sent EUR 12,000 to a supplier. A pacs.002 status report came back saying the payment was rejected. The customer sent the payment again. The supplier was paid twice. The first payment had never been rejected at all. The debit had already happened. One thing to remember: A status report describes the ledger. It does not replace it.

WC-34.agenda: Work through this case: The case was closed as resolved, and the money was still missing. A customer reported a missing payment of EUR 9,800. An investigation case was opened, and a pacs.028 was sent. Three days later, the case was marked resolved. The customer had not been paid, had not been contacted, and had not agreed to anything. The money was still missing. The queue simply looked better. One thing to remember: A case is resolved when the money is found, not when the queue is cleared.

WC-35.agenda: Work through this case: The branch said sent, operations said queued, and the customer heard both. A customer sent a payment from a branch at 3.40 in the afternoon. The branch officer said it had been sent. The customer called the contact centre an hour later and was told it was queued. The customer called the branch again and was told, again, that it had been sent. The payment went out the next morning, after the. One thing to remember: Sent must mean one thing, everywhere, or it means nothing to the customer.

WC-36.agenda: Work through this case: Four hundred repairs, two people, and an SLA breach by Friday. On a Monday morning, the repair queue held 400 items. Two analysts were available to work it. The SLA for the oldest items expired on Friday. Some items were worth millions. Some were worth very little. Every item could not be fixed in time, so the team had to choose what would break. One thing to remember: Triage is a decision about what breaks first, so it must be a rule, not a habit.

WC-37.agenda: Work through this case: The screen said pending, but the payment had already settled. A customer checked the status of a EUR 60,000 payment. The screen said pending. The customer waited, called, and was told it was still pending. The beneficiary confirmed the funds had arrived two days earlier. The payment had settled. Only the status had not. One thing to remember: Status must come from settlement evidence, not from a mapping table.

WC-38.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 0.01 nostro break hid a EUR 100,000 error. At the end of the month, the nostro reconciliation showed a break of EUR 0.01. The team noted it, and moved on. One cent is not worth chasing. Three weeks later, a EUR 100,000 payment was found to have settled to the wrong account. The one cent break had hidden it. Two errors had netted off, and the net looked like. One thing to remember: Breaks that net to nearly nothing can still hide a very large error.

WC-39.agenda: Work through this case: Pay urgently, with no value date: who decides what urgent means. A customer sent an instruction to the bank: pay urgently. The instruction named the beneficiary and the amount, EUR 75,000. It gave no value date and no definition of urgent. The payment went out as a next day payment. The customer had meant same day, and the supplier's deadline was missed. One thing to remember: Urgency is a value date, not a feeling. If it is not specified, it must be confirmed.

WC-40.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 1,850 approved at the hotel, and the clearing never arrived. A guest checked out of a hotel on a Friday morning. The card payment of EUR 1,850 had been approved four days earlier. The hotel never sent the clearing record. The money stayed in limbo for three weeks, and the customer ended up paying twice. One thing to remember: An expired hold is not a cancelled payment, and an approved authorisation is not money moved.

WC-41.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 640 headphones, delivery proof, and a fraud claim. A customer reported a EUR 640 card payment as fraud. The merchant produced a delivery photo, a signature, and a matching delivery address. The issuer had to decide who to believe, and the evidence pointed both ways. Whatever the decision, one honest party would feel betrayed. One thing to remember: In a chargeback, evidence decides, not the loudest claim.

WC-42.agenda: Work through this case: A EUR 2,400 flight booking lost to a failed security check. A customer tried to book flights worth EUR 2,400. The security check failed twice, and the booking was abandoned. The customer booked with a competitor within the hour. The fraud that the check prevented never existed. One thing to remember: A security check that blocks good customers is not secure, it is expensive.

WC-43.agenda: Work through this case: The charity whose payments looked like money laundering. A small charity sent EUR 4,500 every month to field partners. Transaction monitoring flagged every payment. The bank closed the account, and the charity started moving cash. The monitoring system had made the money less visible, not more. One thing to remember: Exiting a customer does not remove the risk, it removes the visibility.

WC-44.agenda: Work through this case: A payment file with 380 account numbers went to the wrong inbox. A payment file with 380 supplier account numbers was emailed to the wrong address. The addresses differed by one letter. The email could not be recalled, and the file could not be unseen. The breach clock had already started. One thing to remember: Data that has been seen cannot be unseen, so the control must sit before the send button.

WC-45.agenda: Work through this case: The bank that held EUR 40 million to protect its liquidity ratio. A bank held back EUR 40 million of customer payments until late afternoon. The payments were valid, funded, and ready to go. The delay protected the bank's liquidity buffer, and the customers paid the price. One corporate missed a settlement window it could not recover. One thing to remember: A payment delayed to protect a ratio is still a payment delayed, and the customer feels it first.

WC-46.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 9,800 stolen at 3am on a Sunday, in 14 instant payments. At 3.07am on a Sunday, an account was emptied in 14 instant payments. No member of staff was on duty. The automated limits allowed every one of them. By Monday morning, the money was gone through a chain of mule accounts. One thing to remember: In instant payments, prevention is the only control, because recovery is a request, not a right.

WC-47.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 300 that expired before it could be spent. A relief payment of EUR 300 arrived with an expiry date. Spend it in 30 days, or lose it. The recipient saved EUR 120 toward rent, and watched it disappear. The money had done exactly what it was programmed to do. One thing to remember: Programmable money changes what money is, so the conditions need the same scrutiny as the payment.

WC-48.agenda: Work through this case: An AI agent created a vendor, then paid it EUR 18,500. A new vendor was onboarded on a Monday. Its first invoice was paid on the same day, EUR 18,500. An AI agent had done both, the onboarding and the payment. The vendor's bank details had come from a spoofed email. One thing to remember: An agent that approves its own setup has not been controlled, it has been trusted blindly.

WC-49.agenda: Work through this case: One wrong character in an LEI held a EUR 250,000 payment. A EUR 250,000 payment was held two hours before the cut-off. The legal entity identifier had one character transposed. Fixing it meant missing the customer's deadline. Sending it meant filing a report the bank knew was wrong. One thing to remember: Validate identifiers at entry, because a defect found at the cut-off has no good outcome left.

WC-50.agenda: Work through this case: After the merger, EUR 75,000 reached the wrong legal entity. Two banks merged, and two payment hubs kept running. The same customer name existed in both, mapped to different accounts. A EUR 75,000 payment followed the wrong mapping. The money reached the wrong legal entity, in the wrong country. One thing to remember: A name is not an identity, and a payment routed by name alone will eventually reach the wrong entity.

WC-51.agenda: Work through this case: A sanctions list update landed at 13:40, with 11 payments in flight. A sanctions list update arrived at 13:40. Eleven payments already in flight matched a newly listed name. Three had settled, five were in clearing, three were still queued. The team had to decide, in the hour, which payments to stop. One thing to remember: Screening is a decision with an expiry date, and the re-screening scope must be written before the list changes.

WC-52.agenda: Work through this case: The EUR 1 test payment that taught the whole journey. A tester sent EUR 1 to prove the new payment chain worked. The euro travelled through instruction, tracking, clearing, liquidity, exception, and return. It never reached the beneficiary. And it taught the team more than a year of successful payments had. One thing to remember: A payment chain is only proven when its exception path works, and a EUR 1 test can prove the whole chain.

XBR-001.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 50,000 sent serial, but the chain had no account to settle through. A supplier invoice for EUR 50,000 was due on Friday. The payment team sent it serial, straight down the chain, and marked the job done. One thing to remember: Serial is a chain of accounts. No account, no chain.

XBR-002.agenda: Work through this case: USD 40,000 cover booked as the bank's own money, supplier never paid. A customer paid USD 40,000 to an overseas supplier. The supplier's bank confirmed it had received funds. The supplier was never credited. One thing to remember: A cover without its MT103 is just money with no owner.

XBR-003.agenda: Work through this case: USD 25,000 "sent" on Monday, beneficiary paid on Thursday. A customer sent USD 25,000 to pay an invoice and was told the payment had gone. Three days later the beneficiary called to say nothing had arrived. One thing to remember: Sent is not settled. The MT103 is the message, the cover is the money.

XBR-004.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 30,000 announced, EUR 29,965 arrived, nobody got paid. An MT103 announced EUR 30,000. The MT202 COV that arrived to settle it carried EUR 29,965. The beneficiary bank credited nobody and raised an exception. One thing to remember: Two legs, one truth. If they disagree, nothing moves.

XBR-005.agenda: Work through this case: USD 10,000 cover arrived USD 35 short, and the payment stopped for two weeks. A cover payment of USD 10,000 was announced. The cover that arrived was USD 9,965. The beneficiary bank refused to credit the full amount, and the USD 35 gap turned into a two-week dispute. One thing to remember: Never take charges from the cover. The cover is the full amount, or it is an exception.

XBR-006.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 5,000 salary sent, EUR 4,940 received, and nobody made an error. A company paid an overseas employee EUR 5,000 in salary by MT103. The employee received EUR 4,940 and asked where the missing EUR 60 had gone. One thing to remember: In a serial payment, every bank in the chain takes its cut from the amount.

XBR-007.agenda: Work through this case: 71A said BEN, the copy said SHA, and the sender paid charges it never agreed to. A sender instructed a payment of GBP 20,000 with field 71A set to BEN, so the beneficiary would bear every charge. The beneficiary was credited almost in full, and the sender was billed for charges it never agreed to pay. One thing to remember: 71A is set once, by the bank that generates the MT103. Nobody downstream may change it.

XBR-008.agenda: Work through this case: USD 75,000 passed screening, but only on the leg that was checked. A payment of USD 75,000 to an overseas supplier passed sanctions screening and was released. The supplier was never paid. The funds were sitting in a hold at an intermediary bank. One thing to remember: One clean leg does not clear a payment. Both legs must pass.

XBR-009.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 8,000 recalled the same day, but the beneficiary had already spent it. A customer sent EUR 8,000 to the wrong beneficiary by mistake. The recall went out the same day. The beneficiary had already spent the money. One thing to remember: Once the money is spent, a recall is a request, not a reversal.

XBR-010.agenda: Work through this case: USD 15,000 returned for a bad account, and the refund took the long way home. A payment of USD 15,000 was returned because the beneficiary account did not exist. The customer waited a week, then asked where the refund was. One thing to remember: A return is the same payment travelling backwards, not a new payment.

XBR-011.agenda: Work through this case: Returned five times in six weeks, the code was in the message but not in field 57A. A payment to Australia was returned five times over six weeks. Each time the note said the same thing: the beneficiary bank's SWIFT code had to appear in field 57A. One thing to remember: The receiving bank reads field 57A. Nowhere else counts.

XBR-012.agenda: Work through this case: EUR 18,000 to a new bank, rejected before it was even read. A company made its first ever payment to a new beneficiary bank: EUR 18,000 for an urgent order. The MT103 was rejected before it was even read. One thing to remember: Authorisation comes before the payment, not after it.

XBR-013.agenda: Work through this case: USD 60,000 paid in full, but the bank could not prove it was the same payment. A payment of USD 60,000 passed through a correspondent bank on its way to the beneficiary. The beneficiary was paid. The originator bank could not prove it. One thing to remember: The UETR is the thread. Break it and the payment cannot be traced.

XBR-014.agenda: Work through this case: Nine days for a payment promised in three, the bank had not bought the currency yet. A customer sent a payment in a less common currency and was told it would arrive in two to three days. Nine days later it still had not arrived, and the customer assumed the money was lost. One thing to remember: The instruction can be complete while the money waits for the bank's currency position.

XBR-015.agenda: Work through this case: USD 30,000 to a dollar account arrived USD 300 short after two conversions. A customer sent USD 30,000 to a supplier's US dollar account. The supplier received USD 29,700 and sent the invoice back unpaid. One thing to remember: No intermediary may change the currency. The sender decides it.

ch100s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in reconciliation matching. Reconciliation is proving that the money that left the bank matches the money that was supposed to leave, and AI helps by matching payments to statements faster than a person can by hand. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch100s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in exception prediction. An exception is a payment that did not go through cleanly, and AI in exception prediction tries to spot the payments likely to fail before they fail, so the operations team can act early instead of fixing the mess. An exception is a payment that did not go through cleanly, and AI in exception prediction tries to spot the payments likely to fail before they fail, so the operations team can act early instead of fixing the mess afterwards.

ch100s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in fraud detection. Fraud detection is the job of spotting a payment that looks wrong before the money is gone, and AI helps by scoring each payment against patterns it has learned from past fraud and from normal behaviour. Take a retail customer who normally spends around three thousand rupees a day in Bangalore, and suddenly there is a payment of one lakh eighty thousand rupees to a new beneficiary in another country at two in the morning.

ch100s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in customer service for payments. Customers ask the same payment questions again and again, where is my money, why has it not arrived, what is the charge, and AI can answer many of those questions fast, but only inside clear limits.
