Imagine a customer who sent fifteen thousand rupees by an instant payment at ten in the morning and asks at noon where it is.

ch100s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing requirements for ai systems. Writing requirements for an AI feature is different from writing requirements for a normal screen or report, because you describe not only what the system must do, but how it must behave when it is uncertain, and what. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch100s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defining success metrics and handling ai failures. An AI feature is not done when it goes live, it is done when you can prove it works, and that proof needs numbers, a review rhythm, and a plan for when it gets things wrong. That is the rollback, and it must be a button the operations team can press, not a change request that takes three weeks.

ch100s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone brief: design an ai-assisted payments feature. This is your capstone brief, the task that pulls the whole AI course together into one piece of work you can show. A good example is AI assisted reconciliation of cross border payments, where a corporate client sends one payment of twelve thousand dollars to cover thirty invoices in different currencies, and the operations team spends hours matching the statement lines, the charges and the exchange rate differences by hand.

ch100s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: specify it end to end. In this final lesson you turn your capstone idea into a full specification, the document a developer, a tester and an operations manager can actually work from. First, the BRD outline, one page that states the business problem, the users, the current process, the proposed AI feature, the benefits in numbers, and the risks, for example cutting the unmatched queue from forty items a week to ten, and saving six hours of analyst time a week.

ch10s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain US payments landscape at a glance. The United States runs its domestic payments on a mix of old and new systems, and the mix can confuse anyone who expects a single national design like the one India built around NPCI. A business analyst working on US payments must learn which operator runs each system, because the operator decides the rules, the hours and the support model.

ch10s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nss, the national settlement service. The National Settlement Service settles the money behind private sector clearing arrangements in the United States, using accounts at the Federal Reserve. Timing is what most often confuses analysts, because clearing, customer posting and interbank settlement happen at different moments.

ch10s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain phixius, the ACH information exchange. Phixius is a payment information network run by Nacha, the organisation that governs the ACH network in the United States. Coverage is therefore the limit an analyst should check first: where no responder covers an account, the bank must fall back on other validation methods, such as a prenote or a small test transaction.

ch10s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain aba routing numbers: how US payments find the right bank. Every electronic payment in the United States needs to identify the receiving bank, and the key for that is the ABA routing number: nine digits that identify a specific financial institution. The two numbers are always used together, and the analyst must treat them as a pair.

ch10s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE: the federal reserve's RTGS system. Fedwire Funds Service is the real time gross settlement system operated by the Federal Reserve. Operating hours and cutoffs are the hard deadlines that operations teams watch closely.

ch10s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDNOW: instant payments around the clock. FedNow Service is the Federal Reserve's instant payment system, launched in July 2023. The analyst must design the funding and alerting rules with treasury, because a bank that runs out of FedNow liquidity on a Sunday night cannot wait until Monday morning.

ch10s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ACH: the batch network that pays america. The Automated Clearing House, or ACH, is the electronic network that moves most of the routine payments in the United States. The whole cycle takes one to two business days for a standard ACH payment, and the analyst must make this timing clear, because the customer experience can look fast while settlement is still a day away.

ch10s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHIPS: private sector netting for large payments. Clearing House Interbank Payments System, or CHIPS, is the private sector system operated by The Clearing House for large value US dollar payments. The analyst must show the cutoff in the product and in the operations manual in Eastern Time, and must design the queue view so operations can see which payments are waiting and what funding is needed to release them.

ch10s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain US payment flows end to end. Consider a company in Chicago that needs to pay a supplier in New York fifty thousand dollars today, pay its employees on Friday, and send two million dollars to a partner bank as part of a securities settlement. A good analyst would route these three payments through three different systems.

ch10s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing between FEDWIRE, FEDNOW, ACH and CHIPS. The choice between the four systems comes down to four questions that an analyst should ask for every payment. The choice between the four systems comes down to four questions that an analyst should ask for every payment.

ch10s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE and CHIPS ISO 20022 migrations: complete. The two largest US dollar payment systems have both completed their ISO 20022 migrations. For a business analyst, the practical impact is that US payment projects now assume ISO 20022.

ch10s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain lynx, canada's high-value RTGS system. Lynx is the system that settles large and time critical payments in Canadian dollars between financial institutions in Canada. The cost is liquidity: a bank must fund each payment in full, not only a smaller net amount at the end of the day.

ch11s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA. The Single Euro Payments Area, known as SEPA, is one of the most ambitious payment projects in the world. For a business analyst, SEPA is a lesson in how standardisation creates scale.

ch11s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA instant payments regulation: phased obligations from 2025. The SEPA Instant Payments Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/886, made instant euro payments mandatory across the euro area in phases, not on a single date. For a business analyst, the IPR creates specific requirements.

ch11s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validating an IBAN by hand: the mod-97 check worked. The MOD-97 check is the arithmetic test that catches most typing errors in an IBAN before a payment is sent, and every analyst who works on European payments must be able to work it by hand. The MOD-97 check is the arithmetic test that catches most typing errors in an IBAN before a payment is sent, and every analyst who works on European payments must be able to work it by hand.

ch11s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain eurosic: euro clearing in switzerland. Switzerland has its own currency, the franc, and its own real time gross settlement system, SIC, the Swiss Interbank Clearing system operated by SIX. For a business analyst, the lesson is about how payment systems follow trade and finance rather than borders: where the flows are large enough, a clearing service appears, and the analyst job is to understand its rules, its settlement, and its place in the routing choices available to the bank.

ch11s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain IBAN and the SEPA account identifier. The International Bank Account Number, or IBAN, is the account identifier that makes SEPA possible, and every analyst who works on European payments must understand its structure. The International Bank Account Number, or IBAN, is the account identifier that makes SEPA possible, and every analyst who works on European payments must understand its structure.

ch11s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA credit transfer: sct. A credit transfer is a push payment. Duplicates and cut off times cause the failures analysts see most.

ch11s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA direct debit: sdd. A direct debit is a pull payment. In the B2B scheme the debtor bank must verify the mandate before it debits, because the business debtor gives up the refund right in exchange.

ch11s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sct inst: instant euro payments. An instant payment settles in seconds, not days. The payee bank must reply with a pacs.002 status report, accepted with status ACCP or rejected with status RJCT, and on acceptance it must credit the payee account at once.

ch11s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain target2 and T2: the eurosystem RTGS. TARGET2, now replaced by its successor system known as T2, is the real time gross settlement system operated by the Eurosystem, which is the European Central Bank together with the national central banks of the euro. A payment submitted after the customer cut off will be processed on the next business day, so the cut off is a hard deadline that corporate treasurers and operations teams plan around.

ch11s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA works across countries: a worked example. Consider a company headquartered in Amsterdam that employs people in Germany, France and Spain, buys goods from a supplier in Italy, and sells a subscription service to customers in eight countries. The analyst's job is to preserve that invisibility in the product design.

ch11s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA instruments in depth: sct, sct inst, sdd core, sdd b2b. SEPA, the Single Euro Payments Area, covers euro payments across 34 countries. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch11s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain messages exchanged in the sct scheme: PAIN, PACS, CAMT. All SEPA messages are based on ISO 20022, using XML syntax. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch12s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UK payments landscape at a glance. The United Kingdom runs its domestic sterling payments on three main systems that have grown up over different decades and now sit side by side, each serving a distinct purpose. Together they move almost every pound that changes hands inside the UK, and a business analyst who works on UK payments must know all three, because a customer requirement that sounds simple, such as pay this supplier today, can mean three different things depending on the value, the urgency and the cost the customer will accept.

ch12s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain faster payments: near real time for everyday payments. Faster Payments moves sterling between UK bank accounts in seconds. Netting keeps the liquidity each bank needs far lower than gross settlement would.

ch12s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHAPS: high value payments with same day finality. CHAPS is the United Kingdom's real time gross settlement system for high value sterling payments. A payment submitted after the cutoff is processed on the next business day, so conveyancers, corporate treasurers and operations teams plan around it.

ch12s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BACS: the three day cycle that pays the nation. BACS is the batch system that has moved most UK regular payments since the late 1960s. Bank holidays extend the timetable, and the analyst must design for the calendar, not just the cycle.

ch12s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain three systems differ. The fastest way to compare the UK systems is to put them side by side on four questions. Timing is where analysts most often make mistakes in the UK, because the words fast and same day mean different things on different systems.

ch12s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain confirmation of payee and the fight against fraud. Confirmation of Payee, known as CoP, is a service that checks whether the name entered by the payer matches the name on the account that the sort code and account number identify, and it is now a standard part of the UK. The reimbursement rules for authorised push payment fraud are a second layer of protection that the analyst must understand.

ch12s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing the right system: a worked example. Consider a small business in Manchester that needs to make four payments on the same morning, fifty pounds to a local supplier for stationery, two thousand pounds to a consultant, one hundred and fifty thousand pounds. A good analyst would not send all four through the same system.

ch12s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sort codes and account numbers: how UK payments find the right account. Every domestic payment in the United Kingdom needs an address, and that address has two parts: a six digit sort code that identifies the bank branch, and an eight digit account number that identifies the account at that. The analyst who understands this structure can read a UK IBAN at a glance, spot a missing or extra digit, and explain to a customer why an international payment needs the IBAN while a domestic payment needs only the sort code and account number.

ch13s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain correspondent banking is. Correspondent banking is the arrangement that lets a bank in one country make payments in another country where it has no branch, no licence and no account with the central bank. New solutions, including payment system linkages, central bank digital currency projects and fintech networks, are trying to reduce the dependence on correspondent banking, but for now it remains the backbone of cross border payments, and the analyst must design for the world as it is, not the world as it might become.

ch13s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chats, hong kong's RTGS system. Hong Kong settles interbank payments through CHATS, its real time gross settlement system. For an analyst, CHATS is best understood as four settlement systems sharing one operator and one design, not as a single multicurrency account.

ch13s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fcdps, china's foreign currency domestic payments. FCDPS and CDFCPS are two names for the same Chinese payment system, and treating them as separate systems is the most common mistake analysts make with this topic. FCDPS and CDFCPS are two names for the same Chinese payment system, and treating them as separate systems is the most common mistake analysts make with this topic.

ch13s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro mirrors. A nostro account is our account with you: a bank holds an account with a correspondent bank in another country, in that country currency, so it can make and receive payments there. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch13s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain lead bank, consortium and syndicate models. Large financings need more than one bank. For a business analyst, syndicated and consortium lending is a payments design problem.

ch13s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro and vostro: two names for the same account. Nostro and vostro are the two words that confuse every new analyst in cross border payments, and the confusion disappears once the perspective is clear. Nostro and vostro are the two words that confuse every new analyst in cross border payments, and the confusion disappears once the perspective is clear.

ch13s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks need correspondent accounts. A bank needs a correspondent account in a currency when it has customers who need to pay or receive in that currency and it cannot settle those payments itself. A bank needs a correspondent account in a currency when it has customers who need to pay or receive in that currency and it cannot settle those payments itself.

ch13s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain account structures: direct, nested and payable through. Not every bank has a direct correspondent relationship with a bank in every country, and the account structures that fill the gaps are important for an analyst to understand. Not every bank has a direct correspondent relationship with a bank in every country, and the account structures that fill the gaps are important for an analyst to understand.

ch13s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity in nostro accounts. Liquidity is the most practical problem in correspondent banking, and it is the problem that operations and treasury teams spend most of their time managing. A business analyst who writes requirements for a cross border payment product must include the funding process, the forecasting, and the cut off handling, because a payment product that cannot fund its nostro account cannot send payments at all.

ch13s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro reconciliation and account statements. Nostro reconciliation is the daily discipline of agreeing the balance of a nostro account between the two banks, and it is one of the most important operational controls in cross border payments. Breaks happen for many reasons, and the analyst must know the common ones.

ch13s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain compliance, sanctions and de-risking. Correspondent banking is one of the most heavily controlled areas in finance, because a correspondent account can be used to move money for money laundering, for terrorist financing, or for evading sanctions, and the. If a payment mentions a sanctioned person, a sanctioned country or a sanctioned entity, it is stopped, and the correspondent bank must decide whether to reject it, to block it, or to report it.

ch13s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: nostro account management systems. Nostro accounts are managed in the core banking system as a special class of account, with one record per currency per correspondent bank. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch13s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cips, china's cross-border payment system. CIPS clears and settles renminbi payments moving across China's borders, giving those payments a dedicated route of their own. For an analyst, the practical questions on a CIPS payment mirror those on any cross border payment, with the participant tier added.

ch14s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain there and apply it to a real banking scenario. Both methods deliver the money and the information, but they do it in different ways, with different speeds, costs and risks, and the analyst must know which one is being used for any given payment.

ch14s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial flow and apply it to a real banking scenario. If the charges are OUR, which means the sender pays all charges, the sending bank must ensure that each bank in the chain is paid separately, or must send the full amount and settle the charges through a separate arrangement, because the beneficiary must receive the full amount.

ch14s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cover flow and apply it to a real banking scenario. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch14s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial versus cover: a side by side comparison and apply it to a real banking scenario. Cover can be faster for the beneficiary, because the instruction arrives directly, but it is more complex to operate, because the receiving bank must match the cover funds to the instruction, and a mismatch creates a reconciliation break.

ch14s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to use each method and apply it to a real banking scenario. The cover method is the right choice when the sending and receiving banks have no direct relationship, when the funds need to travel through a different route from the instruction, and when the beneficiary bank needs the full information quickly.

ch14s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain inda, inga, cove and clrg codes and apply it to a real banking scenario. The bank must screen the cover payment using the originator and beneficiary information carried in the COVE message, and it must pass the funds on to the next bank in the cover chain.

ch14s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tracing a payment through either method and apply it to a real banking scenario. The analyst asks each bank in turn whether it received the MT103, when it received it, when it passed it on, and what charge it deducted.

ch14s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain method-specific cancellations: cancelling a direct, serial or cover payment. Cancelling a payment is not one process. The usual practice is to cancel the cover first, so that no funds are in flight, and then cancel the customer payment, but the exact order depends on the state of each leg, and the analyst must design the coordination as a single case with two cancellation requests, not as two independent cases.

ch15s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain our, sha and ben: who pays the charges. Every cross border payment passes through several banks, and every bank that handles it charges a fee. The analyst must know whether the bank offers a guaranteed OUR or a best efforts OUR, and must explain the difference to the customer.

ch15s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked examples: what the beneficiary actually receives. Consider a payment of ten thousand US dollars from a company in India to a supplier in Germany, where the sending bank charges twenty five dollars, the intermediary bank charges fifteen dollars, and the receiving bank. A business analyst who prepares a worked example like this for a customer or for a training session makes the abstract codes concrete, and the customer can then make an informed choice instead of discovering the deduction when the supplier complains.

ch15s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange: rates, spreads and conversion. Most cross border payments involve a foreign exchange conversion, because the sender holds one currency and the beneficiary needs another. A customer who sends ten thousand dollars and receives the equivalent in euros may not realise that the bank's rate was one percent worse than the market rate, which means the customer paid one hundred dollars for the conversion without seeing a separate charge.

ch15s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT GPI: what it is and how it changed tracking. SWIFT gpi, which stands for Global Payments Innovation, is a service launched by SWIFT in 2017 that transformed cross border payments by making them faster, more transparent and trackable. A customer who sends a payment can now see that it has been received by the intermediary bank, that it has been forwarded, and that it has been credited to the beneficiary, with timestamps at each step.

ch15s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UETR: the unique tracking reference. The Unique End to end Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, is the identifier that makes gpi tracking possible, and every analyst who works on cross border payments must understand it. The Unique End to end Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, is the identifier that makes gpi tracking possible, and every analyst who works on cross border payments must understand it.

ch15s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transparency: fees, rates and time in the open. Transparency is the direction in which cross border payments are moving, driven by regulation, by competition from fintech companies, and by customer expectation. In the past, a customer who sent money abroad was told the amount to be sent and the charge of the sending bank, but was not told the exchange rate, the spread, the charges of the intermediary banks, or the time the payment would take.

ch15s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain complete cross border payment: putting it together. Consider a company in Bengaluru that needs to pay a supplier in Frankfurt ten thousand euros for a shipment of machinery, and the company holds rupees. A business analyst who can walk through this example, explain each step, and answer the questions that arise at each step, has understood cross border payments at a practical level.

ch15s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT universal confirmation. SWIFT Universal Confirmation is the rule that a bank receiving a cross border payment must confirm what happened to it. For a business analyst, the design work is to make confirmation automatic: generate the confirmation from the posting event, monitor the two business day window daily, queue unconfirmed items for same day follow up, and test all four outcomes, including the hold and the transfer outside SWIFT.

ch15s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange market: how currencies are bought and sold for payments. Every cross border payment that changes currency passes through the foreign exchange market, and the analyst who designs payments must understand how that market works, because the rate, the value date and the. Every cross border payment that changes currency passes through the foreign exchange market, and the analyst who designs payments must understand how that market works, because the rate, the value date and the settlement of the currency conversion decide when the beneficiary is paid and how much they receive.

ch16s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross border payments fail. Most cross border payments arrive without a problem, but a small percentage fail, and the failures matter out of proportion to their number because each failure involves a customer who is waiting for money, a supplier. Most cross border payments arrive without a problem, but a small percentage fail, and the failures matter out of proportion to their number because each failure involves a customer who is waiting for money, a supplier who has not been paid, or a salary that has not arrived.

ch16s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rejects: stopped before the money moves. A reject happens when a payment is stopped before the funds have moved, usually because the receiving bank or an intermediary bank cannot process the instruction as it stands. The analyst must design the reject handling to be fast and clear.

ch16s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain returns: the money comes back. A return happens when a payment has been sent and the funds have moved, but the receiving bank cannot credit the beneficiary and sends the money back. The analyst must design the return handling to match the return to the original payment by UETR, to calculate the amount actually returned, to identify any deduction, and to notify the customer with the amount and the reason.

ch16s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recalls: asking for the money back. A recall, also called a payment recall or a request for recall, happens when the sending bank asks the receiving bank to return a payment that has already been credited to the beneficiary, usually because the payment. The recall is not guaranteed to succeed, and the analyst must make that clear to the customer.

ch16s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigations and reason codes. An investigation is the process of finding out what happened to a payment that has not arrived, has arrived for the wrong amount, or has arrived with the wrong information, and it is the most common exception task in. The investigation starts with the customer reporting the problem, and the operations team then traces the payment using the UETR, the gpi tracker, the SWIFT messages, and the correspondent account statements.

ch16s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain timelines, costs and who bears them. Every exception has a timeline, and the timeline is set by the rules of the payment system, the agreements between banks, and the law of the countries involved. The analyst must include the cost allocation in the requirements, must ensure that the charges are applied correctly, and must ensure that the customer is told upfront what an exception will cost.

ch16s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain handling exceptions well: a practical playbook. The best exception handling starts before the exception happens, with validation at payment capture, with clear customer instructions, and with a payment flow that prevents the most common errors. The system should detect a reject, a return, a recall or an investigation automatically, should match it to the original payment by UETR, and should alert the operations team without waiting for the customer to complain.

ch17s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing really means. Clearing is the process that sits between a payment instruction and its final settlement. For a business analyst, understanding clearing means understanding where in the flow a payment can be stopped, corrected or returned, and what information is needed at each step to keep the process reliable and auditable.

ch17s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rtfs and rtns settlement models. RTFS and RTNS are two labels for two different answers to the same question, namely when a payment that is processed in real time actually becomes final. For an analyst, the working question about any system is therefore not how fast it looks, but when finality happens, and the answer decides how credit, customer funds and failure handling must all be managed.

ch17s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bilateral and multilateral limits. Netting and clearing systems let participants exchange payments through the day and settle the net amounts later. This matters because clearing and settlement are where money actually moves between banks. A mistake here is a settlement failure, a liquidity shortfall, or a loss.

ch17s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from gross payments to net positions. Every payment has a gross value, which is the full amount instructed by the payer. By netting first, a bank needs a much smaller balance, and the cost of holding that balance falls.

ch17s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bilateral netting in practice. Bilateral netting is the simplest form of netting, and it involves just two parties. An analyst turns this into three artefacts.

ch17s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain multilateral netting and the clearing house. Multilateral netting extends the same idea across many participants at once. A clearing house coordinates, while a central counterparty guarantees, and an analyst should not confuse the two.

ch17s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example with three banks. Consider three banks, A, B and C, exchanging payments during one clearing cycle. Operations teams monitor this closely, because a sudden change in net position changes the liquidity a bank must have ready at settlement.

ch17s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing houses and central counterparties. A clearing house is more than a calculator. For a business analyst, the distinction matters when designing system requirements.

ch17s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain netting matters for risk and liquidity. Netting reduces the amount of money that must move at settlement, and that directly reduces both liquidity risk and settlement risk. There is a trade off that analysts must understand.

ch17s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: clearing house architecture. A clearing house processes millions of instructions every day, often 10 to 50 million in a large domestic system, with peak rates of 5,000 to 10,000 instructions per second. This reduces the liquidity each bank needs by 90 percent or more in a typical cycle.

ch17s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hybrid payment systems. A hybrid payment system settles some payments the gross way and others the net way inside a single system. An analyst should never assume that a payment in a hybrid system is final merely because it was accepted.

ch18s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement means after clearing. Settlement is the moment when value actually moves and a payment becomes final and irrevocable. A business analyst needs to know the finality point for every system they work on, because it drives reconciliation, customer funds availability, exception handling and the wording of terms and conditions.

ch18s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real-time gross settlement. Real time gross settlement, known as RTGS, settles each payment individually and immediately, as soon as it is received by the system. For an analyst, the queue is a feature to specify, not a detail to leave to the vendor.

ch18s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain deferred net settlement. Deferred net settlement, often called DNS, is the model used by most retail payment systems. An analyst documents three things for a DNS system.

ch18s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain prefunded settlement models. In a prefunded settlement model, participants deposit funds in advance into a settlement account, and payments are settled only to the extent that prefunded balance allows. A business analyst designing a prefunded system needs to model the prefund sizing problem carefully, because getting it wrong directly affects customer experience, either through rejected payments or through wasted liquidity.

ch18s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain comparing the three models. RTGS, deferred net settlement and prefunded settlement each solve a different problem, and the choice between them is a trade off between risk, liquidity and speed. Understanding these regulatory drivers helps a business analyst explain why a system is designed the way it is, rather than simply describing its mechanics.

ch18s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing a model for a payment system. When a new payment system is designed, the settlement model is one of the earliest decisions, because it shapes everything else. A business analyst working on such a project spends much of their time mapping these interfaces and confirming that the new system and the existing settlement system agree on timing, amounts and responsibilities.

ch18s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement finality and legal certainty. Settlement finality is the legal protection that makes a payment system trustworthy. A business analyst who is asked to add a reverse button for settled payments should refuse with the legal reason, not with a technical excuse, because the business needs to understand that this is a legal boundary, not a missing feature.

ch19s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity. Liquidity, in the context of payment systems, is the ready availability of funds in a bank's central bank account to settle payments as they fall due. For a business analyst, liquidity management is where payment operations meet treasury.

ch19s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain available, reserved and blocked: liquidity position states. A liquidity position is not one number. For a business analyst, position states are a reporting and control design.

ch19s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intraday liquidity and central bank accounts. Every bank that participates directly in a payment system holds a settlement account at the central bank. Intraday credit is usually collateralised, meaning the bank must pledge securities such as government bonds to secure it, and it is usually free or very cheap, because the central bank wants payments to flow smoothly.

ch19s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity saving mechanisms and queuing. When a bank does not have enough funds to settle a payment immediately, the payment system does not necessarily reject it. The analyst's job is to specify the rules that govern the queue, because the rules decide who waits and who does not.

ch19s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gridlock and how systems resolve it. Gridlock is a situation where several banks are each waiting for funds from another bank in the group, and no bank can settle its queued payments because each one is waiting for the next. For a business analyst, gridlock is a reminder that payment systems are networks, and the behaviour of one participant affects all the others.

ch19s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity pools and shared arrangements. A liquidity pool is an arrangement where a group of banks, often part of the same banking group, combine their liquidity for settlement purposes. An analyst documents a pooling arrangement in the same way as any shared service.

ch19s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank facilities and collateral. Central banks provide several facilities that help banks manage intraday liquidity. A business analyst does not need to be a monetary policy expert, but should understand how these facilities affect the cost and availability of liquidity on a given day.

ch19s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks manage liquidity day to day. In practice, liquidity management is a daily routine with a clear rhythm. A business analyst involved in building or improving such a dashboard needs to understand which metrics matter and how quickly they must update to be useful.

ch19s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nsfr and lcr in depth: the basel liquidity ratios. The Basel III framework added two liquidity ratios that every bank must live with: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio, the LCR, and the Net Stable Funding Ratio, the NSFR. For a business analyst, the ratios are a data and reporting project.

ch19s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bcbs intraday liquidity monitoring tools. A bank can be solvent at the end of the day and still fail during it. For a business analyst, the monitoring tools are an intraday data project.

ch1s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Understanding payments in this way helps a business analyst avoid a common mistake, which is to treat every money movement as the same thing.

ch1s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus transfer and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst should be precise even when others are loose.

ch1s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment instruments and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst must know which instrument fits which use case.

ch1s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain push versus pull payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst documents push and pull as two different products, not as one payment flow with a flag.

ch1s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus settlement and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the practical lesson is to never confuse a customer credit with final settlement.

ch1s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value date, finality and irrevocability and apply it to a real banking scenario. Analysts must capture value date rules explicitly in payment specifications.

ch1s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain this foundation matters for a BA and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst who understands what a payment really is can ask better questions, write clearer requirements, and spot risks earlier.

ch20s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement risk really is. Settlement risk is the risk that a payment will not settle as expected, either because the sending party fails to deliver the funds or the asset, or because settlement happens at a different time or in a different. The risk has two dimensions that analysts must separate.

ch20s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain herstatt collapse of 1974. The most famous example of settlement risk is the collapse of Bankhaus Herstatt, a small German bank, on 26 June 1974. An analyst uses Herstatt as a test, not just a story.

ch20s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain principal risk, replacement cost and liquidity risk. Settlement risk is usually broken down into three types, and it helps to keep them distinct. This matters because clearing and settlement are where money actually moves between banks. A mistake here is a settlement failure, a liquidity shortfall, or a loss.

ch20s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS reduces settlement risk. Real time gross settlement reduces settlement risk by settling each payment immediately and individually in central bank money. Until eleven fifteen in the morning the receiving bank must not release anything against it, because a queued payment is not a settled payment, and treating it as settled is exactly the mistake RTGS is designed to prevent.

ch20s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment versus payment. Payment versus payment, usually shortened to PVP, is the principle that the two legs of a foreign exchange transaction should settle simultaneously, so that one cannot settle without the other. A business analyst working on foreign exchange systems needs to know for each currency pair and each settlement channel whether PVP applies, because that determines the risk profile of the trade and the controls that must surround it.

ch20s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CLS and foreign exchange settlement. CLS, originally known as Continuous Linked Settlement, is a global system that provides payment versus payment settlement for foreign exchange trades in eighteen major currencies. Any business analyst working on cross border payments should understand how CLS fits into the overall flow.

ch20s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain managing residual risk in practice. No system eliminates settlement risk entirely, so banks and payment system operators manage the residual risk with a combination of limits, collateral, monitoring and contingency plans. An analyst writes the default procedure as a runbook, not as a paragraph in a policy document.

ch20s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clsnow, same-day fx settlement. CLSNow is the service that brings payment versus payment protection to foreign exchange trades that settle on the same day they are agreed. Eligibility can change over time as the service develops, so an analyst should confirm the current list in the CLS rulebook or with the settlement member before assuming a pair is covered.

ch20s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CLS in detail: timetable and member structure. Foreign exchange settlement carries a famous risk: Herstatt risk, named after the bank whose failure in 1974 left counterparties who had paid one currency leg without receiving the other. For a business analyst, CLS teaches the settlement design pattern that recurs everywhere: link the legs, net the funding, schedule the window, and tier the membership so that the obligations sit with those who can meet them.

ch21s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four parties and the card transaction. The four party model is the foundation of every card payment. The cardholder is the customer who owns the card and makes the purchase.

ch21s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorization in real time. Authorisation is the real time check that happens while the customer is still at the till or on the checkout page. Step four is the hold, and the analyst must understand how long it lasts.

ch21s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain happens after the customer leaves. Once the customer has left, the merchant's work is not finished. For a business analyst, the authorisation to capture gap is a source of many edge cases.

ch21s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain batching and clearing files. Batching is how the acquirer collects captured transactions and prepares them for clearing. A business analyst working on a clearing interface needs to understand the file layout, the field definitions, the validation rules and the error handling procedures.

ch21s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interchange fees and how money moves. Interchange is the fee that the acquirer pays to the issuer on every card transaction, and it is the largest component of the cost a merchant pays to accept cards. For business analysts, interchange matters because it drives pricing, product design and negotiations.

ch21s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement between issuer, acquirer and scheme. Settlement is the movement of money that follows clearing, and it is the stage where promises become payments. A transaction that was authorised but never cleared does not appear in settlement at all, which is why clearing discipline, including timely presentment, is a control the analyst must watch.

ch21s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain things go wrong. Card transactions can fail at every stage, and each failure has a different cause and a different remedy. The merchant is not funded on time, and the acquirer's operations team works through the night to fix the three records and resubmit.

ch21s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: card authorization at scale. Card authorization systems process thousands of transactions per second, with large issuers handling 5,000 to 15,000 authorizations per second at peak, such as during holiday shopping or major sales events. The model is updated regularly with new fraud patterns, and its decisions are logged with the score and the top contributing features, so analysts can review why a genuine transaction was blocked and tune the rules.

ch22s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card payments need extra protection. Card payments face a basic problem. Every extra step at checkout, every password to remember and every code to type, increases the chance that a genuine customer will abandon their purchase.

ch22s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain 3D secure 2 works. Three D Secure, often called 3DS, is a protocol that adds an authentication step to online card payments. An analyst specifies 3DS as a data contract, not just a feature.

ch22s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain frictionless flow versus challenge flow. The frictionless flow and the challenge flow are the two outcomes of EMV 3D Secure version 2, and the choice between them decides the customer experience of every online card payment. Both flows give the same protection and the same liability shift, but they feel very different at checkout, so the analyst must understand what drives the issuer to choose one or the other.

ch22s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tokenization and network tokens. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a surrogate value that has no meaning on its own. For the analyst, this is a measurable benefit to track: approval rate and fraud rate, tokenized against non tokenized, for the same merchant.

ch22s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain device tokens and mobile wallets. Device tokens are the form of tokenization that powers mobile wallets such as Apple Pay and Google Pay. The analyst should confirm that refunds, chargebacks and reporting all carry the token through, end to end.

ch22s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chargeback lifecycle. A chargeback is the process by which a cardholder disputes a transaction and the funds are returned to them through the card system, rather than directly by the merchant. A business analyst working on dispute processes needs to understand the full lifecycle and the deadlines, because missing a deadline can mean losing a dispute that could have been won.

ch22s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reason codes and dispute handling. Every chargeback carries a reason code, and the code is the starting point for the whole dispute. The analyst must map each code to its evidence and its workflow.

ch23s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions exist. Sanctions are restrictions that governments and international bodies place on specific countries, organisations and individuals to achieve a foreign policy or security goal without using military force. For a business analyst, the practical point is that sanctions are not a policy document, they are a live data problem inside the payment flow.

ch23s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain main sanctions lists. The OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list, usually called the SDN list, is the most widely screened list in the world. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.

ch23s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain screening works in a payment flow. Screening happens at defined points in the payment lifecycle, and the timing matters as much as the matching itself. A possible match creates an alert in a work queue for a sanctions analyst to review, and the payment waits until the analyst clears it or escalates it.

ch23s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain name matching and fuzzy logic. Exact name matching would be useless for sanctions screening, because real payment data is messy. A score above a threshold creates an alert, and the threshold is a tuning decision that balances catching real matches against flooding analysts with noise.

ch23s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain false positives and alert triage. A false positive is an alert where the payment party shares a name with a listed person but is not that person. Each one still has to be reviewed by a trained analyst, because the bank cannot simply assume that a match is harmless.

ch23s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain true hits and what happens next. A true hit means the payment genuinely involves a sanctioned party, and the response depends on the sanctions programme. For a BA, this is a requirements point: the workflow must distinguish a blocking programme, where funds are frozen in a blocked account, from a rejection programme, where funds are returned to the sender, and it must record every step for the audit trail.

ch23s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fines, enforcement and lessons. Sanctions failures have produced some of the largest fines in banking history. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.

ch23s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT sanctions screening service. Every payment a bank sends or receives must be checked against sanctions lists: the lists of persons, entities, and countries that the law forbids doing business with. When a sanctions list changes, the bank needs to know what the change will do to its alert volumes before the change goes live.

ch24s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain money laundering really looks like. Money laundering is the process of making money from crime look like it came from a legitimate source, so that it can be spent or invested without attracting attention. For a business analyst, the key point is that anti money laundering controls are embedded in ordinary payment and account processes, not bolted on as a separate system.

ch24s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain KYC and customer due diligence. Know Your Customer, or KYC, is the process of identifying and verifying a customer before the bank does business with them. The bank must be satisfied that it knows who it is dealing with, and that the customer's expected activity makes sense for who they are.

ch24s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction monitoring. Transaction monitoring is the automated surveillance of customer activity after onboarding, looking for behaviour that does not fit the customer's profile or that matches known laundering patterns. A sudden change, such as a dormant account becoming active, or a customer whose usual pattern is domestic payments suddenly sending money to three new countries, is more suspicious than the absolute value alone.

ch24s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain suspicious activity reports. A Suspicious Activity Report, known as a SAR in the United States and a Suspicious Transaction Report in many other countries, is the formal report a bank files with its national Financial Intelligence Unit when it. For a BA, the requirements here cover the SAR workflow itself.

ch24s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain common fraud patterns in payments. Payment fraud takes many forms, but a few patterns account for most losses. For a BA, fraud requirements cover the full lifecycle.

ch24s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain machine learning in fraud detection. Traditional fraud detection relied on fixed rules, such as flagging any transaction above a set amount, but criminals learn the rules and stay just below them. Explainability matters too, because when a customer's payment is blocked, the bank must be able to explain why, and a regulator may ask how a model reached its decision.

ch24s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain building a fraud prevention culture. Technology alone will not stop fraud, because criminals adapt faster than systems do. Front line staff are often the first to spot something wrong, such as a customer who seems confused or pressured while making a large transfer, or a business customer whose invoice details have changed unexpectedly.

ch24s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain APP fraud and the UK psr reimbursement rules. Authorised push payment fraud, known as APP fraud, happens when a customer is tricked into sending money to a criminal. For a business analyst, the reimbursement rules create a full set of requirements.

ch25s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment hub. A payment hub is a central platform that processes many different payment types through one shared set of services, instead of each product having its own separate system. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch25s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain channels and the gateway. Channels are the places where a payment starts. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch25s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validation, enrichment and the processing engine. Validation is the set of checks that confirm a payment is complete, correct and allowed before any money moves. For example, take a payment from a corporate customer who sends EUR 50,000 to a supplier but leaves the beneficiary bank identifier blank.

ch25s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud, sanctions and compliance services. Fraud and sanctions services sit in the middle of the hub pipeline, and a payment cannot proceed until they have cleared it. The audit trail is critical, because a regulator may ask why a particular payment was released, and the bank must be able to show the fraud score, the sanctions result, the analyst's decision and the timestamp for each step.

ch25s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain routing, clearing and settlement. Routing is the decision about how a payment leaves the bank and reaches the beneficiary. The hub's settlement handling also covers liquidity management, because the bank needs enough funds in the right accounts to settle its payments.

ch25s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ledger, reconciliation and reporting. The ledger is the accounting heart of the hub, recording every movement of money as a double entry. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch25s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain design patterns and what good looks like. Several design patterns appear in almost every well built payment hub. For a BA, the practical takeaway is that hub requirements are never just about the happy path.

ch25s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: building a payment hub. A payment hub is built around five core components that work in sequence. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch26s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from files and SWIFT to real time APIs. For most of banking history, payments moved through files and messages that were exchanged in batches. For a business analyst, the API shift changes the nature of the work.

ch26s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain REST APIs for payments. Most modern payment APIs use REST, which is an architectural style built on standard HTTP methods and on resources that have clear identifiers. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch26s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 APIs. ISO 20022 began as a messaging standard for payment instructions, with well known messages such as pain.001 for customer credit transfers and pacs.008 for interbank transfers. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch26s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain PSD2 and open banking. The European Union's second Payment Services Directive, known as PSD2, changed the relationship between banks and their customers by giving customers the right to share their account data with third parties. For a BA, open banking work means understanding the regulatory requirements, the consent model, the API specifications, and the liability rules, because when a third party initiates a payment that goes wrong, the question of who is responsible must have a clear answer.

ch26s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer authentication: mfa, SCA and step-up. Customer authentication is the step where the customer proves who they are to the bank before an API is allowed to act for them, and it is separate from what the API is then allowed to do. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every channel and every payment type, which authentication method applies, what triggers a step-up, what happens when authentication fails, and what evidence is kept.

ch26s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain webhooks and event driven payments. Polling is the simplest way for a client to learn what happened to a payment. The bank must sign each webhook payload so the client can verify it really came from the bank, and the client must return a success response quickly, so the bank knows the notification was received.

ch26s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment initiation and the developer experience. Payment initiation is the API use case that changes the checkout experience most visibly. For a BA, the commercial requirements, pricing, service levels, and support commitments, are as important as the technical ones, because they shape what the API can promise to its users.

ch26s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: payment APIs at scale. The API gateway is the front door for all payment APIs, and it handles routing, security, and traffic management before any request reaches a backend service. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch26s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system authentication: OAuth2 grants, scopes, tokens and certificates. System authentication is the control where one system proves its identity to another system, with no person involved. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every system to system call, which grant type applies, which scopes the token carries, how long the token lives, how it is refreshed, whether mTLS is required, and how certificates are rotated.

ch27s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank digital currencies. A central bank digital currency, or CBDC, is digital money issued directly by a central bank, as a liability of the central bank itself, in the same way that physical cash is. For a BA, the practical point is that CBDCs are not a distant theory, they are a real product area, and the requirements skills used for any payment product, user journeys, limits, privacy, reconciliation and reporting, apply directly to them.

ch27s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ripple overview: ripplenet, xrp and on-demand liquidity. Ripple is a company whose products aim at the same problem as SWIFT gpi and the instant payment links: making cross border payments faster and cheaper. For a business analyst, the lesson is to evaluate the approach on its mechanics: how does the payment move, where does the liquidity come from, who bears the risk, and what does the regulator say.

ch27s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain agentic payment protocols, part 1: mcp, a2a and the agent stack. An AI agent is software that perceives, decides, and acts on behalf of a user, carrying out multi-step tasks without a human driving each step. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch27s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain agentic payment protocols, part 2: ap2, tap, agent pay, acp, ucp and x402. Six protocols, from six different parts of the industry, aim at the same problem: how does an AI agent pay safely?. For a business analyst, the evaluation questions are the same for all six: what is the trust model, which rails carry the money, who governs the protocol, and what happens when something goes wrong?

ch27s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain stablecoins and crypto payments. A stablecoin is a crypto asset designed to hold a stable value, usually by being pegged to a fiat currency such as the US dollar. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch27s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in fraud detection and operations. Artificial intelligence is already embedded in payment fraud detection, and its role is growing. Generative AI is being used to help analysts, by summarising a case, drafting a suspicious activity report narrative, or searching through transaction histories in response to a question in plain language.

ch27s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross border innovation: mbridge and project nexus. Cross border payments have been slow and expensive for decades, because they rely on correspondent banking, where a payment passes through several banks, each taking a fee and adding a delay, and where the sender often. For a BA, the lesson from both projects is that cross border innovation is not about one technology winning, it is about solving the same problems in different ways.

ch27s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain tokenisation and programmable money. Tokenisation is the process of representing a real world asset, such as a bank deposit, a bond, or a property, as a digital token on a ledger, so that it can be transferred and settled more efficiently. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch27s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain is real and what. Payments attract more hype than most industries, because money is universal and every new technology claims it will transform how money moves. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch27s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain this means for a payments BA. The emerging topics in this chapter all point in the same direction for a business analyst. The emerging topics in this chapter all point in the same direction for a business analyst.

ch27s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain stablecoin regulation in 2026: MICA and beyond. Stablecoin regulation has moved from discussion to law. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch27s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai across payments: reconciliation, fraud, customer service and operational decisions. Artificial intelligence is already working in payments, and it works in four places: reconciliation, fraud, customer service, and operational decisions. It predicts the liquidity a bank must hold for instant payments by learning the pattern of outbound flows through the day.

ch28s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain requirements gathering for payments projects. Requirements gathering is the first and most important phase of any payments project, because a requirement missed at this stage becomes a defect, a delay or a failed audit later. A business analyst starts by identifying every stakeholder group that touches the payment flow.

ch28s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business process modelling: as-is and to-be flows. Business process modelling turns a spoken description of how payments work into a diagram that everyone can read, challenge and agree on. The analyst always models the As-Is process first, which is how the payment flows today, including every manual step, every workaround and every delay.

ch28s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business rules and processing conditions. Business rules are the conditions that decide how a payment is processed, and in payments they are numerous, precise and often invisible until one of them is broken. The analyst's job is to find every rule, write it down in plain language, and make sure the system enforces it exactly.

ch28s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing jira user stories for payments. A user story is a short description of a feature written from the perspective of the person who needs it, and it is the unit of work that agile payments teams build, test and release. A story without a testable acceptance criterion cannot be built or tested, so the analyst who writes the criterion decides whether the developer builds the right mapping and whether the tester can prove it.

ch28s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain API analysis and interface specifications. An application programming interface, or API, is how one system asks another system to do something, and in payments the most common API is the payment initiation API, which lets a channel such as internet banking ask. The interface specification is the contract between the two systems, and the business analyst reads it to confirm that it covers every field, every validation and every error the business needs.

ch28s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BRD and FSD documents for payments. The Business Requirements Document, or BRD, records what the business needs and why, without describing how the system will be built. Consider a project to integrate UPI collect requests into a bank's corporate banking portal, so that a merchant can raise a collect request of 2,500 rupees against a customer who then approves it in their UPI app.

ch28s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain workshop facilitation: running a payments discovery workshop. A discovery workshop brings all the stakeholders into one room, or one video call, for a focused session to agree on requirements, and it is the fastest way to resolve the questions that stall a payments project. The analyst plans the workshop like any other deliverable.

ch28s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BA artefacts that carry a payment design: mapping sheets, sequence diagrams and flow diagrams. A payment design lives or dies by its artefacts. The business analyst does not just describe what should happen; the analyst produces documents that developers can build from, testers can test from, and operations teams can support.

ch29s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone brief: BA on a SWIFT MT to ISO 20022 migration. You are the business analyst assigned to a migration project at a mid-sized bank in Mumbai that sends around 12,000 outward cross-border payments a day, and your job is to move those payments from SWIFT MT format to ISO. You are the business analyst assigned to a migration project at a mid-sized bank in Mumbai that sends around 12,000 outward cross-border payments a day, and your job is to move those payments from SWIFT MT format to ISO 20022.

ch29s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT MT103 to ISO 20022 pacs.008 message mapping. A mapping document is a table that lists every field in the source message, the matching field in the target message, and the rule that converts one into the other, and it is the single most important deliverable of the migration. A mapping document is the single most important deliverable of the migration: if a field maps to the wrong element, the payment fails schema validation or settles the wrong amount, so the analyst who writes it decides whether the migration works.

ch29s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain API business data, rules and validations. The payment initiation API is the front door to the new ISO 20022 world, and it accepts payment instructions from channels such as internet banking, mobile banking and the corporate file upload service. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.

ch29s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain user stories and acceptance criteria for the migration. The first user story covers the core conversion. As a reconciliation analyst, I want a daily report showing every MT103 received and its converted pacs.008, so that I can prove no payment was lost or altered during migration.

ch29s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UAT scenarios and end-to-end test cases. A test case is a structured instruction that tells the tester exactly what to do and what result to expect, and it has a fixed format. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.

ch29s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hands-on BA deliverables checklist. The Business Requirements Document is the first deliverable on the checklist, and it is complete only when it states the business objectives, the scope with explicit exclusions, the prioritised requirements, the. The analyst keeps the signed version in the project repository and versions every change after sign-off.

ch29s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone exercise: trace a card payment end to end. The exercise starts at checkout, where a customer in Bengaluru buys a laptop for 85,000 rupees on an e-commerce website and pays with a Visa debit card. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.

ch29s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: an australian bank joins the npp. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a mid-sized Australian bank in Brisbane that has decided to join the NPP. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a mid-sized Australian bank in Brisbane that has decided to join the NPP.

ch29s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone: a US bank joins the rtp network. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a regional bank in Ohio joining the RTP network to offer real-time payments. The capstone brief places you as the business analyst for a regional bank in Ohio joining the RTP network to offer real-time payments.

ch2s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain credit transfers, the default business payment. A credit transfer is a payment instruction in which the payer, known as the debtor, instructs the debtor agent to transfer funds to the account of the payee, known as the creditor. For a business analyst, the two questions that matter most about a credit transfer product are how files are processed and when the cut off falls.

ch2s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain direct debits and pull collections. A direct debit is a pull payment in which the creditor, with the prior authorisation of the debtor, instructs the creditor agent to collect funds from the debtor account through the debtor agent. For a business analyst, direct debits require careful attention to mandates, notifications, and returns.

ch2s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cards, how a card payment really works. A card payment involves more parties than a simple transfer, and understanding the flow is essential for anyone working in retail payments. A business analyst must distinguish between authorisation, clearing, settlement, and dispute, and must know which system holds the truth at each stage.

ch2s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheques, still relevant in some markets. A cheque is a written, signed instruction from an account holder to a bank to pay a named payee a stated amount from the drawer account. For an analyst, cheque work is mostly about the exceptions.

ch2s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain e-money, wallets and newer instruments. E-money is electronically stored monetary value that represents a claim on the issuer and is accepted as a means of payment by parties other than the issuer. For an analyst, the key is to identify where the value is actually held, who is liable if the wallet provider fails, and how a payment from a wallet settles with the merchant.
