ch2s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real time versus batch payments. Real time payments settle individually, within seconds, at any time of day, including weekends and holidays. A business analyst must be able to explain when to use each model and what the customer should expect.

ch2s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain domestic versus cross border, retail versus wholesale. A domestic payment is one where the debtor and creditor accounts are held in the same country and usually in the same currency, and it is processed through a national clearing system. An analyst should state the classification of every payment product in the first paragraph of its specification, domestic or cross border, retail or wholesale.

ch30s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment gateway does. A payment gateway is the technology layer that sits between a merchant website or mobile application and the banking system. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch30s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway services. The payment page is the customer facing part of a gateway, and it must be fast, secure and easy to use. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch30s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway APIs. A gateway REST API is a set of secure web endpoints that a merchant system calls to create payments, check status and issue refunds. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch30s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain routing and retries. Smart routing is the decision a gateway makes, in milliseconds, about which acquirer should handle a given transaction. A gateway that offers only one acquirer cannot fail over, so multi acquirer support is a key question for a business analyst to ask during vendor evaluation.

ch30s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment aggregators vs gateways. A payment gateway is primarily a technology service. A business analyst must check the authorization status of any aggregator on the Reserve Bank website before recommending it, because an unauthorized aggregator puts the merchant at risk of frozen settlements and regulatory action.

ch30s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bas write gateway integration requirements. The work starts with a clear business objective and scope, written before any technical detail. The analyst also documents edge cases, error handling and the go live checklist, which are easy to forget.

ch30s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway fees and commercial models. The merchant discount rate, usually shortened to MDR, is the main fee a merchant pays on each card transaction, expressed as a percentage of the transaction value. The analyst must model the total cost, not just the headline percentage.

ch31s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card network roles. A card network is the rails that connect the issuing bank, which gives the card to the customer, with the acquiring bank, which serves the merchant. The cardholder is the customer who holds the card and makes the purchase.

ch31s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain visa message flow. A Visa authorization starts when the merchant sends a request through the acquirer to VisaNet, which is Visa global processing network. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch31s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mastercard message flow. A Mastercard authorization also starts with an ISO 8583 message from the merchant, through the acquirer, to the Mastercard network. When a business analyst writes an integration requirement for a Mastercard connection, the MIP is the component that must be installed, certified and tested, and certification includes test cases for approvals, declines, reversals, refunds and stand in processing.

ch31s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorization, capture, clearing, settlement. Authorization is the real time check that the card is valid and the funds are available. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch31s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interchange and scheme fees. Interchange is the fee that the acquirer pays to the issuer on every card transaction, and it is the largest component of the merchant discount rate. A business analyst who evaluates a gateway or acquirer must ask for the full fee schedule, including the rate for each card type, the cross border surcharge, the chargeback fee and the monthly minimum, and must model the cost using the merchant real transaction mix.

ch31s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NFC and contactless. Near field communication, known as NFC, is a short range wireless technology that lets a card or phone communicate with a payment terminal when held within about four centimetres. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch31s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chargebacks. A chargeback starts when a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank, instead of asking the merchant for a refund. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch31s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 8583 in depth: message types, data elements and the clearing message. ISO 8583 is the message standard for card transactions, and it is the language that the terminal, the acquirer, the scheme and the issuer use to talk to each other. For a business analyst, ISO 8583 is a message specification subject.

ch32s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain digital wallet architecture: where the money actually sits. A digital wallet is a prepaid stored value account held by a licensed issuer, and the balance you see on your phone is a claim on the issuer rather than money sitting in your own bank account. A business analyst must document this clearly, because confusing a wallet balance with a bank deposit leads to wrong requirements for interest, deposit insurance and account closure.

ch32s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet transactions: load, pay, send and withdraw. Loading money into a wallet is a pull from a funding source, and the most common sources are UPI, a debit card, net banking or a bank transfer. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch32s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet KYC: minimum KYC, full KYC and RBI PPI rules. Minimum KYC is the lighter tier, designed to let a customer start using a wallet quickly with only a mobile number verified through an OTP and basic details such as name and date of birth. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch32s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain wallet security: device binding, pin, biometrics and tokenization. Device binding ties a wallet to a specific phone, so that the wallet cannot simply be opened on a different device with a stolen password. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch32s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain POS systems overview: terminals, taps and swipes. A POS terminal is a certified payment device that captures card data, encrypts it immediately, and sends an authorisation request to the acquiring bank through the card network. From a business analyst perspective, a POS project is not just about the device, it is about the whole merchant journey, onboarding, terminal deployment, transaction processing, settlement, dispute handling and support.

ch32s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment acceptance at POS: authorization, settlement and reconciliation. Authorisation is the real time check that happens while the customer waits at the counter, and it usually takes two to three seconds. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch32s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain QR codes and soundbox: payments for small merchants. A QR payment starts with a code that contains the merchant payment address, usually a UPI ID or a merchant identifier, and sometimes the amount and a transaction reference as well. This matters because card payments are the highest-volume payments most banks process, and the four-party model decides who pays whom, when, and what happens when it goes wrong.

ch33s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH mandate processing in depth: from creation to activation. NACH is the centralised bulk payment system run by NPCI that allows banks and institutions to collect recurring payments from customers through mandates, and to make bulk credit payments such as salaries and dividends. The BA must specify the scanning quality, the image format, the rejection reason codes, and the customer communication for each rejection, because a customer whose EMI mandate is rejected may not know until the first EMI bounces.

ch33s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sfms: the structured financial messaging system. India domestic interbank payments run on a messaging system most people outside Indian banking have never heard of: SFMS, the Structured Financial Messaging System. For a business analyst working on Indian payments, SFMS is foundational knowledge.

ch33s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sdmc, mdmc and umrn: bulk file accounting and the NACH mandate reference. Three identifiers that look like alphabet soup carry real operational meaning in Indian bulk payments and mandates: SDMC, MDMC, and UMRN. For a business analyst, the lesson is that identifiers are infrastructure: the UMRN, like the accounting types, is a small piece of data that the whole operation depends on.

ch33s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ccil: the clearing corporation of india. A central counterparty, a CCP, stands between buyers and sellers in financial markets, guaranteeing settlement even if one side defaults. For a business analyst, CCIL teaches the CCP pattern that applies well beyond India.

ch33s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH debit and credit: presentation, settlement and returns. A NACH debit presentation starts when the user institution prepares a file of all the debits due on a given date and submits it to NPCI, usually one working day before the debit date. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch33s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bbps: how bharat bill payment works. BBPS is an integrated bill payment system that connects billers, such as electricity distribution companies, telecom operators, gas companies and insurers, to the customers who pay them, through a network of agent. Reconciliation is critical because a customer who has paid must never be marked as a defaulter by the biller.

ch33s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI mandate and autopay: requirements from a BA perspective. A UPI mandate is a standing instruction registered on the UPI platform that authorises a merchant to collect payments from a customer bank account through UPI, up to a defined maximum amount and within a defined period. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch33s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI architecture in depth: vpa, psp apps and the NPCI switch. The Virtual Payment Address, or VPA, is the identifier that makes UPI easy to use, because it replaces the bank account number and IFSC with a simple handle such as learner@okhdfcbank. That is why the bank needs a robust reversal and reconciliation process.

ch33s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fema compliance for payments it projects. FEMA is the Indian law that regulates foreign exchange transactions, and its core principle is that foreign exchange can only be dealt with through authorised persons, such as banks licensed as authorised dealers, and. A customer who has already remitted 240,000 dollars cannot remit a further 20,000 dollars in the same financial year.

ch33s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border payments from india: SWIFT, nostro, vostro and a worked example. SWIFT messaging is the network that carries the payment instructions between banks, and it is important to understand that SWIFT does not move money, it moves messages about money. A BA must document the charge options offered to the customer, the fee schedule for each option, and the disclosure that the customer sees before confirming the payment, because a customer who expected to receive 10,000 dollars and received 9,950 dollars will raise a complaint if the charges were not explained.

ch33s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain aeps: aadhaar enabled payment system. AEPS, the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System, is India interoperable banking service that lets a customer perform basic banking transactions at a micro ATM using only their Aadhaar number and their fingerprint, without a. For a business analyst, AEPS is a financial inclusion and operations subject.

ch33s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain dmt: domestic money transfer. DMT, Domestic Money Transfer, is India service that lets a person send money to any bank account in India using only the recipient mobile number or account number, without needing the recipient bank details or a bank. For a business analyst, DMT is an agent network and compliance subject.

ch34s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payments explained. A recurring payment is a payment that a merchant initiates on a schedule the customer agreed to in advance, without the customer being present for each charge. From a business analyst perspective, recurring payments are a rich area because they touch almost every system a merchant owns.

ch34s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain 3D secure requestor initiated (3ri) transactions. 3RI is a message type defined in the EMV 3D Secure version 2 specification, and it allows a merchant to request authentication for a transaction that the merchant initiates rather than the cardholder. For a business analyst, the important details of 3RI are the data elements and the error handling.

ch34s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain subscribe n save: the mycommerce project scenario. The myCommerce project describes an e-commerce merchant that sells everyday products such as groceries, household goods, and personal care items. The project scenario is used in business analyst training because it forces the analyst to think about the full lifecycle of a subscription, not just the checkout page, and that lifecycle is where the real complexity lives.

ch34s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing a use-case document for system-triggered payments. A use-case document starts with the basic identification fields, and these matter more than people think. A business analyst writes these as a numbered list so that testers can verify each one, and so that developers can code the checks in the right order.

ch34s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payment failure handling. The most common cause of recurring payment failure is an expired card. Dunning is the process of communicating with a customer whose payment has failed, and it is a mix of messaging, timing, and tone.

ch34s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card-on-file and tokenization for recurring. A card-on-file transaction is any transaction that uses payment credentials a merchant stored from an earlier transaction. From a business analyst perspective, card-on-file design means documenting several connected requirements.

ch34s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain recurring payments compliance. The Reserve Bank of India introduced its e-mandate framework for recurring card payments in 2019 and tightened it in 2021, and it changed the Indian subscription market completely. The pre-debit notification is the most important customer protection in the RBI framework, and it is a requirement that business analysts must design carefully.

ch34s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ebpp and eipp: electronic bill and invoice presentment and payment. A bill or an invoice is a request for payment, and presenting it electronically, with the payment attached, removes the friction of paper, post, and manual entry. For a business analyst, EBPP and EIPP design is three disciplines at once.

ch35s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain end-to-end payment platform design. Designing a payment platform from scratch starts with the business requirements, not with the technology. Data flow through the platform follows a consistent pattern that a business analyst must understand.

ch35s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment channels, hubs, engines and gateways. Payment channels are the points where customers and businesses start a payment. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch35s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement and reconciliation. Settlement is the process by which the money behind a payment actually moves between financial institutions. When a reconciliation break happens, the operations team follows a structured investigation process.

ch35s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payments certifications compared. The Payment Domain Certification is the most directly relevant certification for a business analyst working in payments, and it is offered by training providers such as . The Payment Domain Certification is the most directly relevant certification for a business analyst working in payments, and it is offered by training providers such as .

ch35s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain salary premium for payments bas. Payments business analysts in India typically earn 25 to 50 percent more than generalist business analysts with the same years of experience, and the premium grows with seniority. Payments business analysts in India typically earn 25 to 50 percent more than generalist business analysts with the same years of experience, and the premium grows with seniority.

ch35s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interview q and a for payments roles. When an interviewer asks what it means when a payment is settled, they want to hear that settlement is the final and irrevocable transfer of funds between banks to cover a payment. The final set of questions covers the business analyst side of payments.

ch35s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain your learning path forward. The eight-session learning path on this site is designed to take a business analyst from zero payments knowledge to job-ready domain expertise, and the best way to use it is in order, with practice between sessions. The eight-session learning path on this site is designed to take a business analyst from zero payments knowledge to job-ready domain expertise, and the best way to use it is in order, with practice between sessions.

ch36s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment hub architecture inside a bank. A payment hub is the central processing engine that receives payment instructions from every channel in a bank and routes each one to the correct destination. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch36s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message routing: from channel to rail. Routing begins with the information in the payment instruction itself. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch36s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain queueing and retry logic. Message queues exist because the systems in a bank do not all run at the same speed and are not all available at the same time. Apache Kafka is the newer technology, and it is used where a bank needs to stream very large volumes of events, such as logging every status change of every payment for analytics.

ch36s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation engines. A reconciliation engine compares two or more sets of records and reports the differences. The analyst starts with the payment reference and traces it through every system, the hub log, the payment engine log, the SWIFT message archive, and the core banking entries.

ch36s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exception queues. A payment lands in an exception queue when an automated check cannot be resolved by the system alone. Manual repair screens are the tools analysts use to fix these payments.

ch36s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain systems connect. APIs, or application programming interfaces, are the modern way for systems to talk to each other in real time. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch36s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain database design for payments. The payment instruction table is the core record. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch37s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain jpmorgan chase and citibank. JPMorgan Chase runs one of the largest payment operations on the planet, moving more than 10 trillion dollars a day across its wholesale payment systems. A business analyst working at either bank spends much of the time mapping fields between the old and new formats and testing that no data is lost in translation.

ch37s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hsbc and standard chartered. HSBC runs one of the largest trade and payments networks in the world, with a presence in more than 60 countries and a particular strength in Asia. A business analyst joining either bank will quickly learn that sanctions compliance is not a separate function; it is built into every step of the payment flow.

ch37s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank of america and wells fargo. Bank of America runs its payments through a central hub that connects to every US clearing system, Fedwire for high value same-day payments, the Clearing House for ACH bulk payments, and the RTP network for real-time. For a business analyst, the lesson from both banks is that domestic scale and global reach need different architectures.

ch37s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain deutsche bank and bnp paribas. Deutsche Bank runs its payment operations from Frankfurt, with a payment hub that connects directly to TARGET2, the real-time gross settlement system of the Eurosystem, and to STEP2, the pan-European clearing system for. The lesson for a business analyst is that consolidation is a long project, often taking five years or more, and it succeeds only when the business, operations, and technology teams agree on a single target design before the migration starts.

ch37s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain barclays and natwest. Barclays runs one of the largest payment hubs in the United Kingdom, processing more than 1 billion payments a year for retail customers, corporate clients, and correspondent banks. For a business analyst, BACS is a good example of a system where the business rules matter more than the technology, the direct debit guarantee, the indemnity claim process, and the rules for failed collections are all defined by the scheme, not by the bank.

ch37s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ubs and goldman sachs. UBS payment operations are built around its private banking and wealth management business. The lesson for a business analyst is that the right technology choice depends on the client base, a wealth manager needs security and service, an investment bank needs speed and integration, and a retail bank needs volume and cost.

ch37s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain more banks and what to learn from them. Morgan Stanley is similar to Goldman Sachs in that its payment operations are built around institutional clients, but it has a different emphasis, wealth management through its acquisition of E*TRADE and its large. The patterns a business analyst should recognise are the same in every large bank.

ch38s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks need a canonical payment model. A large bank receives payment instructions from many different places, and each place speaks its own dialect. When each channel connects directly to each payment system, the bank must build and maintain a separate translation for every pair, and a small change in one system can break several others without warning.

ch38s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain canonical model: core entities and fields. At the centre of the canonical model sits the payment instruction, the single record that represents one instruction to move money. This central record is the anchor that every other entity connects to, and it is the record that operations teams search for when a customer asks where a payment is.

ch38s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain source-to-target mapping and field transformation. Mapping starts with a mapping table that lists each source field, the canonical field it feeds, and the rule that governs the transfer. A good mapping table is a controlled document, reviewed by business analysts, developers, and operations staff, and changed only through a formal change request so that no one edits a live mapping by accident.

ch38s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data enrichment, normalisation and reference data. Enrichment adds information the customer did not supply, using data the bank already holds. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch38s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment identifiers, parties, accounts and amount precision. Every payment carries several identifiers, and each one has a different job. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch38s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data lineage, retention and auditability. Data lineage records the full journey of every field in a payment, from its source to its final destination. It records the customer who created the instruction, the operator who released it, the second approver who authorised a payment above GBP 50,000, the sanctions officer who cleared a false alert, and the system that rejected a payment for an invalid IBAN.

ch38s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hands-on exercise: pain.001 to canonical model to pacs.008. Emma Wilson logs in to Barclays online banking on the morning of 5 November 2026 and creates a new international payment. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch39s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain catalogue at a glance: PAIN, PACS, CAMT, admi and head. The ISO 20022 catalogue is organised into families, and each family is named by its first four letters. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch39s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.009 adv: the advice that accompanies a financial institution transfer. A pacs.009 is a financial institution credit transfer, the ISO 20022 message that moves money between banks. The ADV code sits alongside the other pacs.009 codes, and the analyst must know the set.

ch39s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain remt.001: the remittance advice. A payment tells the receiver that money is moving. For a business analyst, remittance advice design is reconciliation design.

ch39s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.035, camt.058 and camt.059: proprietary investigations and the notification to receive lifecycle. Three camt messages complete two pictures: the lifecycle of a notification to receive, and the handling of investigations that do not fit a standard format. For a business analyst, the lesson is about lifecycle and edge cases.

ch39s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.010: the financial institution direct debit. The pacs family has a credit message for customers, the pacs.008, and a credit message for financial institutions, the pacs.009. For a business analyst, the pacs.010 requirements cover the agreement data, the authorisation check, the debit posting, and the failure handling.

ch39s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer-to-bank: pain.001, pain.002, pain.008. The pain.001 message, Customer Credit Transfer Initiation, carries a customer instruction to move money from the debtor account to one or more creditor accounts. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch39s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank-to-bank: pacs.002, pacs.003, pacs.004, pacs.008, pacs.009. The pacs.008 message, FI to FI Customer Credit Transfer, is the most widely used message in cross border payments, and it carries a customer payment from the debtor bank to the creditor bank. Returns must be processed promptly, because a return that sits unmatched can look like a missing payment, and a customer who is not told about a return may believe the supplier has been paid when the money is on its way back.

ch39s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash management: camt.029, camt.052, camt.053, camt.054, camt.056. The camt.053 message, Bank to Customer Statement, is the formal end of day statement for an account, and it is the document a treasurer reconciles against the company ledger. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch39s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message identification, correlation, group header vs transaction info. Four identifiers do most of the work in ISO 20022, and confusing them is a common source of errors. An operations analyst who can follow those identifiers across five messages can answer a customer query in minutes, while an analyst who searches only by amount may find several payments of EUR 8,750.00 and choose the wrong one.

ch39s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mandatory, optional and conditional fields, schema validation, external code sets, version management and market practice rules. Every field in an ISO 20022 message has a usage rule, mandatory, optional, or conditional. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch39s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain practical exercise: transform an MT103 into pacs.008. Here is a pre-migration MT103 we will transform, sent before coexistence ended on 22 November 2025. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch39s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.060: the account reporting request. A treasury team needs to know the balance of its euro account at 11 in the morning, before it decides whether to fund a large payment. For a business analyst, the camt.060 is a small message with a clear use case, and the requirements around it are straightforward.

ch39s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.057 in depth: the notification to receive. A bank that expects a large credit needs to know it is coming, so that it can plan its liquidity, match the credit when it arrives, and chase it if it does not. The message carries the facts the receiving bank needs to prepare.

ch3s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain debtor and creditor, the two ends of every payment. The debtor is the party who owes the money and who instructs the payment, and the creditor is the party who is owed the money and who receives it. Analysts must therefore treat party data as a core part of the payment, not as a decorative extra.

ch3s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain debtor agent and creditor agent, the banks that act. The debtor agent is the bank or payment service provider that holds the debtor account and executes the payment instruction on behalf of the debtor. For a business analyst, the agent roles are essential for tracing a payment and for assigning ownership of a failure.

ch3s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intermediary banks and correspondent banking. An intermediary bank is a bank that sits between the debtor agent and the creditor agent in a payment chain and helps to move funds when the two agents do not have a direct relationship. As an analyst, you must be able to draw the chain for any payment you work on, name each intermediary, and explain why it is there.

ch3s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing houses and central banks. A clearing house is an institution that receives payment instructions from multiple banks, sorts them, calculates net positions, and prepares them for settlement. Analysts must understand the clearing cycle for each system they work with, including the cut off times, the settlement windows, and the consequences of a bank failing to settle.

ch3s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to name the scheme for a given payment, read a rulebook extract, map the parties in the four-party card model, trace the money and the fees through authorisation, clearing and settlement, and write a requirement that cites a scheme rule. A scheme is the rulebook that makes payments interoperable. Every payment you build must be traceable to a rule in that book, and a feature that violates scheme rules will be rejected in testing or lead to fines after launch.

ch3s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain regulators, compliance and oversight. A regulator is a public authority that oversees payment systems, payment institutions, and banks to ensure safety, stability, fairness, and compliance with the law. A business analyst must work closely with compliance teams and must understand the basics of anti money laundering, counter terrorist financing, sanctions screening, and fraud prevention.

ch3s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain players interact, a single payment story. Consider a simple example. A business analyst who can tell this story, name each player, and explain what each player does is able to diagnose problems quickly, write requirements that reflect reality, and communicate with operations, compliance, and technology teams in a common language.

ch3s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bank does. A commercial bank is the institution that holds money for people and businesses and moves it when they ask it to. For a business analyst, the practical point is that every payment design must name both layers: which commercial banks hold the customer accounts, and which settlement system and central bank accounts carry the final movement of value.

ch40s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation. A payment can pass every upfront check and still end up in the wrong place, which is why reconciliation exists as an independent control after processing. For a business analyst, reconciliation is also where business knowledge meets operational reality, because every break tells a story about a process gap.

ch40s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro reconciliation. A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency, and its name comes from the Latin word for ours, because the money in it belongs to the holding bank. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch40s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain internal ledger, clearing and settlement reconciliation. Every payment creates at least two ledger entries inside the bank, a debit and a credit, and the discipline of double-entry bookkeeping requires those entries to balance exactly. The practical lesson for analysts is that internal reconciliation is not one check but a chain of checks, and a break in any link can hide a break further down the chain.

ch40s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction-level matching: references, amounts, currencies and value dates. The payment reference is the primary key that links an internal record to an external statement line, and it must survive the whole payment journey unchanged. For example, a reference of sixteen characters sent through a system that allows only fifteen will lose its final digit, and the statement line will sit unmatched until an analyst manually links it by amount and date.

ch40s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain breaks: suspense accounts, unmatched transactions, duplicates and date mismatches. A suspense account holds funds temporarily when the bank knows money has moved but does not yet know where it belongs, and it must never become a permanent home. The operations team posts it to a suspense account, opens an investigation, and contacts the correspondent bank to ask who sent the money and why.

ch40s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain automated vs manual reconciliation and end-of-day processing. Automated reconciliation uses rules to match internal records against external statements at high speed and at high volume, and it is the only practical way to reconcile a large bank. Automation therefore removes the routine work and leaves the exceptions, which is exactly where skilled analysts add the most value.

ch40s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example and exercise: a bank sends 10,000 payments, 9,850 settled, 100 rejected, 30 returned, 20 have no corresponding settlement record. The starting point is the control total, because the engine must first prove that it is looking at the complete population before it matches anything. A return arrives as a pacs.004 message, often with reason code AC04 for a closed account or MD07 for an end customer who is deceased, and the engine matches it to the original payment by reference.

ch40s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain three-way reconciliation. Reconciliation proves that two records of the same activity agree. For a business analyst, reconciliation design is a requirements exercise with three inputs.

ch41s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exception landscape: what can go wrong. A payment exception is any payment that does not complete its intended journey cleanly, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit, and the scale of the problem is larger than most people expect. The exceptions range from a simple typing error in an account number to a clearing system outage that stops thousands of payments at once, and the operations team must triage them by value, by age, and by customer impact before it starts fixing them.

ch41s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain technical rejection vs business rejection. A technical rejection happens when a payment message fails a structural or format check, so the receiving system cannot even begin to process the business content. The reporting of the two types is different, and analysts must know which message to expect for each.

ch41s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment repair, return, recall and cancellation. Repair means correcting a payment that has been stopped before settlement, so that it can proceed without the customer having to start again. A payment of USD 60,000 may be held because the beneficiary address is incomplete, or because the intermediary bank details are missing, and the operations team can repair it by adding the missing information from the customer instruction or from a standing arrangement.

ch41s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigations, duplicate payments, timeouts and pending payments. An investigation begins when a customer reports that a payment has not arrived, or when reconciliation shows a payment with no matching settlement, and the analyst must reconstruct the payment journey from the available. An investigation begins when a customer reports that a payment has not arrived, or when reconciliation shows a payment with no matching settlement, and the analyst must reconstruct the payment journey from the available evidence.

ch41s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain unknown payment status, failed beneficiary credit and clearing system outage. Unknown payment status means the bank has sent a payment but has received no acknowledgement, no rejection, no return, and no settlement confirmation, so it cannot state with confidence whether the money moved. The bank must not assume the payment failed, and it must not assume it succeeded, because either assumption can cause a duplicate or a missing payment.

ch41s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 messages and reason codes for exceptions (pacs.002, pacs.004, camt.056, camt.029, pain.002 with real reason codes). The pacs.002 message, known as the payment status report, is the standard way for a bank to tell the sender whether a payment was accepted, rejected, or is still pending. Common codes include AC01 for an incorrect account number, AC04 for a closed account, AM04 for insufficient funds, AM05 for a duplicate payment, and MD07 for an end customer who is deceased.

ch41s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: trace one payment through every possible failure scenario (one USD cross-border payment traced through reject, return, recall, duplicate, timeout and outage, with what happens at each step). The payment begins as a customer instruction for USD 85,000, sent by the Mumbai company through its corporate banking channel, with the beneficiary account at a bank in New York and the value date set for 6 November. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch41s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain automating exceptions and investigations. Exceptions are the work that straight through processing cannot finish: the payment that failed validation, the funds that cannot be applied, the claim that money never arrived, the return that needs a decision. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch41s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message repair. Repair is the work of fixing a message that failed, so that it can proceed. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch42s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment testing. Payment testing is different because every test case touches value, and value cannot be undone with a simple refresh. When a payment system sends a pacs.008 for 125,000 pounds to the wrong beneficiary account, the bank must start a recall, contact the receiving bank, and explain the error to the customer.

ch42s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain test levels: unit, SIT, UAT and regression. Unit testing checks the smallest piece of code in isolation, and in payments that precision matters. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch42s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing test scenarios for happy path and negative path. A happy path scenario proves that the normal journey works from start to finish. If an operations user resubmits the same pain.001 file twice, or if a system retries a pacs.008 after a timeout, the bank must not send the money twice.

ch42s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme certification: what schemes and clearing systems demand. Scheme certification proves that a bank can exchange payment messages correctly with a scheme or clearing system. Before a bank can join SWIFT, it must prove that its MT103 and pacs.008 messages pass validation, that it can handle acknowledgements, and that its operations team can manage exceptions.

ch42s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain test data, environments and simulators. Good test data looks like real payment data, but it must never be real customer data. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch42s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defect management, entry and exit criteria. A defect in payments must be recorded with enough detail for a developer to reproduce it without guessing. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch42s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: build a UAT pack for a pacs.008 change. Start the exercise with a clear change description, because a UAT pack without a scope is impossible to sign. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch42s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain boundary, time-out and duplicate testing for real-time flows. Testing a real time payment flow is different from testing a batch flow, because the flow has hard edges: amount limits that reject a payment one unit over the line, time limits that turn a slow payment into a failed. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch43s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain threat model for payment systems. A threat model for payments starts with the simple fact that payment systems move money, and money attracts determined attackers. A payment operations analyst who can create, approve and release payments on their own could send 250,000 dollars to a personal account and hide the transaction.

ch43s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authentication: passwords, mfa, certificates and OAuth2. Passwords are the weakest form of authentication, yet they remain common in payment portals. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.

ch43s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain encryption in transit and at REST, key management and hsms. Encryption in transit protects payment data while it moves between systems. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.

ch43s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mTLS, API security and secure connectivity. Mutual TLS, known as mTLS, is TLS where both sides prove their identity with certificates. This matters because a compliance failure is not a process error, it is a regulatory breach, a fine, or a frozen payment. The controls in this lesson are what keep the bank out of trouble.

ch43s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT customer security programme and network security. The SWIFT Customer Security Programme, known as CSP, was created after a series of high profile frauds in which attackers used stolen SWIFT credentials to send fraudulent payment instructions. The bank must log every SWIFT session, every message sent and received, and every change to configuration or user access.

ch43s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud controls, monitoring and incident response. Fraud controls start before a payment is sent, with checks that look for risk in the instruction itself. A monitoring system might flag a customer who receives a large credit and then sends the full amount onward within an hour, a pattern known as money mule activity.

ch43s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: security review of a payment API. Start the review with the integration itself, so that you know exactly what you are checking. The treasury system will send payment instructions as JSON, the bank will return a pacs.008 reference and a pacs.002 status, and the customer will check balances through a separate read only API.

ch43s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system authentication: OAuth2 grants, scopes, token lifetimes and certificate rotation. System authentication is how one system proves its identity to another, and it is different from customer authentication in kind, not just in degree. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the scope for each operation, the scope each client type is entitled to, and the error returned when a client asks for a scope it does not have.

ch44s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain day in payment operations. A payment operations day starts before most customers wake up, because the first files and instructions are already waiting in the queues. When it does not, an analyst opens the repair screen, reads the error code, fixes the missing beneficiary account number and releases the payment again.

ch44s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cut-off management and processing calendars. A cut-off time is the last moment a payment instruction can be accepted for processing on a given value date. A customer who submits a payment of 500,000 pounds at 5 past 5 in the afternoon for CHAPS will therefore see a value date of the next working day, even though the money leaves the account immediately.

ch44s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain end-of-day processing, close and start-of-day checks. End of day processing begins when the last clearing system closes and no new same day payments can be released. The payment hub stops accepting instructions for the current value date and switches to the next value date, while the operations team runs the closing batches.

ch44s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intraday liquidity operations and monitoring. Intraday liquidity is the cash a bank has available to settle payments during the working day, as distinct from the cash it holds at the end of the day. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch44s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain operational controls, queues and exception handling. Operational controls are the rules and checks that prevent errors, detect them quickly when they happen, and limit the damage. A third control is the limit on what one analyst can release in a day, so a single compromised account cannot drain a large sum.

ch44s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain incident management, outages and business continuity. An incident is any event that stops or degrades payment processing, from a single system failure to a full site outage. The analyst who notices the problem logs it, states the impact in plain language and calls the incident manager.

ch44s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: run the operations shift. The scenario starts at 8 in the morning on a Tuesday in London. You are the operations team leader for a bank that processes 1.8 million payments a day.

ch44s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain kpi and kri: payment analytics. A payment operation that cannot measure itself cannot manage itself. The business analyst uses indicators to size problems, to justify change, and to prove improvement after it lands.

ch45s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment product manager actually does. A payment product manager owns a product from the first idea to the day it is retired, and is accountable for whether it makes money, serves customers well and stays within the rules. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.

ch45s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain product lifecycle: discovery, build, launch, grow, retire. Discovery is the stage where the manager learns whether a problem is real, who has it and whether they will pay to solve it. Discovery also checks the competition, for example whether Faster Payments already solves the problem, and checks the regulation, for example whether the bank needs a new licence.

ch45s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pricing, fees, interchange and commercial models. The cost of a payment has several layers, and a product manager must understand each one before setting a price. The manager chooses the model that matches how the customer values the service and how predictable the bank needs its revenue to be.

ch45s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain slas, kpis and measuring product health. A service level agreement, or SLA, is a formal promise about the service a customer will receive, with a remedy if the promise is broken. A service level agreement, or SLA, is a formal promise about the service a customer will receive, with a remedy if the promise is broken.

ch45s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain roadmaps, prioritisation and stakeholder management. A roadmap is a plan that shows the major features and changes for a product over the next twelve to eighteen months, grouped by quarter. Stakeholders in a payment product include the customers who use it, the sales team who sells it, the operations team who runs it, the risk team who approves it, the technology team who builds it and the senior executives who fund it.

ch45s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme changes, regulatory change and product impact. Scheme changes are updates to the rules, fees and technical standards published by the payment schemes, and they arrive on a fixed calendar. This matters because this is the work a payments BA, PO or SME actually produces: requirements, mappings, stories, test cases and traceability. It is the job, not the theory.

ch45s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: write a business case for an instant payments product. The market for this product is small and medium businesses in the United Kingdom that need to pay suppliers and staff quickly. A typical customer will make 180 payments a month, so the customer will pay 15 pounds plus 130 payments at 40 pence, which is 52 pounds, giving a total of 67 pounds a month.

ch46s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real-time really means. A real-time payment is a payment that moves from the sender account to the receiver account within seconds, with confirmation returned to the sender in the same session. A customer who sends EUR 1,000 to the wrong account in a SEPA Instant payment cannot recall it through the scheme in the same way as a standard transfer.

ch46s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain designing for 24/7 availability and low latency. Active-active architecture is the foundation of a real-time payment platform, because it keeps two or more data centres processing live traffic at the same time. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch46s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain timeouts, duplicate prevention and idempotency. A timeout is a decision point, not just a delay, because it forces the system to choose a next step when an answer does not arrive. The bank must therefore query the scheme for the status of that specific payment before deciding whether to retry, reverse, or mark it as unknown.

ch46s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real-time validation, screening and fraud checks in milliseconds. Account validation is the first check, and it must confirm that the beneficiary account exists and can receive funds. An analyst reviews the case in a workbench that shows the full payment details, the screening hits, and the fraud score.

ch46s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain instant settlement, liquidity and prefunding. Instant settlement means the receiver bank is paid at the same time as the beneficiary is credited, rather than hours later in a net batch. Treasury analysts study patterns by hour, by day of the week, and by season, and they build forecasts that predict the peak outflow.

ch46s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI, FEDNOW, faster payments and SEPA instant do it differently. UPI in India is built around a simple addressing model that hides account numbers behind a virtual payment address. A business analyst designing a new instant service must therefore start from the market, the regulation, and the customer need, and only then choose the technical pattern that fits.

ch46s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: design an instant payment flow (initiation to confirmation with timeouts, retries and failure handling). Start with the scenario and the actors, because a design without a scenario is only a diagram. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch46s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain comparing instant schemes through four design choices. The design choice framework compares instant schemes on four questions that every scheme must answer, whatever market it serves. The four questions cover addressing, message standards, settlement models, and overlay services, and answering the same four questions for any two schemes produces a comparison a business analyst can defend.

ch46s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain faster-payment non-functional targets: latency, availability and recovery. A faster payment system lives or dies on its non-functional targets: how fast, how available, and how recoverable. For a business analyst, non-functional requirements must be written like functional ones: quantified, measurable, and testable.

ch47s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain integration landscape inside a bank. A typical large bank runs several hundred applications, and a single payment can touch twenty of them before it completes. The business analyst must therefore map what exists before proposing what should exist, and must design integration that works with the legacy estate rather than pretending it will be replaced.

ch47s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain balance enquiry, account validation and posting: the core banking services every payment needs. Every payment integration makes three calls into the core banking system, and each call answers a different question before money moves. The business analyst must specify the queue rule, the rejection message, the reversal path, and the suspense handling before the integration goes live.

ch47s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain earmarking and fund reservation: holding money before the payment settles. A payment does not always move money the moment it is authorised. Release is not a reversal, and the distinction matters for the analyst and for the auditor.

ch47s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain host-to-host connectivity. A corporate treasury system and its bank can talk to each other in two ways: through a person at a portal, or directly, system to system. For a business analyst, H2H onboarding is an integration project.

ch47s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain core banking integration patterns. A synchronous call is the simplest pattern, and it fits real-time payments where the caller needs an immediate answer. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch47s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ledger, general ledger and accounting integration. A payment creates at least two ledger entries, because double-entry accounting requires a debit and a credit for every movement of value. Automated matching handles more than ninety-five percent of items, and the remainder go to analysts with the full message trail.

ch47s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gateway, aggregator and third-party service integration. A payment gateway is a service that accepts payment instructions from a bank or a merchant and forwards them to the correct scheme. The bank must test the service under load before launch, because a slow provider becomes the slowest step in the whole payment.

ch47s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain APIs, messaging queues, files and event streaming. Application programming interfaces, known as APIs, are the standard way for one system to ask another system to do something and receive an immediate answer. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch47s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain partner onboarding, certification and change management. Onboarding starts with a discovery workshop, where the bank and the partner agree on the business need, the volumes, and the technical approach. The bank must pass every case and provide evidence, such as message logs and screenshots, before it is allowed into production.

ch47s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: design the integration for a new payment rail (choose patterns, draw the integration map, define contracts and failure handling). Start with the scenario and the constraints, because they decide which patterns are possible. This matters because APIs and integrations are how systems talk to each other. A badly specified API is a failed payment, a duplicate, or a security hole.

ch47s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain openapi contracts: designing a payment API contract. Before a developer writes a single line of code, a bank publishes a contract for its payment API. For a business analyst, writing an OpenAPI contract is a requirements exercise, not a coding exercise.

ch47s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain event-driven payments and KAFKA: topics, partitions, ordering and replay. A payment hub processes thousands of payments a minute, and every important change is an event. For a business analyst, event-driven design changes how requirements are written.

ch48s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hub components: what a hub is and what it contains. A large bank rarely processes payments through one system. Each system has its own validation rules, its own sanctions screening, its own ledger posting logic and its own operations team.

ch48s10.agenda: This lesson is a cross-reference. The full Hub operations lesson is taught in ch48s9, Hub operations: running a payment hub day to day. Hub operations is taught once, in ch48s9, so that monitoring, queues, exception handling, incident response, change and release, capacity, and the worked example stay in one place.

ch48s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain components 1 to 6: from channel to screening. Payment Channels are where every payment instruction begins. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch48s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain components 7 to 12: from fraud checks to clearing. The Fraud Detection Engine scores every payment for the likelihood that it is unauthorised, manipulated or part of a scam. If it fails, payments stall in unknown states, duplicate processing becomes likely, and operations teams cannot tell a customer whether a 1 million dollar payment is sent, held or lost.

ch48s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain components 13 to 18: from settlement to audit. The Settlement Engine moves value to finalise a payment once clearing has accepted it. If it fails, payments settle in the clearing system but never appear on customer accounts, or debits are applied twice, so a customer who sent 25,000 dollars sees the money leave twice and calls the bank to complain about a duplicate debit.

ch48s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain architecture patterns: sync, async, events and idempotency. Synchronous processing means the caller waits for a reply before continuing, while asynchronous processing means the caller sends a request and continues, receiving the result later. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch48s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain resilience at scale: transactions, breakers and recovery. Distributed transactions are the hardest problem in hub design, because a payment touches many systems that cannot share one database transaction. Disaster recovery is the plan for losing a whole data centre, and it is measured with two numbers every analyst should know.

ch48s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain capstone exercise: draw the hub. Start with a blank page, landscape orientation, and draw four horizontal lanes labelled Channels, Hub Core, External Systems, and Books and Control. This matters because the architecture decides what the bank can build, how fast it can change, and where a payment can fail. Most payment requirements live in the architecture.

ch48s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cloud and deployment architecture for payment platforms. A payment platform that runs in the cloud does not run on one server. For a business analyst, the cloud architecture requirements are therefore about resilience, data residency, deployment safety and responsibility, not about which cloud provider is fashionable.

ch48s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hub operations: running a payment hub day to day. A payment hub is not finished when it is built; it must be operated every day, and the operational model is as much a design decision as the component catalogue. Hub operations is where most payment failures happen, so a BA must be able to specify monitoring, queue priority, exception handling, incident response, change control and capacity, not just the happy path.

ch49s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain standby letter of credit is. A standby letter of credit is a written undertaking by a bank to pay a stated amount to a named beneficiary if the applicant fails to perform a stated obligation. If the applicant defaults, the beneficiary can present a demand and the required documents, and the bank must pay.

ch49s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain standby vs commercial letter of credit. A commercial letter of credit is a payment instrument. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch49s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain parties involved and their roles. The applicant is the customer who asks the issuing bank to create the standby. The applicant is the customer who asks the issuing bank to create the standby.

ch49s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain issuance process. The process starts with the underlying agreement between the applicant and the beneficiary. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch49s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain notification, advising and confirmation. Notification starts when the issuing bank sends the standby to the advising bank. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch49s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain it is used and how banks process a drawing. A standby is used to guarantee payment of an advance. If the documents comply, the bank must pay.

ch49s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain risks, ucp 600 and isp98 rules. The applicant bears the risk that the beneficiary will draw even when the applicant believes it has performed. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch4s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain initiation, where every payment begins. Every payment travels through seven stages, and this chapter maps the whole journey before it looks at any one stage in detail. A good analyst documents the initiation channel, the mandatory fields, the validation rules, and the error messages for each failure, so that customers and operations teams know exactly what to fix.

ch4s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validation, screening and fraud checks. Once a payment instruction is accepted, it enters a stage of validation, screening, and fraud checking that is invisible to most customers but critical to the safety of the system. For a business analyst, this stage requires careful requirements.

ch4s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorisation and debit, committing the funds. Authorisation is the step where the debtor confirms that the payment should proceed, and the debtor agent commits the funds. If the debit happens early, the customer sees the money leave quickly, but the bank must manage the funds until settlement.

ch4s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain clearing, routing and message exchange. Clearing is the process by which payment instructions are exchanged between banks, sorted, and prepared for settlement. The message must carry all the information the next bank needs to process the payment, including the debtor and creditor details, the amount, the charges, and the remittance information.

ch4s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interbank settlement, moving value between banks. Interbank settlement is the movement of value between banks that makes the payment final. Analysts must understand the settlement model for each system they work with, the liquidity requirements, and the contingency arrangements.

ch4s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain crediting the beneficiary and notification. The final stage of the lifecycle is the credit to the beneficiary and the notification that the payment has arrived. Analysts must document the crediting rules, the return codes, the suspense account handling, and the notification content.

ch4s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exceptions, returns, recalls and investigations. No payment lifecycle is complete without exception handling, because a significant minority of payments will fail, be delayed, or need investigation. For a business analyst, exception handling is where much of the real work lies.

ch4s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: how the lifecycle is built inside a bank. A payment lifecycle is implemented as a finite state machine, and every state has a clear owner, a set of allowed transitions, and a set of actions that must complete before the payment can move on. Operations teams use this trail to answer customer queries, investigate delays, and prove compliance during audits.

ch4s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authentication: proving who you are before the money moves. Authentication is the control that proves who you are before a payment is allowed to move, and it is not the same control as authorisation. For a business analyst, product owner or subject matter expert, the test is to state, for every channel and every payment type, which authentication method applies, what triggers a step-up, what happens when authentication fails, and what evidence is kept.

ch50s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt101. MT101 is a SWIFT message type called Request for Transfer. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch50s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt101 structure: sequence a and sequence b. Sequence A is the general information sequence. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch50s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field 50a ordering customer in sequence a vs sequence b. Field 50a in Sequence A names the ordering customer for the whole MT101 message. Option F carries structured party identification, with name, address, and account details in a coded format, and is used when the bank needs a precise identification for regulatory reporting.

ch50s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain two domestic transactions in one mt101. A corporation may need to make two domestic payments on the same day, for example a salary payment and a supplier payment, or two supplier payments to different cities. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch50s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain paying from multiple debit accounts. A corporation may hold an operating account, a tax account, and a payroll account at the same bank, and it may need to pay from more than one of them in a single run. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.
