ch50s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain paying from a subsidiary account and paying on behalf of subsidiaries. Paying from a subsidiary account means the money leaves an account owned by the subsidiary, even though the parent treasury team sends the instruction. The bank must hold a mandate for either pattern before it will act.

ch50s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain funds repatriation and a full worked example. Funds repatriation is the transfer of surplus cash from a subsidiary to its parent, often as a dividend, a loan repayment, or an intercompany settlement. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch51s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain documentary collection is. A documentary collection is a payment method in which an exporter ships goods and then asks banks to handle the shipping documents on agreed terms. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch51s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain roles: remitting bank and collecting bank. The remitting bank is the exporter bank, the bank to which the exporter entrusts the documents and the collection instruction. If the instruction says release documents only against payment of EUR 95,000, the collecting bank must not release them for EUR 90,000, or against a promise to pay next week.

ch51s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain documents against payment and documents against acceptance. Documents against payment, usually written as D/P, means the collecting bank may release the documents to the importer only after the importer has paid the full amount stated in the collection instruction. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch51s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain collection process. The process begins with the sales contract between exporter and importer, which must state the collection terms clearly. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch51s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT category 4 messages explained. SWIFT Category 4 covers collections, cash letters and related advices, and it exists so that banks can exchange collection instructions and status updates in a standard structured form. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch51s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt400: advice of payment and announcing the proceeds. Before an MT400 is sent, the collecting bank must have completed the presentation and obtained payment or its equivalent. Before an MT400 is sent, the collecting bank must have completed the presentation and obtained payment or its equivalent.

ch51s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a EUR 250,000 documentary collection from a french exporter to a spanish importer, traced from remitting bank to collecting bank to mt400 and final credit. The trade begins in Lyon, where a French exporter, Rhone Packaging SA, sells EUR 250,000 of pharmaceutical packaging to a Spanish importer, Iberia Pharma SL in Madrid. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch52s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reporting messages matter. A reporting message tells an account holder what has happened to its account, after the payments have been made. If the two records differ by even one cent, or by one day, the item becomes a break that an analyst must investigate.

ch52s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt941: the balance report. The MT941 is the Balance Report, the answer to the MT920 request. A treasurer deciding whether to fund an account, a liquidity manager checking a buffer, or an operations team confirming that an expected receipt has landed all read the same message for the same reason: to know where the account stands.

ch52s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT910 confirmation of credit. The MT910 Confirmation of Credit is sent by an account servicing bank to its account holder to advise that a specified amount has been credited to a specified account. If the MT910 arrives but the statement line is missing, the operations team must raise a query with the bank the same day.

ch52s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT940 customer statement. The MT940 Customer Statement Message is sent by an account servicing bank to its customer, or to another bank on behalf of a customer, to provide a statement of the account for a defined period, usually one business day. A statement line for EUR 85,000 with no narrative is almost useless to a reconciliation analyst, who must guess whether it is a supplier refund, a customer payment or an intercompany transfer.

ch52s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT950 statement message. The MT950 Statement Message is sent by an account servicing bank to the owner of an account, and it provides a statement of the account for a defined period, in a format designed for bank to bank use. The key difference is that the MT950 does not carry Field 86 information to account owner lines in the same way as the MT940, because the receiving bank needs the entries and balances for its own ledger, not customer facing narrative.

ch52s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT940 balances: f60a opening balance, f62a closing balance (booked funds), f64 closing available balance (available funds), f65 forward available balance. Field 60a, the opening balance, is the balance of the account at the start of the statement period, before any of the transactions in this statement are applied. If the previous closing balance was EUR 480,000 and this opening balance is EUR 475,000, the statement is broken before a single transaction is read, and the bank must be asked to correct it.

ch52s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciling statements: MT940, MT950 and camt.053. Reconciliation of an MT940 starts with three control checks before any transaction is matched. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch52s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a full MT940 with opening balance, transactions, closing balance and forward available balance, reconciled line by line. The account is a euro current account held by Meridian Foods GmbH at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, account DE89 3707 0060 0123 4567 89, statement number 142, for 2 November 2026. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch52s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from MT900 and MT910 to camt.054: debit and credit notifications across the migration. The camt.054 Bank to Customer Debit Credit Notification is the ISO 20022 message that advises an account holder of a single debit or a single credit, and it is the successor to MT900 and MT910. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch52s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt920: the request message that asks for a balance report. Balances change all day. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch53s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain basic MT103 decrypted: mandatory fields only. An MT103 is a single customer credit transfer instruction sent through SWIFT FIN. If two payments carry the same reference on the same day, operations teams cannot tell them apart, so uniqueness is a control, not a courtesy.

ch53s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field 52a ordering institution: when and why it appears. Field 52a identifies the ordering institution, the financial institution that ordered the payment on behalf of the ordering customer, when that institution is different from the sender of the MT103. Operations teams check this rule first when they validate a payment, because a wrong 52a can misdirect a compliance query.

ch53s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field 57a account with institution: when and why it appears. Field 57a identifies the account with institution, the bank at which the beneficiary holds the account that must be credited. A payment of 250,000 pounds to a beneficiary in London that names the wrong account with institution can sit in a repair queue for three days while operations teams exchange MT199 free format messages to correct it.

ch53s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain 52a and 57a change across the serial chain. In the serial method, each bank in the chain sends a fresh MT103 to the next bank, deducts its own charge if the charge option allows it, and forwards the remaining amount. Field 50a, the ordering customer, also stays the same, because the customer who ordered the payment does not change as the money moves.

ch53s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field 53b sender's correspondent and how cover differs. Field 53B identifies the sender correspondent, the bank at which the sender holds the account that will be debited to fund the payment. Serial is simpler to trace because each MT103 carries the full customer details and the funds move with it, but it can be slower because each bank must process the message in turn.

ch53s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field 70 remittance information and field 71g receiver's charges. Field 70 carries remittance information, the free text that tells the beneficiary what the payment is for. Operations teams use fields 70, 71F and 71G to resolve the two most common beneficiary queries.

ch53s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: the full USD 367,574.90 payment from bnp paribas paris (bnpafrpp) to banco santander madrid (bschesmm) via wells fargo (pnbpus3n, USD 20 charge) and bank of new york mellon (irvtus3n, USD 22 charge), reference 103ref405775, charges sha, beneficiary account es6300491800132710387658, final settled USD 367,532.90, with every optional field explained as it appears and disappears across the three mt103s. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as MT103s. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch53s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT103 stp variants, the :77t: envelope and message user group registration. The MT103, the single customer credit transfer, exists in three forms, and the form is signalled by a single code in the message header. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch54s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT. SWIFT is a member owned cooperative based in Belgium that provides secure messaging services to more than 11,000 financial institutions in over 200 countries and territories. Analysts who understand this boundary can trace a delayed payment correctly, ask the right bank the right question, and avoid blaming the messaging network for a liquidity or compliance problem that belongs to a bank.

ch54s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain finplus: the channel that carries ISO 20022 on swiftnet. The FINplus service is the SWIFTNet channel that carries ISO 20022 messages between banks, and it is the successor to FIN. The bank must send the right format to the right counterparty, because a counterparty that is ready for ISO 20022 receives FINplus traffic while a counterparty still on MT receives FIN traffic.

ch54s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment controls: the SWIFT service that screens payments in flight. A fraudulent payment that has left the bank is hard to recover, so the best place to stop it is while it is still in flight, between the back office and the network. The analyst must design the alert handling process with the same care as the screening rules, because a screening service that nobody watches is worse than no service: it creates delay without creating safety.

ch54s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain uak and unk: how SWIFT knows a message was delivered. Sending a SWIFT message is not the same as delivering it. Operations teams watch these alongside the ACK, NAK, UAK, and UNK flow, because a message can be ACKed by the network and still never reach the receiver: it can sit undelivered, it can be aborted, or the receiver interface can fail to acknowledge it.

ch54s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT browse: the interactive channel of swiftnet. SWIFTNet, the network that carries SWIFT traffic, offers three service families, and only two of them move messages between applications. For a business analyst, the practical point is to ask, for every SWIFT service in scope, which channel it uses.

ch54s14.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain routing restrictions: controlling where SWIFT messages can go. A SWIFT message does not go everywhere by default. A business analyst who understands routing restrictions can diagnose a rejected message in minutes; one who does not will chase the message format while the real problem sits in an authorisation table.

ch54s15.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message user groups in depth: how communities agree on message use. A message standard is a skeleton. For a business analyst, the working rule is simple: never implement a message, implement a guideline.

ch54s16.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain score, ma-cug and trco: how corporates connect to SWIFT. Corporates connect to SWIFT through closed user groups, and three models dominate. For a business analyst, the CUG model matters at onboarding and at troubleshooting.

ch54s17.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain snl and the alliance products: the software that connects a bank to SWIFT. A bank does not connect to SWIFTNet by plugging a cable into the wall. A business analyst specifying a SWIFT integration must specify the interface behaviour alongside the message behaviour: the queue, the routing, the validation, and the failure handling.

ch54s18.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT y-copy: when a third party gets a copy of the message. Sometimes a payment message needs a third reader. A central bank needs to see the flows in its currency, for oversight and liquidity management.

ch54s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain swiftnet: how banks connect. SWIFTNet is a private, closed network that connects member institutions to SWIFT services. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch54s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT message types, groups and categories. SWIFT message types are three digit numbers, and the first digit is the category. Category 1 is the most familiar to payment operations teams.

ch54s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BIC code: ISO 9362 and how a BIC identifies an entity. A BIC, or Business Identifier Code, is defined by the ISO 9362 standard and identifies a financial institution or a branch of that institution. A payment sent to DEUTDEFFXXX will be handled by the head office, while a payment sent to DEUTDEFF500 will be handled by that specific branch, which may have its own accounts and operations team.

ch54s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BIC routes a message across swiftnet. Routing begins when the sender enters the receiver BIC in the payment system. That acknowledgement is the evidence operations teams use when a customer asks whether a payment was sent.

ch54s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fin, interact and fileact. FIN is the original SWIFT service, and it carries MT messages such as MT103, MT202 and MT950 in a store and forward model. Operations teams must know which service carried each leg, because the investigation path is different for a FIN message, an InterAct exchange, and a FileAct transfer.

ch54s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: follow one message from a bank in paris to a bank in singapore. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as an MT103. Its operations team screens the ordering customer and the beneficiary against sanctions lists, checks the account number 003912345678, and confirms that the value date of 5 November 2024 has been met.

ch54s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rma: the authorisation that lets banks exchange messages. RMA, the Relationship Management Application, is the authorisation that decides whether one bank may send a SWIFT message to another bank. Harbour Bank might authorise Meridian Bank to send customer payment messages only, while Meridian Bank must grant its own separate authorisation for messages in return.

ch54s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ack and nack and what network validation checks. ACK and NACK are the short answers SWIFT sends back after a bank transmits a message, and together they tell the sending bank whether the message entered the network. Operations teams monitor ACK and NACK traffic as a routine control over every message the bank sends, because an unmatched message is a payment whose fate is unknown.

ch55s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 and one leg out: what changes next. One leg out describes a payment where one part of the journey uses ISO 20022 and the other part does not. A bank must therefore decide, field by field, what is preserved, what is mapped and what is lost, and it must record that decision in a mapping table that operations and compliance teams both understand and test.

ch55s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CBPR+ after migration: what comes next for cross-border payments. CBPR+ moved cross border payments onto ISO 20022, but migration alone did not make payments faster or cheaper. A business analyst should ask, for every new requirement, whether it uses ISO 20022 data to remove a manual step or only adds another field to an old process.

ch55s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain open banking reshaping payments. Open banking lets a regulated third party start a payment directly from a customer bank account, with the customer consent, instead of using a card network. For a business analyst, this means the payment flow has extra steps that a normal transfer does not have, including consent capture, consent storage and consent expiry.

ch55s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cryptocurrencies reshaping payments. A cryptocurrency is a digital asset that moves on a distributed ledger, without a central bank or a traditional clearing system in the middle. That speed is valuable, but it also means a mistaken payment cannot be recalled through a banking operations team in the same way.

ch55s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain open banking meets crypto: two forces together. Open banking and crypto are usually discussed separately, but together they describe a payment that starts in a regulated bank account and settles on a digital ledger. A business analyst working on this design should map every handoff, name the party responsible for each one, and test the failure cases, including a failed conversion, a lost peg and a wallet that cannot be reached.

ch55s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain this means for banks, bas and architects. Banks must rethink their operating model, not just their technology. The change needs product owners who understand the whole payment journey, operations teams who can work across rails, and compliance teams involved from the start.

ch55s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: design a 2026-ready payment product. Your brief is to design a payment product for a small business that imports goods from three countries and pays suppliers in euros, dollars and pounds. This matters because the next payment product you work on may use one of these technologies. Knowing what is real and what is still a proposal is what separates a good analyst from a confused one.

ch56s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain target2 does not exist anymore: what went live on 20 march 2023. TARGET2 stopped operating after business on Friday 17 March 2023, and the new TARGET services went live on Monday 20 March 2023. A business analyst who writes TARGET2 on a new design document will confuse developers, testers and operations teams, because the accounts, the messages and the connection are all different.

ch56s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain three target services: T2, T2S and TIPS. TARGET is now a family of three services, and each one settles a different type of business. A customer who sends EUR 500 to a friend on a Sunday evening does not wait until Monday morning.

ch56s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain inside T2: CLM central liquidity management and the main cash account (MCA). Central Liquidity Management, known as CLM, is the component of T2 that manages central bank money for each participant. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch56s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain inside T2: RTGS real-time gross settlement. RTGS, which stands for Real-Time Gross Settlement, is the component of T2 that settles large value euro payments. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch56s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain T2S securities settlement and TIPS instant settlement. T2S settles securities transactions in central bank money, and it does so for the whole euro area on one platform. A retail customer who sends EUR 250 to a friend at 20 minutes to midnight on a Saturday expects the money to arrive in seconds, not on Monday morning.

ch56s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain esmig, multi-currency support and the legal framework (guideline (EU) of the ecb on target, repealing guideline ecb/2012/27). ESMIG, the Eurosystem Single Market Infrastructure Gateway, is the single entry point through which banks reach T2, T2S and TIPS. A bank that joins T2 signs up under the new Guideline, not under the old TARGET2 rules, and its lawyers, compliance team and operations team all work from the same legal text.

ch56s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a EUR 10 million payment through T2 and a EUR 5,000 instant payment through TIPS, traced step by step. A German car maker, a customer of Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, instructs a EUR 10 million payment to an Italian supplier, a customer of UniCredit in Milan. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch56s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain T2 ISO 20022 message catalogue: which messages the eurosystem uses. T2 is the Eurosystem real time gross settlement system, the platform on which euro high value payments settle in central bank money, and every message that moves through it is an ISO 20022 message. The analyst who builds a T2 connection starts from the catalogue, not from the general ISO 20022 standard.

ch57s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain addressing works in the RTGS component of T2. Addressing in T2 RTGS starts with the BIC, the Bank Identifier Code that names a bank or a branch in the payment. A bank that sends a EUR 750,000 payment with the wrong value date will see it sit in a queue, not settle, and its operations team must check the date before it calls the payee bank.

ch57s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS directory and crdm common reference data management. The RTGS Directory is the published list of every party that can be addressed in the RTGS component of T2. The directory is the single source of truth for addressing, and every T2 bank must use it.

ch57s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain participation types: direct, indirect, multi-addressee and addressable BIC (05, 06, 07, 08). A direct participant, code 05 in the RTGS Directory, is a bank that holds its own RTGS Dedicated Cash Account in T2 and connects directly to the system through ESMIG. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch57s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain indirect participation plays no direct role in EUR settlement. Indirect participation is registered as a participation type in the RTGS Directory, but it plays no direct role in euro settlement, because no euro settlement is ever booked on an indirect participant account. The practical lesson for a business analyst is simple, and it prevents a common design error.

ch57s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain technical layer: every message is addressed to the system itself. Every message sent to T2 is addressed to the system itself in the Business Application Header, known as the BAH. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch57s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain T2 with a CBPR+ leg: multi-addressee in practice. A direct participant can authorise its branch to submit and receive payments directly to T2 without their involvement, and that branch is the multi-addressee. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch57s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: address three payments in T2. Read the three cases carefully, and write down your answer for each one before you check it against the text that follows. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch58s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reject vs return: the one rule that decides. The one rule that decides reject versus return is timing, and it is simple to state. Operations teams that learn this rule first make far fewer errors than teams that try to memorise lists of reason codes.

ch58s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.002 payment status report. A pacs.002 is a status report that an agent sends to the previous agent in the payment chain to report the outcome of a payment instruction. These optional reports help corporate treasurers who need to know where a USD 250,000 supplier payment stands, and they help operations teams to spot a stuck payment before the customer calls.

ch58s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.004 payment return. A pacs.004 is a separate settlement instruction from the original payment, and that separation is the most important thing to understand about returns. Operations teams must read the settlement method on every pacs.004 before they post it, because the method is the settlement instruction itself.

ch58s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro and vostro relationships and the inda/inga settlement method in reject and return flows. A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency, and the word means our account with you. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch58s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a rejected USD 100,000 payment traced bank by bank. The payment starts with a corporate debtor in New York, a textile importer called Hudson Trading, which owes USD 100,000 to a supplier in Germany called Rhein Textil GmbH. Because the payment has reached a final negative status, Deutsche Bank must send a pacs.002 to inform the previous agent, which is Citibank in London.

ch58s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a returned EUR 50,000 payment with a partial amount and charges. The payment starts in London, where a property company called Thames Estates pays EUR 50,000 to a contractor in Paris called Seine Renovations, for work on an office building. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch58s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exercise: decide reject or return. Scenario one. The funds are already in the beneficiary account, so the correct answer is a return, and Citibank must send a pacs.004 for USD 120,000 with reason DUPL and settlement method INDA, while the return chain lists Citibank, the intermediary bank, and the original debtor in order.

ch58s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT103 and MT202 reject and return flows: what happens when a payment comes back. A payment that cannot be completed does not simply disappear. The analyst must design for both flows.

ch59s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain TIPS. TIPS stands for TARGET Instant Payment Settlement, and it is a service of the Eurosystem that settles instant payments in central bank money, around the clock, every day of the year. Under the SCT Inst scheme, the maximum execution time for an instant payment is ten seconds from the moment the payer bank receives the instruction until the payee bank must have the funds available.

ch59s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain instant payment between two TIPS participants: process flows. The SCT Inst scheme is the rulebook that governs instant credit transfers in euro across the Single Euro Payments Area, and it sets the ten second deadline that every participant must meet. Under SCT Inst, the payer bank must send the payment, the payee bank must accept or reject it, and the funds must be available to the payee, all within ten seconds.

ch59s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain messages and statuses: pacs.008.001.08 and pacs.002.001.10. The payment instruction in TIPS is a pacs.008.001.08, which is version eight of the FI to FI Customer Credit Transfer message. The status trail for a successful payment therefore reads Received, then Validated, then Reserved, then Settled, and each step is recorded so that operations teams and auditors can reconstruct the payment in seconds if a customer asks.

ch59s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity transfers in TIPS: the deposit model and the three basic rules. TIPS uses a deposit model for liquidity, which means that a participant holds its instant payment liquidity in a TIPS Dedicated Cash Account, known as a TIPS DCA, and that account is funded by moving money from the. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch59s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.050, camt.025 and camt.054, a2a and u2a modes, TIPS DCA vs TIPS as technical account. The camt.050 Liquidity Credit Transfer message is the instruction that starts a liquidity transfer in TIPS. The camt.025 is therefore the receipt that closes the instruction, and operations teams match every camt.050 to its camt.025 before they treat a liquidity transfer as complete.

ch59s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain inbound and outbound liquidity transfers via transit accounts. A transit account in TIPS is a technical account that sits between TIPS and TARGET, and it is used to move liquidity between the two services. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch59s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a EUR 2,000 instant payment and a EUR 500,000 inbound liquidity transfer, traced. The instant payment starts with a customer in Lyon, a freelance designer called Claire Moreau, who owes EUR 2,000 to a supplier in Berlin called Weber Studio. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch59s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rt1 and how it differs from TIPS. RT1 is the instant payment system operated by EBA Clearing for SCT Inst payments in euro, and it clears and settles those payments between banks across Europe around the clock. A bank with a long clearing relationship with EBA Clearing may start with RT1, because the operator, the rules, and the funding pattern are already familiar to its operations team.

ch5s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT MT is. SWIFT MT, where MT stands for Message Type, is the long established messaging standard used by banks around the world to exchange payment instructions and related information. The fixed field structure also makes MT messages relatively easy to parse, to test, and to repair, which operations teams value.

ch5s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT message blocks 1 to 5: how to read a raw message. Every SWIFT MT message is built from up to five blocks, each wrapped in curly brackets and numbered 1 to 5. That skill lets an analyst read any MT message without a tool.

ch5s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: SWIFT connectivity inside a bank. A bank connects to SWIFT through Alliance Access and Alliance Gateway, which together form the bank's SWIFT interface. Operations teams use it to prove that a payment was sent, to investigate a missing payment, and to reconcile SWIFT traffic against the payment engine.

ch5s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt102, many customer transfers in one message. The MT102 is the SWIFT message that carries many customer credit transfers inside a single message. An analyst who meets one should still be able to read it: find the batch total in Sequence C, count the transactions in Sequence B, and reconcile the two before investigating any single payment inside it.

ch5s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt210, notice that funds are coming. The MT210 is an advance notice that funds are on their way, and it moves no money itself. For a business analyst, the MT210 is a control message rather than a payment, and the design questions are about matching rules, suspense handling, and the reconciliation of notices against statements.

ch5s14.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt191: requesting payment of charges, interest and other expenses. When a bank has incurred charges or interest on behalf of another bank and cannot deduct them from the payment itself, it needs a way to ask for the money. The analyst must check which of the two the business process needs before specifying either.

ch5s15.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt195, mt196, mt199 and mt299: queries, answers and free format messages. Not every message between banks fits a structured payment format. Sometimes one bank needs to ask another a question, answer one, or send a message that does not fit any other type.

ch5s16.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt104: direct debits and requests for debit transfer. The MT104 is the SWIFT message that pulls money instead of pushing it. A direct debit is a pull on somebody else account, so the debtor bank must be satisfied that the debtor agreed to the debit before it acts.

ch5s17.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt200, mt201, mt203 and mt204: financial institution transfers and direct debits. Category 2 of the SWIFT MT standard holds the messages banks use to move money between themselves. Four of them form a family that every payments analyst should be able to tell apart: the MT200, the MT201, the MT203, and the MT204.

ch5s18.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt670 and mt671: exchanging standing settlement instructions through SWIFT. Every payment needs to know where to settle, and that knowledge is a standing settlement instruction, usually shortened to SSI. For a business analyst, the lesson is about static data discipline.

ch5s19.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt198: the proprietary message. Not every exchange between banks fits a standard message. A business analyst should treat every proprietary message as a liability to be managed: documented, versioned, and reviewed regularly against the question of whether a standard message now covers the need.

ch5s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT103, the customer payment. The MT103 is a single customer credit transfer message, and before the CBPR+ migration it was the most widely used cross border payment message in the world. A business analyst must understand the MT103 field structure, the mandatory versus optional fields, and the business meaning of each field, because those details determine whether the payment is processed automatically or falls into a repair queue.

ch5s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT202, bank to bank cover payments. The MT202 is a general financial institution transfer, and it is used for bank to bank payments where the originator and the beneficiary are both financial institutions. An analyst must be able to explain the cover method, draw the two message flows, and identify where the customer data is visible and where it is not.

ch5s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT900 and MT910, confirmations of debit and credit. The MT900 is a confirmation of debit, and the MT910 is a confirmation of credit. Analysts should include MT900 and MT910 in their payment flow diagrams and in their reconciliation requirements, because they are the link between the payment instruction and the actual movement of funds.

ch5s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT940 and mt942, account statements. The MT940 is a customer statement message that provides the end of day statement for an account, usually a nostro or vostro account held with another bank. An analyst who understands MT940 and MT942 will find the camt messages familiar, because the business concepts of opening balance, transactions, and closing balance are the same.

ch5s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain field structure, how to read an MT message. An MT message is divided into blocks, and the text block contains tagged fields. A business analyst who can read an MT103 can investigate a payment delay, can explain a deduction to a customer, and can write test cases that reflect real payment data.

ch5s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to read a real MT103, worked example. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, when an MT103 was still the message for a cross-border customer payment. If the beneficiary receives less than ten thousand dollars, the analyst can use the MT103 to explain why.

ch5s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: cover method, paris to madrid in USD. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as an MT103 announcement with an MT202 COV cover. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch5s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: serial method, the same payment in three mt103s. This worked example is set before the CBPR+ migration, so the payment travels as MT103s. A business analyst who can trace both methods through the same payment, field by field, understands correspondent banking at a level most practitioners never reach.

ch60s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.001.001.09 customer credit transfer initiation: what it is and what it carries. pain.001.001.09 is the ISO 20022 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation message, and it is the standard way a customer tells a bank to move money from the customer account to a named beneficiary. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch60s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.009 to pain.018 mandate message family. A direct debit needs a mandate: the debtor authorisation that lets the creditor pull funds. For a business analyst, the mandate lifecycle is a state machine.

ch60s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.002.001.10 customer payment status report: statuses and reason codes. pain.002.001.10 is the ISO 20022 Customer Payment Status Report, and it is the reply a bank sends after it receives and checks a pain.001 file. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch60s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.001 initiates pacs.008,. The journey from pain.001 to pacs.008 begins when the customer system creates the pain.001 file and sends it to the debtor agent, which is the bank that holds the debtor account. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch60s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.001 in customer-to-bank space. In customer to bank space, pain.001 is a direct instruction from a customer to its own bank, and the bank is the debtor agent for every payment in the file. If the payment has already been executed and sent as a pacs.008, cancellation is no longer a customer to bank matter, and the bank must use a recall or return process in the interbank space.

ch60s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.001 in bank-to-bank space: the relay scenario (bank a forwards pain.001 to the debtor agent). In the relay scenario, a customer sends its pain.001 file to Bank A, but Bank A does not hold the debtor account, so it cannot debit the customer and cannot create the pacs.008 itself. Relay creates a clear division of responsibility, and each bank must know where its responsibility starts and ends.

ch60s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain authorised party initiation and financial institution payment initiation. Authorised party initiation allows a party other than the debtor to send a pain.001 instruction on the debtor behalf, provided that party has been authorised to do so. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch60s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a corporation sends pain.001 through a relay to pay EUR 750,000, with the pain.002 status reports at each step. A corporation based in Rotterdam, with its EUR operating account held by a bank in Frankfurt, needs to pay EUR 750,000 to a supplier in Vienna for a delivery of industrial pumps. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch60s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.013 creditor payment activation request: structure, fields and mandate use. The pain.013 Creditor Payment Activation Request is the message a creditor sends to ask for a payment arrangement to be activated before money is collected. The creditor sends pain.013 before the first collection, when a new mandate has been agreed and the debtor bank needs to record it.

ch60s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pain.014 and the request to pay flow: activation status and the payto mandate pair. The pain.014 Creditor Payment Activation Request Status Report is the answer to a pain.013 activation request, and it tells the creditor whether the activation was accepted or rejected. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch61s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four-corner sct model and the EUR 48,250 worked example. The four-corner model describes a SEPA Credit Transfer as a flow between four parties. The originator is the customer who instructs the payment, and the beneficiary is the customer who receives it.

ch61s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reading ISO 20022 names: PAIN, PACS and CAMT explained. Every ISO 20022 message name has three parts, and each part carries meaning. When a business analyst writes a requirement, the full name with its version must be stated, or developers and testers may build against the wrong definition and fail certification testing.

ch61s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer to bank space: pain.001, pain.002 and the exchange periods. In customer to bank space, Loire Components creates a pain.001.001.09 file and sends it to Meridian Bank Paris through its host to host channel. Cut-off times are the practical consequence of exchange periods, and a business analyst must make them visible in any requirement.

ch61s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interbank space: pacs.008, pacs.002 and pacs.004. Once Meridian Bank Paris has debited the Loire Components account, it builds the pacs.008.001.08 Customer Credit Transfer message for the interbank leg. The pacs.008 message and the settlement are separate things, and a business analyst must keep them separate in any design.

ch61s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain exceptions and investigations: camt.056, camt.029 and pacs.004 returns. A camt.056 is the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request, and it is the message Meridian Bank Paris sends when Loire Components asks it to stop a payment that has already left the bank. Timing decides whether a camt.056 can succeed, and a business analyst must design the process around that fact.

ch61s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer reporting and the SEPA 2024 transition to 2019 messages. Customer reporting in SEPA uses the camt family, and each message has a distinct job. The migration work behind a message version change is larger than it looks, and a business analyst should plan for it explicitly.

ch61s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sct inst becomes mandatory, schemes, instruments and the SEPA area map. The Instant Payments Regulation made SCT Inst mandatory across the European Union, and the change is already in force. The product decision is about which rail the customer chooses, and the bank must offer both rails, price them correctly, and make the cut-off and value date clear for each one.

ch62s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sdd core and b2b: two schemes, two risk profiles. A SEPA Direct Debit is a payment in which the creditor pulls funds from the debtor account, under a mandate that the debtor has signed in advance. First, the debtor bank must check that a valid mandate exists before it allows a B2B collection, and it must refuse the collection if no mandate is on file.

ch62s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four-corner sdd model and mandate flows. The four-corner model for SDD has the same shape as the SCT model, but the direction of the instruction is reversed. This flow is used in some countries and for some B2B arrangements, where the debtor bank must have the mandate on file before it will allow any collection.

ch62s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain e-mandate service and its ISO 20022 messages. An e-mandate is a mandate that the debtor signs electronically, usually on the creditor website, and it is validated by the debtor bank during the signing process. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch62s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain collections: pain.008 and pacs.003. The collection begins when Stadtwerke Linden creates a pain.008.001.02 Customer Direct Debit Initiation file and sends it to its bank, Harbour Bank Frankfurt. A creditor that collects without pre-notification gives the debtor grounds to claim a refund, and a business analyst should make the pre-notification step visible in every collection design.

ch62s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rejects, returns and refunds: pacs.002, pacs.004 and the 8 week rule. A reject happens before the due date, when the debtor bank refuses the collection during validation. Within eight weeks of the debit, the debtor can claim a refund with no questions asked, and the debtor bank must return the funds.

ch62s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reversals: pain.007, pacs.007 and reason codes am05, ms02, ms03. A reversal is a creditor initiated instruction to undo a collection that has already been settled, and it is used when the creditor discovers its own error. The code matters for reporting, because a creditor with many AM05 reversals has a duplicate generation problem in its billing system, and the operations team should investigate the source rather than reversing each duplicate by hand.

ch62s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: EUR 89.99 monthly utility collection, end to end and how to test it. The worked example begins on 14 September 2026, when Jonas Weber signs the e-mandate on the Stadtwerke Linden website and Meridian Bank Munich authenticates him and accepts mandate SWL-JW-2026-0417. This matters because the rail decides how fast the money moves, what it costs, when it settles and what can go wrong. Choosing the wrong rail is a product and an operations failure.

ch62s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mandate management in depth: the lifecycle of a direct debit mandate. A direct debit mandate is the authorisation that lets a creditor collect money from a debtor account, and mandate management is the discipline of creating, storing, amending, using and cancelling that authorisation. The debtor can also ask the debtor bank to refuse collections, and the bank must honour that instruction.

ch62s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sdd settlement model: how direct debit collections settle between banks. A SEPA Direct Debit collection is a pull payment: the creditor asks for money from the debtor account, and the settlement model must move the money from the debtor bank to the creditor bank on the due date, while. The creditor bank must present the collection to the debtor bank ahead of the due date, and under the current rulebook the presentation deadline is one business day before the due date for both first and recurrent collections.

ch63s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain types of payment cards and their services. A credit card lets the cardholder borrow money from the issuing bank up to an agreed credit limit, and the cardholder repays the balance later, either in full or in monthly instalments with interest. For a business analyst, the card type decides the questions to ask in a requirements workshop, and getting it wrong creates rework later.

ch63s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain card-present vs card-not-present transactions. A card-present transaction happens when the physical card is at the point of sale, for example when a cardholder inserts a chip card into a terminal in a shop and enters a PIN, or taps a contactless card on the reader. A business analyst must map these outcomes in the requirements, because the checkout screen, the authentication step and the error messages all change with the authentication result, and the test cases must cover success, failure and abandonment at the authentication step.

ch63s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain anatomy of a bank card. The front of a card carries the cardholder name, the card number, the expiry date and usually the scheme logo, while the back carries the magnetic stripe, the signature panel and the three digit security code. Each element of the card maps to a data field in the transaction, and a business analyst must know which field carries which value.

ch63s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain main players and the three-corner and four-corner models. The cardholder is the person who holds the card and uses it to pay, and the merchant is the business that accepts the card as payment for goods or services. The difference between the models matters for a business analyst, because it changes the number of parties, the messages and the places where a payment can fail.

ch63s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four-party scheme flow. The flow starts when the cardholder at Meridian Bank London buys goods worth EUR 120 from an online merchant and enters the card number, expiry date and security code at checkout. A business analyst must define the decline codes, the reversal rules and the customer messages, and a product owner should consider how the checkout explains a decline without revealing fraud logic that criminals could exploit.

ch63s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment processors, fees and how they are shared. A payment processor is a company that runs the technology that moves card transactions between the parties, and most banks use a processor rather than building the whole system themselves. Fees create risks and design questions that a business analyst and a product owner must handle explicitly.

ch63s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ATM cash withdrawals, the SEPA cards framework, clearing and settlement. A cash withdrawal at an ATM follows the same authorisation pattern as a purchase, but the merchant is replaced by the ATM owner. For a business analyst, the framework matters because it defines the standards a new card product must meet, and for a product owner it matters because it opens the market to acquirers and processors from across Europe.

ch64s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheque. A cheque is a written instruction from an account holder, called the drawer, to the bank that holds the account, called the drawee, telling the bank to pay a stated amount to a named person or business, called the payee. For a business analyst, a cheque is a pull payment, which means the payee pulls the money from the drawer account by presenting the cheque, rather than the drawer pushing the money to the payee.

ch64s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain types of bank cheques. A bearer cheque is payable to whoever holds it, because the payee line says bearer or is left blank, so anyone who presents it can be paid. Choosing the right cheque type is a product and risk decision, and a business analyst should capture the rules in the requirements.

ch64s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain four-corner model for a cheque payment. The four-corner model for a cheque has four parties, the drawer, who writes the cheque, the payee, who receives it, the collecting bank, which is the payee bank, and the paying bank, which is the drawer bank. A business analyst must design for the delay between presentment and credit, because the payee sees the cheque as deposited on day one but cannot safely spend the money until the clearing completes, and a product owner must decide what the app shows during that window.

ch64s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheque clearing: physical, image-based truncation and timelines. In physical clearing, the paper cheque itself travelled from the collecting bank to a clearing centre and then to the paying bank, which checked the signature and the paper before paying. If the image is too dark, cropped or blurred, the collecting bank must ask the payee to deposit the cheque again, which adds a day to the timeline.

ch64s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheque bounces. A cheque bounces when the paying bank returns it unpaid, and the most common reason is insufficient funds, which means the drawer account does not hold enough money to cover the amount. A business analyst must know the local law for the market being served, because the return codes, the notice periods and the customer letters all change with the jurisdiction, and the product must support the right process for each country.

ch64s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment systems modernisation: the canada example. Canada modernised its payment systems through Payments Canada, the organisation that operates the country clearing and settlement systems, because the old infrastructure was built for paper and batch processing and. Modernisation changes what a business analyst must design, because the same payment can now travel on different rails with different speeds, costs and data.

ch64s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain on-us transactions, intrabank groups, push vs pull revisited. An on-us transaction is a payment where the payer and the payee hold accounts at the same bank, so the money never leaves the bank and no clearing or settlement between banks is needed. A business analyst should always ask whether a payment is on-us, because the flow, the timing and the cost all change with the answer.

ch64s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cheque conversion: turning a paper cheque into an electronic payment. A cheque is a paper instruction, but the clearing system that processes it no longer needs the paper. There are two distinct ideas here, and the analyst must not confuse them.

ch65s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain open banking. Open banking is a regulated way for a customer to give a licensed third party access to a bank account, either to read information or to start a payment. For a business analyst, the point is that PSD3 is not a new idea, it is PSD2 made stronger, clearer and fairer, and the work it creates is in fraud controls, verification, consent screens and accessible authentication journeys.

ch65s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain key players: pisps, aisps and piisps. A payment initiation service provider, known as a PISP, starts a payment from a customer bank account on the customer instruction. For a business analyst, the licence type is a requirement, not a detail, because the consent screen, the API scope, and the error handling all change with it.

ch65s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain strong customer authentication and PSD3 enhancements. Strong customer authentication requires two out of three factors, something the customer knows, such as a password or PIN, something the customer has, such as a phone or a card, and something the customer is, such as a. For a product owner, this means the authentication journey is a risk decision, not a fixed screen, and the rules for when to challenge and when to trust must be written, tested and monitored.

ch65s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain accessibility, inclusive payments and PSD3. Strong customer authentication can exclude people, and that exclusion is a real risk, not an edge case. The bank must also make its screens readable, with clear language, good contrast, and compatibility with screen readers.

ch65s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud prevention under PSD3 and customer education. Fraud in open banking takes many forms, but the most harmful is authorised push payment fraud, where a criminal tricks a customer into sending money to a criminal account. If a payment was unauthorised, meaning the customer did not approve it, the bank must refund it promptly unless it can prove the customer acted fraudulently or with gross negligence.

ch65s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain verification of payee and fraud information exchange. Verification of payee is a check that runs before a payment is sent, and it compares the payee name the customer entered with the name held on the payee account. For a business analyst, the requirement is not just a check box, it is a full journey, the name entry screen, the match result screen, the warning wording, and the audit record of what the customer saw and chose.

ch65s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a customer pays EUR 240 through a PISP. Claire Dubois, a customer of Meridian Bank in Lyon, buys EUR 240 of kitchen goods from an online retailer called Maison Nord. A business analyst should note that the mismatch warning, the consent record, and the authentication record are all stored, because they are the evidence if Claire later disputes the payment.

ch66s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain trade finance basics: why exporters and importers need banks. An exporter and an importer face opposite risks, and that tension is the heart of trade finance. A business analyst should ask which side bears the risk in each method, because that answer drives the whole design.

ch66s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain documentary credit: definition, main actors and how it works. A documentary credit is an undertaking by a bank, the issuing bank, to pay a named beneficiary, usually the exporter, when the beneficiary presents documents that comply with the credit terms. If the documents comply, the bank must pay even if the importer later claims the goods are faulty, and if they do not comply, the bank must refuse even if the goods are perfect.

ch66s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain documentary credit with a confirming bank. A confirming bank is a bank, usually in the exporter country, that adds its own independent undertaking to pay the beneficiary when complying documents are presented. If the documents do not comply, the confirming bank must refuse them, just as any nominated bank would, and it must tell the presenter why, listing each discrepancy.

ch66s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain documentary credit with a notifying bank. A notifying bank is a bank that tells the beneficiary that a documentary credit has been issued, without taking on the advising role in the usual sense. For a business analyst, the distinction matters for the message flow, because the credit may pass through a notifying bank before it reaches the advising bank, and each hop must be recorded with its date and its role.

ch66s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain simple collection, payment against invoice and cash on delivery. A simple collection, also called a clean collection, is a collection that involves only a financial document, such as a bill of exchange or a cheque, with no shipping documents attached. Choosing between these methods is a commercial decision, and a business analyst should frame it as a risk and cost trade off.

ch66s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bills of exchange and promissory notes: parties and the four-corner model. A bill of exchange is a written, unconditional order by one person, the drawer, telling another person, the drawee, to pay a fixed sum to a named person, the payee, on a set date or on demand. This matters because cross-border payments involve more banks, more charges, more time and more ways to fail than any domestic payment. Getting the chain right is the job.

ch66s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: a EUR 180,000 machinery export and a EUR 12,000 spare parts collection. Harbour Bank in Hamburg acts for the exporter, a machinery maker called Rheinwerk GmbH, and Meridian Bank in Warsaw acts for the importer, a factory called PolTech Sp. z o.o. A business analyst should note that the trade system must show both deals in one customer view, with the credit status, the bill maturity date, and the expected cash date for each.

ch67s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reading an ISO 20022 schema: xsd patterns. An XSD, or XML Schema Definition, is a formal description of what a valid message may contain. A business analyst must know the difference between schema mandatory and business rule mandatory, because a message can pass schema validation and still be rejected by the scheme.

ch67s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain currency and amount: decimal precision and minor units. An ISO 20022 amount is carried as a decimal value together with a three letter currency code from ISO 4217, for example EUR 10000.00 or JPY 125000. A business analyst should check the currency table in the requirements, because a missing currency or a wrong exponent is a defect that only appears for certain currencies.

ch67s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain utc offsets and timestamps: why every time is utc with offset. UTC, or Coordinated Universal Time, is the world reference time, and every ISO 20022 timestamp is written as a UTC time plus an offset that shows the local time difference. A business analyst should include daylight saving cases in the test pack, including a payment created on the day the clocks go forward and one on the day they go back, because those are the days when timestamps fail in production.

ch67s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain market practice: pmpg, CBPR+, SEPA, FEDWIRE, CHAPS and FEDNOW. The Payments Market Practice Group, known as the PMPG, is an industry group that writes market practice guidelines on top of the ISO 20022 standard. A business analyst should treat the PMPG guidelines as requirements, because the development team will ask which practice applies, and the answer decides the field mapping.

ch67s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain t-accounts and wash accounts in payment accounting. A T-account is a simple way to show a ledger account, with debits on the left and credits on the right, and every payment creates at least one debit and one credit of equal value. The wash account exists because the two legs may happen at different times, in different systems, or on different days, and the bank needs a place to hold the money in between.

ch67s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain LEI, FATF recommendation 16 and mandatory versus optional elements. A Legal Entity Identifier, known as an LEI, is a 20 character code that uniquely identifies a legal entity, such as a company, a fund, or a bank, anywhere in the world. A business analyst must therefore build a rule table that shows, for each field, whether the schema requires it, whether the scheme requires it, and whether the bank own policy requires it.

ch67s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worked example: the same EUR 10,000 payment as pacs.008 under CBPR+ and SEPA. The payment is EUR 10,000 from a Paris customer, Atelier Lumiere, to a Frankfurt supplier, Rheinwerk GmbH, for a delivery of lighting equipment. A business analyst should build a per rail mapping table, a tester should run the same payment through both rails and compare the results, and a product owner should make sure the screen asks for the right data for the rail the customer chose.

ch67s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain validating an ISO 20022 XML file: schemas, errors and fixes. An ISO 20022 message is an XML file, and before a bank can process it, the file must be validated. For a business analyst, validation requirements cover what happens when a file fails.

ch68s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment state machines and correlation. A payment state machine lists every state a payment can sit in and every move between states that is allowed, and it is the single control that keeps operations, settlement and customer service looking at the same truth. If an operator or a system tries one of these moves, the state machine blocks it, logs the attempt, and raises an alert to the operations team.

ch68s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain throughput requirements for payment systems. A payment system can have perfect technology and still fail if every participant submits all its payments at the end of the day. For a business analyst, throughput belongs in the requirements alongside the technical targets.

ch68s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain idempotency and duplicate prevention. Duplicates happen because payments move across networks where a sender cannot always tell whether the first attempt succeeded. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch68s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain retries, dead letter queues, timeouts and unknown outcomes. A retry policy defines how many times a payment is sent again, how long to wait between attempts, and how the wait grows with each failure. The limit is usually a number of attempts or a total elapsed time, and once it is reached the payment moves to a failed state and the operations team is alerted.

ch68s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain out of order events: messages and acknowledgements arriving out of order. Out of order arrival is normal in payment networks, because messages travel different routes, systems process at different speeds, and a fast acknowledgement can overtake a slow settlement confirmation. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch68s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ledger posting versus settlement. Acceptance means the bank has checked the instruction and agreed to process it, and it happens before any money moves. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch68s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation matching hierarchies and suspense account management. Reconciliation compares the internal ledger with the external statement, and it starts with exact matching on the reference, the amount and the value date. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch68s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain operational dashboards, kpis, resilience and disaster recovery. An operational dashboard shows volumes, straight through processing rate, exception ageing, settlement positions and queue depths in one view, so the duty manager can see the health of the payment service at a glance. This matters because operations is where payments are reconciled, investigated and fixed. The work in this lesson is what keeps the money right.

ch68s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain incident communication: who is told, what they are told. A payment system goes down at 10:14 on a Monday morning, and 2,000 salary payments are stuck. For a business analyst, the incident communication requirements are therefore about severity levels, notification lists, message templates, update timing, and the post-incident report.

ch68s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain queue expiry and re-sequencing. When a payment cannot settle immediately, because funds are insufficient or a limit is reached, it waits in a queue. For a business analyst, queue requirements cover the discipline, the expiry rules, the re-sequencing rights, and the notifications.

ch69s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain functions of money. Money performs four functions that every payments professional must be able to separate, because a payment can succeed on one function and fail on another. Takeaway: money is not one thing, it is four functions performed by an issuer that others trust, and a payment is only as good as the money it moves.

ch69s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fiat money. Fiat money is money whose value rests on trust and on law rather than on a commodity backing it. Takeaway: fiat money is declared by the state, issued by the central bank, and trusted because it settles taxes, debts and central bank settlement.

ch69s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank money versus commercial bank money. Central bank money and commercial bank money are two different liabilities, and a payment system exists to convert one into the other safely. A payment that looks settled can still fail at the interbank layer. Knowing which layer a payment is in tells you who bears the risk, when finality is reached, and what a Herstatt failure actually costs, which is the full principal of the leg already paid.

ch69s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain e-money as a claim. E-money is a claim on its issuer, stored electronically, and issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions. Takeaway: e-money is a claim on an authorised electronic money institution, issued on receipt of funds, redeemable at par, and protected by safeguarding, not by deposit guarantee.

ch69s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain money on a bank balance sheet. A bank balance sheet shows money from two sides at once, and reading it correctly is a core skill for a payments professional. Takeaway: every payment is a balance sheet event, with a debit and a credit that must be equal, and a customer deposit is a liability of the bank while reserves at the central bank are an asset.

ch69s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain money and payment instruments. Every payment instrument is a way of moving a particular form of money, and the instrument decides the speed, the finality, the data and the risk. Takeaway: the instrument is the vehicle and the money is the cargo, and the choice of vehicle changes cost, timing, data, finality and failure.

ch6s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 is. ISO 20022 is an international standard for financial messaging that defines a common language for exchanging payment, securities, trade, and other financial information. For a business analyst, ISO 20022 is important because it changes how payment data is modelled.

ch6s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business application header, head.001. The Business Application Header, known as head. Takeaway: head.001 is the envelope for an ISO 20022 business message, with From, To, BizMsgIdr, MsgDefIdr, BizSvc and CreDt, and it is read before the business content.

ch6s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value versus non-value messages. Payment messages divide into two kinds, and the division shapes how they are processed, controlled, and tested. For a business analyst, the classification drives requirements, testing, and monitoring.

ch6s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain actc: the accepted technical validation status. When a bank receives a payment instruction, the first thing it checks is whether the message itself is valid: is it well formed, properly authenticated, and compliant with the schema and the usage guideline?. For a business analyst, status mapping is precision work.

ch6s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 replaced MT.
