SWIFT MT served the industry well for decades, but it has limitations that became more pressing as payments became faster, more complex, and more regulated. An analyst must be able to explain these benefits to stakeholders who see only the cost of migration, because the business case depends on those benefits being realised in operations, not just on the technical ability to send a new message format.

ch6s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain XML structure, how an ISO 20022 message is built. An ISO 20022 message is an XML document with a clear, hierarchical structure. A business analyst does not need to be an XML developer, but must be able to read an ISO 20022 message, identify the key elements, and explain what each element means.

ch6s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business model behind the messages. Behind every ISO 20022 message is a business model that defines the concepts, the relationships, and the rules that the message expresses. For an analyst, the business model is a tool for writing clear requirements.

ch6s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message catalogue, PACS, PAIN and CAMT. The ISO 20022 message catalogue is organised by business area, and the three most important areas for payments are pacs, pain, and camt. The catalogue is large, and it continues to grow, but an analyst does not need to memorise every message.

ch6s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain adoption timeline and CBPR plus. ISO 20022 adoption followed a phased timeline, and the cross-border migration is now complete. For a business analyst, the timeline matters because it explains the state of the systems you work on.

ch6s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain changes for banks, corporates and operations. For banks, ISO 20022 migration requires changes to payment engines, to screening systems, to reconciliation systems, and to customer channels. Analysts who work with corporates must be able to explain both the benefit and the cost, and must help corporates plan their own migration.

ch6s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 fundamentals with annotated XML samples. ISO 20022 is a standard for financial messaging that defines messages in XML, and the best way to learn it is to read a real message, line by line, with each element explained. Takeaway: a pacs.008 is a Document with a Group Header, a Payment Information block and a Credit Transfer Transaction Information block, and each element has a purpose, a format and a rule.

ch6s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain MT versus mx worked comparison: the same payment as MT103 and as pacs.008, field by field. The same payment can be written as an MT103 and as a pacs.008, and comparing the two field by field is the fastest way to understand why ISO 20022 replaced MT. Takeaway: the same USD 25,000 payment is an MT103 with numbered fields and 140 characters of remittance, and a pacs.008 with named elements, structured addresses and structured remittance.

ch70s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain account taxonomy: current, savings, nostro, vostro, suspense, settlement, clearing, transit and wash. An account is a record of a claim, and the type of account decides what the claim is, who can move it, and what happens when it is wrong. Takeaway: current and savings accounts hold customer deposits, nostro and vostro accounts are the two views of the same correspondent balance, suspense holds items that cannot yet be posted, settlement holds amounts due to or from a clearing system, and transit and wash accounts must net to zero.

ch70s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ledger versus available balance. The ledger balance and the available balance are two different numbers for the same account, and the difference between them is the money that is already committed but not yet settled. Takeaway: the ledger balance is what has been posted, the available balance is what can be spent, and the difference is holds, pending authorisations, uncleared funds and future dated instructions.

ch70s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value dates and booking dates. The value date and the booking date are two different dates for the same payment, and confusing them causes interest errors, reconciliation breaks and customer complaints. Takeaway: the booking date is when the entry is posted, the value date is when interest starts and funds are considered available, and the two can differ by days.

ch70s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement and clearing accounts. A settlement account and a clearing account are the two accounts that sit between banks, and they do different jobs. Takeaway: a clearing account holds items in transit and must clear to zero at the end of a cycle, and a settlement account holds the net amount owed to or by the clearing system and settles in central bank money.

ch71s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain double-entry bookkeeping. Double-entry bookkeeping is the rule that every financial event is recorded as at least one debit and at least one credit of equal value, so the books always balance. Takeaway: every payment is at least one debit and one credit of equal value, and the books must balance at every step, in every bank and at the central bank.

ch71s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain posting rules. A posting rule is the instruction that tells the ledger which account to debit and which to credit, for how much, in which currency and on which value date, for a given payment event. Takeaway: a posting rule names the event, the trigger, the debit account, the credit account, the amount, the currency, the value date and the reversal rule, and finance owns and versions it.

ch71s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain booking versus non-booking entries. A booking entry changes the ledger balance, and a non-booking entry does not. Takeaway: a booking entry changes the ledger balance, a non-booking entry changes only the available balance, and every payment moves from non-booking to booking on a defined trigger.

ch71s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain booking entries per message: pacs.008, pacs.004 and camt.056, with the debit and credit entry at each step. This lesson is the distinctive depth that separates a payments professional from a message reader: the exact debit and credit entry at each step, for a pacs.008, a pacs.004 return and a camt.056 recall. A message that is not posted correctly is a payment that has not happened in the ledger. Knowing the exact debit and credit at each bank tells you where the money is, what a return reverses, and why a recall posts nothing until the beneficiary bank agrees.

ch71s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain loro, mirror and shadow accounts. A loro account is a bank account held by a bank for another bank, and the word comes from the Italian for theirs, because the account holds their money. Takeaway: a nostro is our account at another bank, a vostro is your account on our books, a loro is an account held for another bank, and a mirror or shadow account is a copy kept for reconciliation.

ch71s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sub-ledger to general ledger. The sub-ledger and the general ledger are two levels of the same accounting, and the payment sub-ledger is where every payment is recorded in detail, while the general ledger is where the totals are recorded by account. Takeaway: the payment sub-ledger holds one entry per payment with full detail, the general ledger holds the totals by account, and the summarisation rules decide how the detail becomes the totals.

ch71s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain value-date correction: camt.087 and camt.027 and apply it to a real banking scenario. A wrong value date is a customer detriment and a regulatory risk: three days of lost interest on EUR 200,000 is EUR 50, and on EUR 20 million it is EUR 5,000, so a corporate customer will claim it, and a pattern of value-date errors is a control failure the auditor and the regulator will ask about.

ch72s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain minute-by-minute timeline for one instant payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Takeaway: an SCT Inst payment of EUR 4,500 moves from pain.001 to pacs.008 to pacs.002 with status ACCC in 10 seconds, with reservation, screening, TIPS settlement in central bank money, and a booking debit at the end.

ch72s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain minute-by-minute timeline for one batch payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Takeaway: a batch salary file of 500 payments totalling EUR 1.2 million moves from pain.001 upload at 08:00 to beneficiary credit at 15:00, through validation, screening, debit, pacs.008 creation, STEP2 clearing and T2 settlement, with 3 IBAN rejections and 2 held payments reported separately.

ch72s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain minute-by-minute timeline for one cross-border payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Takeaway: a USD 85,000 cross-border payment from London to Singapore moves from pain.001 at 09:00 to supplier credit at 12:00 London time, through Bank A, intermediary Bank C and Bank B, by the serial method, with pacs.008 at each step, pacs.002 with status ACCC, and charge arrangement OUR so the supplier receives the full amount.

ch72s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain timeline comparison across rails and apply it to a real banking scenario. Takeaway: SCT Inst settles in 10 seconds, SEPA Credit Transfer credits by the next business day, a correspondent payment takes 4 hours to 2 days through a chain, and a card payment authorises in seconds but settles the next day.

ch72s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain failure at each lifecycle stage. Every payment passes through seven lifecycle stages, and each stage has its own failures, its own messages and its own recovery, and a business analyst must know all seven, because a failure at initiation needs a. Takeaway: initiation fails on bad data and is rejected by pain.002, validation and screening fail on data, parties or behaviour and are held or rejected by pacs.002, authorisation fails on insufficient funds with reason AM04, clearing fails on a bad message or a wrong route, settlement fails on funding or an outage under the system default procedure, and beneficiary credit fails on a closed account and is returned by pacs.004 with reason AC04.

ch72s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain forward-dated payment rules. A forward-dated payment, also called a future-dated payment, is an instruction with a value date in the future: pay this amount, to this beneficiary, on that date. For a business analyst, forward-dating requirements cover the acceptance window, the business day calendars, the revalidation scope, the amendment and cancellation windows, and the warehousing reconciliation.

ch72s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment warehousing: holding future-dated payments. Payment warehousing is the holding of future-dated payments until their release date. For a business analyst, warehouse requirements cover storage, release rules, revalidation scope, reconciliation, and operator visibility.

ch73s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain admi messages: the administration layer of ISO 20022. Administration messages, the admi set in the ISO 20022 catalogue, carry no payment value at all, and that is exactly why they matter: they keep the messaging system itself alive, acknowledged and recoverable. Takeaway: admi is the control that makes every other message trustworthy, so for every message name the acknowledgement, the timeout, the resend rule and the escalation.

ch73s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction manager: the shared record of an ISO 20022 payment. Transaction Manager is the SWIFT platform that holds a shared, central record of an ISO 20022 cross-border payment, so that every bank in the chain can see the same transaction data, in the same format, even when the. Takeaway: Transaction Manager protects the rich ISO 20022 data through the chain, so the beneficiary receives the remittance the debtor sent.

ch73s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.037 claim non-receipt: the newer claim message and how it differs from camt.027. The camt.037 Claim Non-Receipt is the newer ISO 20022 message a creditor bank sends when expected funds have not arrived by the value date. A single case must use one claim message, and the bank must not send both messages for the same missing payment.

ch73s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.036 and camt.055: the debit authorisation response and the customer cancellation request. A customer who has sent a payment and changes their mind has one structured route to stop it: the camt.055, the CustomerPaymentCancellationRequest. A customer who has sent a payment and changes their mind has one structured route to stop it: the camt.055, the CustomerPaymentCancellationRequest.

ch73s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.026 in depth: unable to apply. A bank sometimes receives funds it cannot apply. For a business analyst, the camt.026 teaches the discipline of holding funds safely.

ch73s14.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain case assignment notification: camt.030. An investigation is a case, and a case needs an owner. For a business analyst, the lesson is about workflow design: every case needs an owner, every handover needs a record, and every assignment needs a deadline.

ch73s15.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain case status reporting: camt.038 and camt.039. An open investigation creates a question that somebody will eventually ask: where is this case?. For a business analyst, the design lesson is to treat status as a first class data model: define the status values, define the transitions between them, define who may change a status and on what evidence, and build the ageing and escalation rules on top.

ch73s16.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain debit authorisation request and response: camt.037 and camt.036. Returning funds sometimes requires taking money out of an account, and taking money out of an account requires permission. For a business analyst, the design lesson is that debits need authority, authority needs a message, and the message needs a deadline, a decision, and a record.

ch73s17.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain claim non-receipt in depth: camt.027 from claim to resolution. The most common investigation in cross border payments starts with a simple complaint: the money never arrived. Claims carry response expectations under scheme rules and service levels: the receiving bank must acknowledge the claim, investigate, and update the claimant within defined periods.

ch73s18.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain duplicate and request for duplicate: camt.033 and camt.034. Sometimes a bank needs a second copy of a message. For a business analyst, the pair teaches two lessons.

ch73s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.057 notification to receive: knowing the money is coming. The camt.057 Notification to Receive is the message a bank sends to its own customer, or to another bank, to say that a credit is expected, before the money actually arrives. Takeaway: camt.057 lets a treasurer plan around money that has not arrived yet, and it must be corrected when the expectation changes.

ch73s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.028 payment status request: asking where a payment is. The pacs.028 Payment Status Request is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends when it needs to know the status of a payment it has already sent, and it is the formal, auditable way to ask where the money is. Takeaway: pacs.028 is the first message to send when a payment goes quiet, before the phone call, because the structured answer is what the case file needs.

ch73s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.027 claim non-receipt: when the money never arrived. The camt.027 Claim Non-Receipt is the ISO 20022 message a creditor bank sends when the money it expected has not arrived, and it is the formal claim that starts a non-receipt investigation. Takeaway: a camt.027 claim turns a missing payment into a case with a deadline, and the expected value date is what makes it a claim.

ch73s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain camt.087 request to modify payment: fixing a payment after it was sent. The camt.087 Request to Modify Payment is the ISO 20022 message a bank sends to ask another bank to change a payment that has already been sent, and its most common use is to correct the value date. Takeaway: camt.087 fixes a payment by agreement with the bank that holds it, and a rejected modification needs a different tool, usually a recall.

ch73s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain case lifecycle and stop or recall: running an investigation to closure. A payment case is the operational container that holds an investigation from the moment it is opened until it is closed, and the case lifecycle is the discipline of moving it through defined states with defined owners. Takeaway: a case must be owned at opening, worked in priority order, and closed only when the money is found, returned or recalled, with every action in the file.

ch73s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain GPI instant: cross-border payments on instant rails. gpi Instant is the SWIFT service that connects a cross-border gpi payment to a domestic instant payment system at the destination, so that the last leg of the journey, the credit to the beneficiary, happens in seconds. Takeaway: gpi Instant makes the last mile instant, and the UETR links the gpi leg and the instant leg in one tracker view.

ch73s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT go: low-value cross-border payments, fast and predictable. SWIFT Go is the SWIFT service for low-value cross-border payments, designed for the payments that individuals and small businesses send every day, such as a EUR 400 payment to a family member or a USD 2,500 payment to a. Takeaway: SWIFT Go sells a predictable low-value payment, and a destination that is not covered must be disclosed before the customer sends it.

ch73s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment pre-validation: checking the beneficiary before sending. Payment Pre-validation is the SWIFT service that lets a sending bank check the beneficiary account details before the payment is sent, so that errors are caught while they are still cheap to fix. Takeaway: pre-validation prevents failures instead of fixing them, and its value is measured in returns that never happen.

ch74s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain npp: australia instant payments and payid. The New Payments Platform, NPP, is Australia instant payment system, launched in February 2018 and operated by NPP Australia Limited, and it lets a payment move between accounts at different banks in seconds, 24 hours a. Takeaway: NPP settles each payment individually in seconds, and PayID plus the name check is what makes it safe to use.

ch74s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain npp overlay services: osko, bpay and payto. An overlay service is a customer-facing service built on top of the NPP rails, and it uses the addressing, messaging and settlement of the platform instead of building new rails. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch74s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain npp credit transfers and returns: inward, outward, solicited and unsolicited. A customer credit transfer, CCT, moves money from a payer account to a payee account, and every NPP payment a customer sends or receives is a CCT. Every flow must end in a clear status, a reconciled ledger and a customer who knows what happened.

ch74s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain npp rejections and recalls: clearing, settlement and camt.056. The four rejection and cancellation flows are the paths an NPP payment takes when it does not complete normally, and each one has a different cause, timing and customer message. The bank must restore its settlement funding and decide on a retry, and the customer message must name the delay and the next step.

ch74s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain npp settles: the fast settlement service and becs. The Fast Settlement Service, FSS, is the settlement engine behind every NPP payment, and it is operated by the Reserve Bank of Australia. The liquidity duty is different on each system, and the bank must staff and fund for both.

ch74s14.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain proxy and alias initiation in depth: paying to a phone number, an email address or a proxy. An account number is hard to remember and easy to mistype, so instant payment systems let people pay to something easier: a phone number, an email address, a national identifier, or another alias that the system. Different systems implement proxies differently, and the analyst must know the local model.

ch74s15.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border instant linking: project nexus, the g20 targets and bilateral links. Domestic instant payment systems settle in seconds inside one country, but a payment between two countries still travels through correspondent banking, with its delays, costs and opacity. Both models are live, both are growing, and the analyst must understand both, because the corridor the business needs will use one or the other.

ch74s16.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rtp funding in depth: positions, watermarks, supplemental funding and the token service. Instant payments settle in real time, which means the funding must be in place before the payment, not after. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch74s17.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ip+ and rtpg: the groups that harmonise instant payments. Every country that built an instant payment system built its own: its own data, its own rules, its own message usage. For a business analyst, the working rule is to start from the guidelines.

ch74s18.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain canada real-time rail and the pcrn. Canada launched its Real-Time Rail, the RTR, on 9 November 2026, joining the group of countries with a national real time payment system. For a business analyst, the RTR is a case study in building a real time system with the lessons of the last decade included from day one.

ch74s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pix: brazil instant payments by key. Pix is Brazil's instant payment system, launched by the Banco Central do Brasil in November 2020, and it lets any person or business send money instantly, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, using a key instead of an account. Takeaway: Pix is instant, free for individuals and open to every licensed institution, and the name shown before confirmation is the control against mistaken payments.

ch74s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain paynow and fast: singapore instant payments. PayNow and FAST are Singapore instant payment systems, and they work together: FAST, Fast and Secure Transfers, launched in 2014, is the real-time interbank transfer system, and PayNow, launched in 2017, is the service. Takeaway: a PayNow payment travels on FAST, and the UEN lets a business be paid without sharing its account number.

ch74s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain promptpay: thailand instant payments by id or mobile. PromptPay is Thailand instant payment system, launched in 2017 and overseen by the Bank of Thailand, and it lets a person or business send money instantly using a national ID number, a mobile phone number, or a bank. Takeaway: PromptPay lets anyone pay instantly by mobile number or ID, and a merchant QR code replaces cash and a terminal.

ch74s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain spei: mexico real-time payments by clabe. SPEI, Sistema de Pagos Electrónicos Interbancarios, is Mexico real-time payment system, operated by the Banco de México since 2004, and it lets a payment move between accounts at different banks in seconds, 24 hours a. Takeaway: SPEI settles each payment in seconds in central bank money, and the CLABE check digit catches typing errors before the payment is sent.

ch74s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain buna: cross-border instant payments for the arab region. Buna is the cross-border payment system for the Arab region, operated by the Arab Monetary Fund and launched in December 2020, and it lets a bank in one Arab country pay a bank in another Arab country in real time, in. Takeaway: Buna lets banks in the region settle directly with each other instead of through correspondents outside the region.

ch74s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rtp: the US real-time payment network. RTP, the Real-Time Payments network, is the United States instant payment system operated by The Clearing House, launched in November 2017, and it lets a payment move between accounts at different US banks in seconds,. Takeaway: RTP is final in seconds because it is prefunded, and a payment above USD 1 million must travel by another rail such as Fedwire.

ch74s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA request to pay: asking for a payment instead of pulling it. SEPA Request to Pay, SRTP, is the European Payments Council scheme that lets a payee ask a payer for a payment, instead of pulling the money by direct debit or waiting for the payer to remember to send it. Takeaway: SRTP gives the payee certainty and the payer control, because the payment is a credit transfer that cannot be refunded like a direct debit.

ch74s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payto: payer-controlled mandates on the npp. PayTo is the mandate service that runs on the NPP, and it lets a payee collect payments only under a mandate the payer authorised in their own bank app. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch75s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the missing MT103. A missing MT103 is the most common cross-border investigation, and it means the customer payment message has not arrived at the bank that should have received it, so the beneficiary has not been credited and nobody can. Takeaway: trace a missing payment hop by hop with pacs.028 and the UETR, and the gap is the bank that cannot answer.

ch75s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: return of funds. A return of funds investigation starts when money comes back to the sender, and the sender, or the sender bank, must work out why it came back, what to do with it, and whether to resend the payment, and the return is. Takeaway: read the pacs.004 reason code, state the fix in plain language, match the return by UETR, and resend with the correction.

ch75s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the missing MT202 cov. A missing MT202 COV is the investigation where the customer payment arrived but the cover did not, or the cover arrived but the customer payment did not, and the two legs of a cover payment have become separated. Takeaway: match the cover and the customer payment by UETR, hold an unmatched cover in suspense, and never credit on one leg alone.

ch75s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the wrong intermediary. A wrong intermediary investigation starts when a payment was sent through a bank that should not have been in the chain, and the payment is now delayed, charged, or held, because the wrong bank applied its own rules,. Takeaway: correct the SSI after the investigation, or the same wrong intermediary will receive the next payment on the corridor.

ch75s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the delayed payment. A delayed payment investigation starts when a payment that should have arrived by its value date has not arrived, and the customer wants to know why, and the bank must give a factual answer, not a guess. Takeaway: check the cut-off and the status history before opening a case, because a payment sent after cut-off is on time for the next business day.

ch75s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the compliance hold. A compliance hold investigation starts when a payment is stopped by sanctions screening, anti-money laundering monitoring or fraud detection, and the customer wants to know why the money has not arrived, and the bank. Takeaway: find the holder, the review and the deadline, tell the customer a factual update without revealing the match, and record the hold.

ch75s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the charges discrepancy. A charges discrepancy investigation starts when the beneficiary receives less than the sender expected, and the difference is the charges deducted along the way, and the sender wants to know who deducted what, and. Takeaway: trace every deduction bank by bank, and a deduction that breaks the arrangement must be reclaimed.

ch75s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: the duplicate payment. A duplicate payment investigation starts when the same payment has been sent twice, and the beneficiary has been paid twice, or the debtor has been debited twice, and the bank must recover one of the payments without. Takeaway: retries must reuse the same identifier so the receiver can deduplicate, and duplicates must be caught by reconciliation on day one.

ch75s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: recall and cancellation. A recall investigation starts when the sender asks for the money back after the payment has been sent, and the request is sent as camt.056, and the answer, camt.029, says whether the return was accepted or rejected, and. Takeaway: send a recall in hours, not days, because a recall sent on day one succeeds and a recall sent on day five usually fails.

ch75s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain investigation: cancellation before the money moves. A cancellation investigation starts when the sender asks for a payment to be stopped before it is credited to the beneficiary, and the request is sent as camt.056, and the difference from a recall is that the money has. Takeaway: act inside the cancellation window, and convert a late cancellation into a recall instead of rejecting it.

ch76s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash management services: what a bank offers a corporate treasurer. Cash management services are the set of products a bank offers a corporate customer to control its money across many accounts, many entities and many countries, and the core idea is that a treasurer should see all the. Takeaway: cash management saves the customer interest by bringing scattered cash together, and the saving must be measurable.

ch76s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sweeping: moving surplus cash to where it is needed. Sweeping is the cash management service that moves surplus cash from a subsidiary account to a header account, automatically, at the end of each day, so that the money is concentrated where it can be used or invested,. Takeaway: sweep on the available balance, not the ledger balance, and respect value dates and known future payments.

ch76s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pooling: offsetting balances without moving money. Pooling is the cash management service that lets a group offset the balances of several accounts against each other, for interest calculation, without physically moving the money between them. Takeaway: pooling gives the interest benefit of concentration without the loan, tax and exchange-control consequences of moving money.

ch76s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain zero balancing: sweeping every account to zero each day. Zero balancing is the cash management service where every subsidiary account is swept to zero at the end of each day, so that all the cash ends the day in one header account, and each subsidiary starts the next day with. Takeaway: zero balancing gives maximum concentration, but a funding that is late or wrong means a supplier is not paid.

ch76s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain notional pooling: offsetting without moving, across currencies and countries. Notional pooling is the cash management service that offsets the balances of several accounts, in different currencies and different countries, for interest calculation, without moving any money, and without converting. Takeaway: notional pooling gives a multinational group the interest benefit of concentration without moving money across borders.

ch76s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash forecasting: predicting the money before it moves. Cash forecasting is the cash management service that predicts the corporate cash position, days and weeks ahead, by combining the known balances, the scheduled payments, the expected receipts, and the seasonal patterns,. Takeaway: forecast by value date, update it daily with actuals, and explain the variance, or the forecast cannot be trusted.

ch76s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash management versus bank liquidity management: two different jobs. Cash management and bank liquidity management are two different jobs, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes a payments professional can make, because they use similar words, similar systems and similar. Takeaway: never use the same balance for both jobs, and never propose a cash management fix for a liquidity problem.

ch76s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pobo: paying on behalf of. A multinational group may have a hundred subsidiaries, each with its own bank accounts, each making its own payments. For a business analyst, POBO design covers the instruction flow, the account structure, the intercompany postings, and the exception handling.

ch76s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cash concentration and the in-house bank. Cash scattered across a hundred accounts in twenty countries is cash the group cannot use. For a business analyst, the design covers the account structures, the sweep rules, the internal payment flows, and the statements.

ch77s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement cycle design: choosing when and how often to settle and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the settlement cycle is a requirements subject, not a background fact.

ch77s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain never reversing finality: erroneous payments as new instructions. Once settlement is final, it cannot be reversed by the system. For a business analyst, error handling requirements must never specify reversing the settlement.

ch77s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity optimisation: queues, offsets and how banks fund a settlement day and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, liquidity optimisation is a functional requirement area with measurable acceptance criteria.

ch77s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gridlock and how it is resolved and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, gridlock is a test scenario, not a footnote.

ch77s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intraday credit and collateral at the central bank and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, intraday credit is a set of requirements around limits, alerts and reporting.

ch77s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain central bank accounts: how settlement actually happens and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, central bank accounts are a data and interface subject.

ch77s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement failures: what happens when a bank cannot settle and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, settlement failure is a requirements and testing subject.

ch77s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the central counterparty default waterfall, who pays when a clearing member fails, and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the default waterfall is a rules and reporting subject.

ch77s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain designing a settlement system: a BA checklist from requirements to go-live and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, this checklist is your deliverable.

ch77s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement commit as a hard gate. In settlement design, the commit is the point of no return: the moment a payment settlement becomes final. For a business analyst, the commit gate is the most safety critical component in a payment system, and it must be specified and tested accordingly.

ch78s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EMV chip and arqc: how a chip card proves it is genuine and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, EMV is a certification and data subject.

ch78s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pci dss: what it requires and who it applies to and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, PCI DSS is a scope and evidence subject.

ch78s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain merchant underwriting: mcc, kyb and risk rating and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, underwriting is a workflow and rules subject.

ch78s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain interchange modelling: how the fee is built and who earns what and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, interchange modelling is a calculation and reporting subject.

ch78s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain chargeback chain: representment, pre-arbitration and arbitration and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the chargeback chain is a workflow and deadline subject.

ch78s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain acquiring economics: pricing a merchant, mdr and the acquirer p and l and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, acquiring economics is a modelling and reporting subject.

ch78s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain bnpl: how buy now pay later works and where the risk sits and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, BNPL is a credit and collections subject.

ch78s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme compliance: mandates, fines and the certification cycle and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, scheme compliance is a tracking and delivery subject.

ch79s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment engine modules: the anatomy of an engine and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the test of a good engine design is simple: every state transition is logged, every failure has a defined recovery path, and no payment can be lost between two modules.

ch79s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain booking entries per message: how a payment posts to the ledger and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the suspense account is a diagnostic: if you want to know where a bank's payment process is weakest, look at what is sitting in suspense and why.

ch79s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain worklists and audit trails: what operators see and what auditors need and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is precise: define which actions need four eyes, what the approver must check, and what happens if the approver rejects the action.

ch79s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain orchestration failure handling: timeouts, retries, compensation and sagas and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the saga for each payment type: the steps, the compensation for each step, and the state in which the payment rests while the saga waits.

ch79s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain observability: metrics, logs, traces and alerting for payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the alerts, the thresholds, the severity, the owner and the runbook for every payment type the engine carries.

ch79s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain microservices for payments: service boundaries and data ownership and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define, for each service, what data it owns, what events it publishes, what events it consumes, and what happens when an event is delivered twice or out of order.

ch79s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain engine performance and capacity: throughput, latency budgets and load testing and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the latency budget per payment type, per step, and the alert threshold for each.

ch79s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cache stampede, ttl jitter and single-flight. Caches protect backends. For a business analyst, cache design is a resilience requirement, not an optimisation detail.

ch79s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain search internals: inverted indexes, posting lists and sharding. Finding a payment among millions, by reference, amount, date, or party, in under a second, needs an index. For a business analyst, search requirements cover what is indexed, how fresh the index is, and how fast queries must return.

ch7s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pacs.008 is and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must be able to distinguish those three messages, because they have different structures, different mandatory fields, and different business meanings.

ch7s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain group header, the message envelope and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the Group Header is important because it is the first place to look when a message fails validation.

ch7s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment information, the batch level details and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must understand this hierarchy, because it affects how messages are constructed, how they are validated, and how errors are handled.

ch7s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain credit transfer transaction, the single payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst must be able to read a transaction block, identify each element, and explain its business meaning.

ch7s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain key fields explained with examples and apply it to a real banking scenario. An analyst should know which codes are used in the relevant usage guideline, and should ensure that test data covers each code that the product supports.

ch7s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain line by line walkthrough of a pacs.008 and apply it to a real banking scenario. If the beneficiary receives less than ten thousand dollars, the analyst can point to the Charge Bearer SHAR and explain that charges were shared.

ch7s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain common errors and validation in pacs.008 and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, validation requirements must be precise.

ch7s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain system design deep dive: processing pacs.008 at scale and apply it to a real banking scenario. This matters because the message is the payment instruction. A wrong field, a missing element or a misunderstood format is a failed payment, a return, or a compliance breach.

ch80s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain API versioning and lifecycle: how to change an API without breaking clients and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the versioning scheme, the deprecation policy, the sunset period, and the error returned for an unknown version, and to write them into the API specification before the first client integrates.

ch80s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pagination, filtering and sorting: returning large result sets safely and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the filter parameters, the validation rules for each, the sort options, and the default sort, and to test each combination.

ch80s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rate limiting and quotas: protecting the API and the client and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the limit per client type, the Retry-After behaviour, and the escalation path when a client is repeatedly limited.

ch80s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain error taxonomy: http status is not the payment status and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the error code for every failure the API can return, the HTTP status for each, and the message text, and to test each one with a real call.

ch80s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain idempotency in depth: keys, replay, conflict and storage and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the key format, the header name, the storage duration, the replay behaviour, the conflict response, and the scoping rule, and to test each with a real retry.

ch80s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain REST resource modelling for payments: resources, state and transitions and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the resource model, the state machine for each resource, the allowed transitions, and the field types, and to write them into the API specification as a contract that both the bank and the client can test against.

ch80s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain webhooks and event delivery: signatures, retries, ordering and replay and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the requirement is to define the event types, the delivery guarantees, the retry schedule, the signature scheme, and the client behaviour for duplicates and out of order delivery, and to test each with a real webhook.

ch81s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain gdpr and payment data: what counts as personal data in a payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, GDPR is a requirements discipline, not a legal footnote.

ch81s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data subject rights in payments: access, erasure and the AML wall and apply it to a real banking scenario. The practical consequence for a product owner is that the export format must be specified in the requirements, and the export must not leak another customer's data, which happens when a joint account or a bulk payment file is exported without filtering.

ch81s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border data transfers: when a payment message leaves the region and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the transfer work is a mapping exercise.

ch81s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain US bank secrecy act: the BSA framework behind every dollar payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the BSA is a set of concrete system requirements.

ch81s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain operational resilience and dora: staying open when things break and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, operational resilience is a requirements discipline.

ch81s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain incident management and reporting: the first 72 hours of a payment outage and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, incident management is a set of requirements and a set of test scenarios.

ch81s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain compliance operating model for a payments firm: putting gdpr, BSA and dora together and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the operating model is the deliverable that ties the whole of this chapter together.

ch82s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment product strategy: choosing who you serve and how you win and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the strategy is the source of every requirement.

ch82s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain business models in payments: where the money comes from and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the business model is a set of numbers that must balance.

ch82s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pricing a payment product: the cost stack and the price the customer sees and apply it to a real banking scenario. The business analyst's first job in pricing is to build the stack, with a number for every layer.

ch82s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer journeys in payments: the moments that decide trust and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the journey map is the deliverable.

ch82s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain from strategy to backlog: product requirements and the roadmap and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the roadmap is a traceability exercise.

ch82s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain go-to-market for a payment product: certification, pilot and launch and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the go-to-market plan is a checklist with owners and dates.

ch82s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain measuring product success: slas, kpis and the numbers that matter and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the metrics are requirements.

ch83s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain joining a payment scheme: membership, adherence and the application and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the scheme application is a requirements package.

ch83s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme certification and test packs: proving the product works and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the test pack is a requirements document.

ch83s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain entering a new market: licensing, local rails and the regulatory map and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the market entry is a requirements package per market.

ch83s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain local payment methods by market: what changes when you cross a border and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the local method is a requirements package per method.

ch83s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain build versus buy: the decision framework for payment technology and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the build versus buy decision is a business case.

ch83s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain vendor selection and management: choosing and controlling a payment supplier and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, vendor management is a set of requirements and a set of tests.

ch83s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain managing scheme change: rulebook updates and the change calendar and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the scheme change is a recurring requirements package.

ch84s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain requirements gathering for payments: workshops, elicitation and the domain language and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the elicitation is judged by the gaps it finds.

ch84s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain writing a BRD and a functional specification for a payment product and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the specification is judged by whether the developers can build from it without asking questions.

ch84s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain user stories and acceptance criteria for payments: gherkin in practice and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the user story is judged by whether a tester can test it and a customer can understand it.

ch84s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain process mapping and BPMN: drawing the payment flow so everyone agrees and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the process map is judged by whether it can be used to build the product and to train the operations team.

ch84s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data mapping and message mapping, MT to MX, and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the mapping document is judged by whether a developer can build from it and a tester can test from it.

ch84s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain test strategy for payments: SIT, UAT, negative testing and the test pack and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the test strategy is a document with test levels, test scenarios, test data, entry and exit criteria, and the regression pack.

ch84s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defect management: severity, triage and the defect lifecycle and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the defect process is a set of requirements.

ch84s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain production support and root cause analysis: keeping payments running and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, production support is a set of requirements: the support model, the runbook, the incident procedure, the root cause process, the reconciliation investigation procedure, and the monitoring.

ch85s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain embedded finance: payments inside another company's product and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, embedded finance is a three-party requirements exercise.

ch85s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banking as a service in practice: the API layer, ledgering and control and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, banking as a service is an API and a ledger specification.

ch85s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain payment data as an asset: what ISO 20022 data enables and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the ISO 20022 data model is a mapping exercise.

ch85s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain analytics on payment data: liquidity, fraud and customer insight and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the analytics are requirements with a question, a data source, a calculation, and a visualisation.

ch85s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain real-time data and streaming: KAFKA, events and the payment event log and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the streaming architecture is a set of requirements: the topics, the schemas, the partitioning, the retention, the idempotency, and the consumers.

ch85s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai in payments operations: reconciliation matching, exception prediction and governance and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, AI in operations is a set of requirements with a use case, a data source, a model, a metric, a governance control, and a human oversight.

ch85s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain future payment stack: what a 2030 payment platform looks like and apply it to a real banking scenario. For a business analyst, the future stack is a roadmap, not a prediction.

ch86s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain PSD2 vs PSD3 vs the Payment Services Regulation and apply it to a real banking scenario. A business analyst must know which legal instrument applies, because a directive and a regulation create different implementation work.

ch86s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain DORA operational resilience and apply it to a real banking scenario. DORA turns resilience from good practice into a testable legal duty, and the analyst writes the requirements that prove it.

ch86s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the EU Instant Payments Regulation 2024/886 and apply it to a real banking scenario. The 10-second rule changes every part of the payment chain, from screening to liquidity to error handling.

ch86s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions screening and apply it to a real banking scenario. Sanctions screening is where a payment system meets criminal law, and a wrong release can cost the bank its licence.

ch86s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain AML and counter-terrorist financing in payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. A risk-based approach is the core of AML law, and the analyst must be able to show the risk rating and the control that follows it.

ch86s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RBI directions and Indian payment regulation and apply it to a real banking scenario. Indian payment regulation is a separate framework from European rules, and a global bank must run both at once.

ch86s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FFIEC guidance and US payment regulation and apply it to a real banking scenario. FFIEC guidance is what examiners actually test against, so requirements must trace to it.

ch86s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ISO 20022 migration and compliance: what richer data changes for screening and reporting. The migration from MT to ISO 20022 is usually described as a messaging change, but for compliance teams it is a data change, and the data changes everything about how screening, monitoring and reporting work. The analyst who treats the migration as a format swap will miss the compliance redesign it requires.

ch86s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain pfmi principles applied to a faster payment system. The Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, the PFMI, are the international standards for payment systems, central securities depositories, central counterparties, and trade repositories, published by the. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch87s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud typologies in payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. APP scams are the largest fraud loss in UK payments, and the controls around them are now a regulatory duty.

ch87s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction monitoring systems and apply it to a real banking scenario. Monitoring is only as good as its tuning, and the analyst defines the thresholds and the triage workflow.

ch87s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SAR and STR filing and apply it to a real banking scenario. SAR and STR filing is a legal duty with criminal penalties for failure, and the workflow must be airtight.

ch87s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain KYC and CDD and apply it to a real banking scenario. CDD is the front door of every control downstream, and a weak onboarding decision poisons everything after it.

ch87s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain access controls and segregation of duties inside a payments operation and apply it to a real banking scenario. Segregation of duties is the oldest fraud control in banking, and every bypass is an audit finding.

ch87s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain audit trails and record keeping and apply it to a real banking scenario. The audit trail is the evidence that every other control worked, and it must survive for years.

ch87s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain scheme rulebooks as control and apply it to a real banking scenario. Scheme rulebooks are a hidden source of requirements, and the analyst must track them like regulation.

ch88s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what a clearing and settlement mechanism is, and where it sits between banks and schemes and apply it to a real banking scenario. The CSM is the invisible middle of every payment, and the analyst must understand it to explain timing and cost.

ch88s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EBA CLEARING STEP2 and apply it to a real banking scenario. STEP2 is the workhorse of European retail payments, and its cycle times drive customer value dates.

ch88s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain national CSMs across Europe and apply it to a real banking scenario. CSM choice is a cost and reach decision, and it changes as volumes and corridors change.

ch88s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain TIPS as a CSM for instant payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. TIPS liquidity is a weekend problem, and the forecast must be right on Friday.

ch88s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain how a bank chooses a CSM and apply it to a real banking scenario. CSM selection is a business case, and the analyst writes the criteria and the scoring.

ch88s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CSM interoperability and routing and apply it to a real banking scenario. Routing across CSMs is where payments get lost or delayed, and the analyst must map every hop.

ch88s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain step2-t and continuous gross settlement: settling SEPA payments one by one. Most retail clearing systems settle in batches: payments accumulate, they are netted or grouped, and settlement happens at fixed times during the day. The participant must manage its prefunded balance actively through the day, topping it up as payments flow out and drawing it down as payments flow in, and the analyst must design the liquidity monitoring that keeps the balance above the level the payment flow needs.

ch88s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain euro1 and step1: eba clearing large-value and retail services. EBA CLEARING, the company owned by European banks, operates the euro payment services that sit alongside the central bank systems. For a business analyst, the lesson is that clearing is a landscape, not a single system, and the routing rules are where the landscape becomes a working operation.

ch89s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain netting versus gross settlement and apply it to a real banking scenario. Netting is the maths that makes clearing cheap, and the analyst must be able to calculate it.

ch89s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement cycles and cut-off times and apply it to a real banking scenario. Cut-off times are where customer expectations meet operational reality.

ch89s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain settlement accounts and central bank money and apply it to a real banking scenario. The settlement account is where liquidity meets finality, and the analyst must understand both.

ch89s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain liquidity management in clearing and apply it to a real banking scenario. Gridlock is the classic RTGS failure mode, and the analyst must know how the system resolves it.

ch89s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain what happens when a participant fails and apply it to a real banking scenario. Default handling is the resilience test of a clearing system, and the analyst must know the rules.

ch89s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS versus deferred net settlement and apply it to a real banking scenario. RTGS versus net settlement is the fundamental design choice in clearing, and it shapes everything else.

ch8s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain migration was needed. Migration from MT to ISO 20022 was needed because MT could no longer carry the rich, structured data that modern payments require, and because domestic schemes around the world were adopting ISO 20022 independently,. For a business analyst, the end of coexistence changes the work.

ch8s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cgi-mp, common usage guidelines for corporates and banks. CGI-MP is the agreed common way for corporates and banks to use ISO 20022 messages in practice. For a business analyst, the requirements should cite the CGI-MP guideline and version, the test plan should include cases that break usage rules as well as cases that pass them, and the onboarding checklist should confirm the bank support statement before the first live file.

ch8s11.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction manager in depth: the central record of an ISO 20022 payment. When a payment travels through several banks, each bank sees only its own leg, and no single bank holds the complete picture of the transaction from end to end. It is the data backbone of the CBPR+ migration, and the analyst who designs cross border flows must understand what it stores, who can access it, and what problems it solves.

ch8s12.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain edifact: the older standard that still carries trade and payment data. Long before ISO 20022, and alongside SWIFT, another messaging standard was already moving business data between organisations: UN/EDIFACT, the United Nations rules for Electronic Data Interchange for Administration,. Any analyst working on legacy integrations will meet it.

ch8s13.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ansi x12 and the 820: payment orders in the north american standard. In North America the dominant electronic data interchange standard is ASC X12, usually shortened to ANSI X12 after the American National Standards Institute that accredits it. The payment transaction set, and the one a payments analyst is most likely to meet, is the 820: the Payment Order and Remittance Advice.

ch8s14.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain message conversion in depth: translating MT to mx without losing meaning. Migration from MT to ISO 20022 needs translation. The analyst job is to make conversion boring: specified, tested, and monitored, so that migration changes the format without changing the money.

ch8s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain translation rules, how MT becomes mx and back. Translation between MT and MX is governed by mapping rules defined by SWIFT and by the CBPR Plus usage guidelines. For a business analyst, the translation deliverables were concrete.

ch8s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mapping types, direct, split, derived and needs care. SWIFT defines several mapping types to describe how MT and MX fields relate to each other, and understanding those types helps an analyst assess the risk of a given translation. SWIFT defines several mapping types to describe how MT and MX fields relate to each other, and understanding those types helps an analyst assess the risk of a given translation.

ch8s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain truncation risk, the silent data loss. Truncation risk is the risk that data is lost when a longer MX field is translated to a shorter MT field, and it is one of the most important risks in the MT to MX migration. An analyst who understands truncation risk can write requirements that minimise it, and can explain to stakeholders why a payment that looks correct in MX may fail after translation to MT.

ch8s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain banks must do, readiness and testing. Banks that migrate to ISO 20022 must undertake a programme of work that covers technology, operations, compliance, and customer readiness. On the compliance side, sanctions screening, anti money laundering, and fraud rules must be updated for the new data model, and the bank must be able to demonstrate to regulators that its controls work in both formats.

ch8s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CBPR plus usage guidelines and scheme rules. The CBPR Plus usage guidelines define how ISO 20022 messages must be used for cross-border payments. For a business analyst, the usage guidelines are the primary reference for any ISO 20022 project.

ch8s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain post-migration checklist for a BA: what to verify now that MT103 and MT202 are gone for cross-border payments. Now that coexistence has ended on 22 November 2025 and MT103 and MT202 are gone for cross-border payments, the BA checklist has changed. Confirm that the operations team can read an ISO 20022 message and investigate a payment without needing to translate it to MT.

ch8s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain mt101 to pain.001: the same corporate instruction mapped field by field. The MT101 Request for Transfer and the pain.001 Customer Credit Transfer Initiation carry the same business instruction in two different formats. The analyst must record a business decision, a fallback behaviour, and a manual review path for each needs care field.

ch8s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hvps+ and CBPR+: the high value rulebook and which rulebook applies. The HVPS+ rulebook is the set of SWIFT ISO 20022 usage guidelines written for high value payment systems and market infrastructures. A bank must therefore validate inbound messages against CBPR+ at the border and against HVPS+ at the settlement system, and it must test the handover explicitly.

ch90s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the core banking ledger, the chart of accounts and double entry and apply it to a real banking scenario. Double entry is the control that makes every payment provable, and the analyst must know the entries.

ch90s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain customer accounts, internal accounts, nostro and vostro ledgers and apply it to a real banking scenario. Nostro and vostro are the language of correspondent banking, and the analyst must use them correctly.

ch90s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain suspense and transit accounts and apply it to a real banking scenario. Suspense accounts are where payments wait, and ageing suspense is a red flag for auditors.

ch90s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain general ledger postings for a payment and apply it to a real banking scenario. Exact ledger entries are the proof that a payment happened, and the analyst must be able to write them.

ch90s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain intraday processing, memo postings, value dating and back-value dating and apply it to a real banking scenario. Memo versus ledger is the reason a customer sees two different balances, and the analyst must explain it.

ch90s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain subledgers and the general ledger and apply it to a real banking scenario. Subledger to general ledger is the accounting spine of the bank, and a break here is a major incident.

ch90s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reconciliation between ledgers and apply it to a real banking scenario. Reconciliation is the detective control that catches everything else, and the analyst defines the break types.

ch90s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain error correction in ledgers and apply it to a real banking scenario. Error correction is where accounting discipline is tested, and the analyst must enforce the reversal rule.

ch90s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain core banking products surveyed: t24, finacle, flexcube and bancs. Every bank runs on a core banking system: the system of record for accounts, balances, and transactions. For an analyst working on Indian banking, Finacle is the core most likely to be in the room.

ch91s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain BACS in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. BACS is the backbone of UK recurring payments, and the three-day cycle shapes every Direct Debit operation.

ch91s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHAPS in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. CHAPS finality is the reason solicitors trust it for house purchases, and the analyst must explain it.

ch91s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain faster Payments in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. Faster Payments is the rail customers expect for everyday instant payments, and its limits matter.

ch91s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain confirmation of Payee and apply it to a real banking scenario. Confirmation of Payee is the front-line fraud control for UK payments, and the analyst must know its outcomes.

ch91s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UK Open Banking payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. Open Banking payments are a new channel, and the analyst must map the consent and liability flow.

ch91s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the Bank of England RTGS renewal programme and apply it to a real banking scenario. RTGS renewal is the biggest UK infrastructure change in a decade, and the analyst must track it.

ch91s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UK payment fraud and apply it to a real banking scenario. APP reimbursement is now a cost of doing business, and the controls that prevent it are a commercial priority.

ch91s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UK standard 18: the BACS file format, record by record. BACS, the United Kingdom system for Direct Debits and Direct Credits, runs on files. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch91s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain link: the UK ATM network. A cash machine in the United Kingdom will usually accept the card of any UK bank, even though the machine belongs to a different bank or to an independent operator. For a business analyst, LINK teaches the economics of shared infrastructure.

ch92s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fedwire in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. Fedwire is the backbone of US large-value payments, and daylight overdraft is its liquidity model.

ch92s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain epn: the electronic payments network. The United States Automated Clearing House, the ACH network, has two operators. For a business analyst, EPN and the ACH network teach the batch pattern and the operator model.

ch92s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CHIPS in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. CHIPS is the private-sector counterpart to Fedwire, and the analyst must know when each is used.

ch92s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ACH in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. ACH is the workhorse of US payments, and the SEC code is the first thing an analyst checks.

ch92s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain same Day ACH and apply it to a real banking scenario. Same Day ACH changed US business payments, and the windows are the operational fact that matters.

ch92s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FedNow in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. FedNow is the newest US rail, and the analyst must know when it fits and when it does not.

ch92s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTP from The Clearing House and apply it to a real banking scenario. Two instant systems means routing decisions, and the analyst writes the routing logic.

ch92s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the US faster payments landscape and apply it to a real banking scenario. Routing across US rails is the treasurer daily decision, and the analyst must map it.

ch92s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain FEDWIRE and CHIPS message detail: the fields that carry a US payment. United States high value payments run on two systems, Fedwire and CHIPS, and each carries field level detail that decides routing, validation, and tracking.
