For a business analyst, field level mapping between Fedwire, CHIPS, and ISO 20022 is core work.

ch92s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain zelle: bank-owned instant person-to-person payments. Zelle is the United States bank owned person to person payment network. For a business analyst, Zelle teaches the alias pattern, the instant and irrevocable trade off, and the scam problem.

ch93s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SCT in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SCT is the default SEPA credit transfer, and its timeline is the baseline every analyst knows.

ch93s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SCT Inst in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SCT Inst is now a mainstream rail, and the 10-second rule is a hard obligation.

ch93s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SDD in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. SDD is the recurring payment scheme of Europe, and the refund rules are its core.

ch93s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain TIPS in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. TIPS is the settlement engine for European instant payments, and its liquidity model is the key fact.

ch93s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain verification of Payee and apply it to a real banking scenario. Verification of Payee is the fraud control that the regulation made mandatory, and the analyst must know its outcomes.

ch93s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain the European Payments Council rulebooks and apply it to a real banking scenario. The EPC change cycle is the calendar that drives SEPA implementation work.

ch93s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA scheme participation, reachability, the EPC register and what happens when a bank is not reachable and apply it to a real banking scenario. Reachability is the directory of SEPA, and the analyst uses it to check whether a payment can arrive.

ch93s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SEPA one leg out: when one leg leaves SEPA. The SEPA schemes assume both legs of a payment are inside the Single Euro Payments Area: the payer bank and the payee bank are both SEPA participants, and the payment travels under SEPA rules from end to end. For a business analyst, a One Leg Out corridor is a mapping exercise with a boundary.

ch94s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain correspondent banking in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. Correspondent banking is the plumbing of cross-border payments, and its decline is reshaping the market.

ch94s10.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sadc-rtgs and comesa: regional settlement in southern and eastern africa. Most cross border payments in Africa settle in dollars or euros, through correspondent banks outside the continent, even when the trade is between two African countries. For a business analyst, regional settlement systems are a study in integration patterns.

ch94s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain SWIFT gpi in depth and apply it to a real banking scenario. gpi changed customer expectations, and the tracker is now a standard service.

ch94s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain CBPR+ and the MT to MX migration and apply it to a real banking scenario. CBPR+ is the biggest messaging change in decades, and the analyst must know the translation rules.

ch94s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain serial versus cover payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. Serial versus cover is the core routing decision in cross-border payments, and the analyst must know both.

ch94s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain foreign exchange in cross-border payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. FX is where cross-border payments make or lose money, and the analyst must price it correctly.

ch94s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain nostro account optimisation and apply it to a real banking scenario. Nostro optimisation is a direct profit lever, and the analyst quantifies the saving.

ch94s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain cross-border instant payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. Cross-border instant is the future of the market, and the links are the new infrastructure.

ch94s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions and compliance in cross-border payments and apply it to a real banking scenario. De-risking is the unintended consequence of tougher compliance, and the analyst must measure it.

ch94s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain eurogiro and tipanet: postal and cooperative bank networks. The payment landscape is not only SWIFT and correspondent banking. For a business analyst, niche networks are a reminder that the payment landscape has many layers.

ch95s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain AML screening in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Name screening is the first line of defence, and its false positive rate decides whether the operations team can cope.

ch95s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain sanctions screening in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. The 50 percent rule is the most commonly failed sanctions test, and it needs ownership data the bank must collect.

ch95s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain when a sanctions hit fires and apply it to a real banking scenario. The sanctions hit workflow is the most time-critical operational process in payments, and it must be rehearsed.

ch95s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud detection in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Fraud detection is a behaviour problem, and the analyst writes the rules that describe normal behaviour.

ch95s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fraud case handling step by step and apply it to a real banking scenario. Fraud case handling is a race against time, and the workflow must be drilled, not improvised.

ch95s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain APP scams and mule accounts and apply it to a real banking scenario. Mule networks are the infrastructure of fraud, and dismantling them stops many scams at once.

ch95s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain transaction monitoring in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Monitoring tuning is a continuous discipline, and the analyst owns the evidence for every change.

ch95s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain controls operations in detail and apply it to a real banking scenario. Controls are only real if they are tested, and the test result is the evidence the auditor asks for.

ch95s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain fatca, gatca and the common reporting standard. FATCA, GATCA and the Common Reporting Standard are three names that describe two regimes and one nickname, and keeping them apart is the starting point for the whole topic. A US person includes a US citizen wherever they live, a US tax resident, and certain US entities, and the bank must also look through foreign entities to substantial US owners.

ch96s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai, machine learning and generative ai actually are. Let us start by clearing up three words that get thrown around as if they mean the same thing, because they do not. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch96s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain machine learning works, at the level a BA needs. Machine learning sounds technical, but the idea is simple, and you already understand it from your own work. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch96s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain generative ai and large language models. Generative AI is the technology behind the chat tools you have probably already tried. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch96s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai agents: what they do and how they differ from a chatbot. A chatbot answers questions. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch96s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai can do well in payments. AI earns its place in payments when the work is high volume, repetitive, and pattern-based, and when a wrong answer is cheap to catch. A payments operations team handles 40,000 customer queries a month.

ch96s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain ai cannot do. AI has hard limits, and a BA who does not know them will sign off on a design that fails in production. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch96s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain vocabulary of ai: a ba's glossary. You cannot challenge a vendor or write a requirement if you do not share the words, so here is the vocabulary you will actually hear in payments AI projects, each in one plain sentence. The guardrail says any score above 80 goes to a human in the loop, so an analyst reviews it instead of the system deciding alone.

ch96s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain hype versus reality. Every new technology arrives with hype, and AI has arrived with more hype than most, so a BA needs a way to separate a real capability from a sales pitch. The AI will replace your analysts.

ch96s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain multi-agent systems and crewai. A single AI agent can do a great deal, but some tasks are better done by several agents working together, each with a role, collaborating toward a result no single agent achieves as well. Agents have roles, goals, and backstories: a senior payments analyst, a compliance reviewer, a technical writer.

ch97s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to draft a BRD. A business requirements document is the hardest artefact to start, and that is exactly where AI helps most, as long as you treat its output as a first draft and never as a finished document. Walk the flow end to end, ask the operations team what breaks, and add the rules and exceptions the draft missed.

ch97s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to write user stories and acceptance criteria. User stories are a good job for AI, because the format is simple and the tool has seen thousands of examples, but the acceptance criteria are where the value lives, and that is where you must check hardest. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch97s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai for process maps and flow diagrams. AI can draft a process map quickly, but a process map is only useful if every leg and every branch is present, and AI is very good at producing a map that looks complete while quietly dropping a branch. So use AI to draw the first version, then walk it with the operations team, step by step, and add every missing leg and branch before anyone builds from it.

ch97s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain using ai to generate test cases and UAT scenarios. Test cases are one of the best uses of AI in BA work, because the tool is good at volume and at combinations a person would take hours to list, but only if you tell it what coverage means for your flow. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch97s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain reviewing and validating ai output: the quality gate. Every AI output that goes into a project needs a quality gate, and the gate is a person, not another AI tool. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch97s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain failure modes: hallucinated fields and missing legs. This is a real case from the industry, and it is the most important lesson in this chapter. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch97s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain prompt patterns that work for payments BA work. A good prompt is not a clever trick. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch97s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain to never let ai decide alone. There is a clear line in payments BA work, and it is this. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch98s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain owning an ai product in payments. Owning an AI product is not the same as owning a regular feature, and the difference matters from the first day. If the model changes after retraining, or the data feeding it changes, the same payment might be treated differently next week, and your customer will notice.

ch98s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain defining the problem and the ai use case. Every AI feature should start from a business problem, not from the technology. Take a payments operations team that spends three hours every morning sorting payment exceptions.

ch98s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain data requirements for an ai feature. An AI feature is only as good as the data behind it, so the product owner has to treat data as a requirement, not as something the engineers will sort out later. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch98s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain model requirements and evaluation. Before you accept an AI model, you have to agree what good looks like, in numbers, and how you will test it. If it wrongly flags a genuine payment of 850 pounds, the customer is annoyed and the operations team does extra work, but no money is lost.

ch98s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain acceptance criteria for ai features. Acceptance criteria for an AI feature have to be testable, and they have to cover failure as well as success. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch98s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain guardrails and human-in-the-loop design. Guardrails are the rules that decide where the model may act alone, where a human must approve, and how the handoff between the two works. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch98s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain managing the ai product backlog. Managing an AI product backlog is different from managing a normal backlog, because the work splits into four kinds that compete for the same team, and if you treat them as one list, the visible work always wins. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch98s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain measuring an ai feature: the metrics that matter. You cannot own an AI feature without measuring it, and you cannot measure it with one number. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain control framework for ai that touches money. When AI touches money, it needs the same control discipline as any system that moves money, and that discipline rests on four separations that must stay apart. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain approval limits and authorisation. Approval limits and authorisation are the two controls that stop a single mistake, or a single bad decision, from becoming a large loss. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain control ownership: naming the owner. Every AI control needs a named human owner. If no one owns that control, the operations team works around it, the holds pile up, and customers start calling.

ch99s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain audit trails and explainability. An audit trail is the record that lets you explain, after the fact, why an AI system did what it did with money. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain regulatory expectations for ai in payments. Regulators expect the same control discipline for AI as for any system that moves money. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 12,000 invoice case: authorisation. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows what happens when the control that makes a payment safe is given to the very thing it is meant to control. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 8,000 API calls case: spend caps. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows how a thousand tiny payments can add up to a large loss when no one sets a limit. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch99s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain EUR 60,000 pilot case: control ownership. This is a real case from the industry, and it shows why an award is not a control. This matters because it is a building block for the payments work in the rest of this course.

ch9s1.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain indian payments landscape at a glance. India runs one of the most layered domestic payment systems in the world, and a business analyst who works on Indian payments needs to understand how the layers fit together rather than treating each rail as a separate. India runs one of the most layered domestic payment systems in the world, and a business analyst who works on Indian payments needs to understand how the layers fit together rather than treating each rail as a separate product.

ch9s2.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain UPI architecture: vpa, psp banks and NPCI. UPI turns a bank account into a simple address. An analyst who confuses the PSP bank with the remitter bank will misassign responsibility when a payment fails.

ch9s3.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain IMPS: instant transfers around the clock. IMPS was India's first truly instant account to account transfer system. Because the service never sleeps, banks must keep their IMPS interfaces available at all hours, and operations teams must handle failures at 3 in the morning just as well as at 3 in the afternoon.

ch9s4.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NEFT: batch settlement and why it still matters. NEFT is the Reserve Bank of India batch based system for transferring money between bank accounts across India. The analyst must never let the screen promise instant credit for an NEFT payment.

ch9s5.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain RTGS: high value settlement with finality. RTGS is the Reserve Bank of India system for high value transfers where each payment is settled individually and immediately in the books of the central bank. To settle a payment, the sending bank must have enough funds in its settlement account at the exact moment of settlement.

ch9s6.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain NACH: bulk debits, credits and recurring payments. NACH is the NPCI system for bulk and recurring payments, and it is the quiet workhorse behind salaries, EMIs, insurance premiums, utility bills, and mutual fund SIPs. Returns arrive in files that the presenting bank must reconcile record by record.

ch9s7.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain rails differ: limits, timing and cost. The fastest way to compare the Indian rails is to put them side by side on four questions. Timing is where analysts most often make mistakes, because the words instant and same day mean different things on different rails.

ch9s8.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain choosing the right rail: a worked example. Consider a mid sized company in Bengaluru that needs to make four payments on the same morning, ten thousand rupees to a vendor who supplied office stationery, one lakh fifty thousand rupees to a consultant, twenty five. A good analyst would not send all four through the same rail.

ch9s9.agenda: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to explain runs indian payments: the RBI, NPCI and the ifsc. Indian payments rest on three distinct parts that a beginner must keep separate, namely the regulator, the operator, and the addressing code. The analyst must state, for each requirement, whether the rule comes from the regulator or the rail is operated by the Reserve Bank, because the RBI acts as both rule setter and operator.
